Esau said to Jacob, "Let me eat some of this red stew, for I am exhausted." Therefore he was called Edom.
Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright today."
Esau said, "Look, I am about to die; what good is the birthright to me?"
Jacob said, "Swear to me today." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank, rose up, and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that had occurred in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.
The LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land that I will tell you."
"Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.
I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.
Because Abraham obeyed My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws."

When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," lest the men of the place kill him because of Rebekah, since she was beautiful to look upon.
When he had been there a long time, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out through a window and saw Isaac caressing Rebekah his wife.
So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then did you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I said, 'Lest I die because of her.'"
Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."
So Abimelech charged all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."
And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him.
The man became rich, and grew richer and richer until he became very wealthy.
He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so the Philistines envied him.
Now all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped up and filled with earth.
And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."
So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.

And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.
Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water.
The herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him.
Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah.
And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
From there he went up to Beersheba.
And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for My servant Abraham's sake."
So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.
Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?"
They said, "We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, 'Let there be a sworn oath between us, between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD.'"
So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
In the morning they rose early and swore an oath to one another. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace.
That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water."
He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite,
and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, "My son." "Here I am," Esau replied.
"Look," Isaac said, "I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death.
Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and bow, and go out into the field to hunt some game for me.
Prepare me the kind of tasty food I love, and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die."
Now Rebekah was listening while Isaac spoke to his son Esau. So when Esau left for the field to hunt game and bring it back,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "Look, I overheard your father speaking to your brother Esau, saying,
'Bring me some game and prepare me a tasty dish, that I may eat and bless you before the LORD before I die.'
Now, my son, listen carefully to my instructions.
Go to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can prepare them as a tasty dish for your father, just as he loves.
Then take it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, "Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, while I am smooth-skinned.
What if my father touches me? Then I would be revealed to him as a deceiver, and I would bring a curse upon myself rather than a blessing."
His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son. Just obey my voice and go get them for me."
So he went and got them and brought them to his mother, and she made the tasty food, just as his father loved.
Then Rebekah took the best clothes of her older son Esau, which she had in the house, and put them on her younger son Jacob.
She put the goatskins on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
Then she handed her son Jacob the tasty food and the bread she had made.
He went to his father and said, "My father." "Yes, my son," Isaac answered. "Who are you?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me."
Isaac asked his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" "Because the LORD your God granted me success," he answered.
Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near so I can touch you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not."
So Jacob came near to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
Isaac did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau; so he blessed him.
"Are you really my son Esau?" Isaac asked. "I am," Jacob replied.
"Serve me," Isaac said, "and let me eat some of my son's game, so that I may bless you." So Jacob brought it to him, and he ate; he also brought him wine, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, "Please come near and kiss me, my son."
So he came near and kissed him. When Isaac smelled the fragrance of his clothes, he blessed him and said: "Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
May God give you the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth—an abundance of grain and new wine.

May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. Be master over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. May those who curse you be cursed, and may those who bless you be blessed."
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had barely left his father's presence, his brother Esau returned from the hunt.
He too made a tasty dish and brought it to his father. "My father," he said, "sit up and eat of your son's game, so that you may bless me."
"Who are you?" his father Isaac asked. "I am your firstborn son, Esau," he answered.
Isaac trembled violently and said, "Who was it, then, who hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him—and indeed, he will be blessed!"
When Esau heard his father's words, he cried out with a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me too, my father!"
But Isaac said, "Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing."
Esau said, "Isn't he rightly named Jacob? He has deceived me twice: He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing!" Then he asked, "Haven't you reserved a blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "Behold, I have made him your master, and I have given him all his brothers as servants. I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What, then, can I do for you, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, my father!" And Esau wept aloud.
His father Isaac answered him: "Behold, your dwelling will be away from the richness of the earth and away from the dew of heaven above.
You will live by your sword and serve your brother, but when you grow restless, you will break his yoke from your neck."
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him, and Esau said in his heart, "The days of mourning for my father are near; then I will kill my brother Jacob."
When Rebekah was told what her older son Esau had said, she sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, "Look, your brother Esau is consoling himself by planning to kill you.
Now, my son, obey my voice: Flee to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him a few days, until your brother's fury subsides.
When your brother's anger has turned away from you and he forgets what you did to him, I will send for you and bring you back. Why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day?"
Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am weary of my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob takes a wife from the Hittite women, like those who are here in the land, what good is my life?"
Isaac summoned Jacob, conferred his blessing upon him, and charged him, “You shall not espouse a wife from among the daughters of Canaan.
Arise and journey to Paddan-aram, to the household of your maternal grandfather Bethuel, and take for yourself a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.”
“May God Almighty bless you, make you fruitful, and multiply you, until you become a multitude of peoples.
May He bestow upon you the blessing of Abraham—upon you and your descendants with you—so that you may inherit the land of your sojournings, which God granted to Abraham.”
Thus Isaac dispatched Jacob, and he traveled to Paddan-aram, to Laban, son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.

Esau observed that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to procure a wife there, and that in blessing him he had charged him, “You shall not espouse a wife from among the daughters of Canaan.”
Jacob obeyed his father and mother and departed for Paddan-aram.
Esau also recognized that the daughters of Canaan were odious in the sight of Isaac his father.
Consequently, he went to Ishmael and took as an additional wife Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, and the sister of Nebaioth.
Jacob departed from Beersheba and journeyed toward Haran.
Upon reaching a certain place, he lodged there because the sun had set; taking one of the stones of that place, he placed it beneath his head and reclined there.
He dreamed, and behold, a ladder was erected upon the earth, its summit touching heaven, while the angels of God ascended and descended upon it.
And behold, the LORD stood above it and declared, “I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land upon which you lie I will give to you and to your descendants.

Your descendants shall become as the dust of the earth, and you shall break forth to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south; in you and in your descendants all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Behold, I am with you, and I will guard you in every way you go; I will restore you to this land, for I will not forsake you until I have fulfilled what I have spoken to you.”
Jacob awakened from his sleep and exclaimed, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.”
Stricken with awe, he said, “How formidable this place is! It is nothing less than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”
Early the next morning Jacob took the stone he had set beneath his head, erected it as a pillar, and poured oil upon its summit.
He named that place Bethel, although the city had formerly been called Luz.
Jacob then vowed, “If God will be with me and protect me along this path I am traveling, and if He will provide me bread to eat and garments to wear,
so that I may return in peace to my father’s house, then the LORD shall be my God.
This stone, which I have erected as a pillar, shall be God’s house, and of everything You give me I will surely tithe to You.”
Jacob set out and traveled to the land of the Eastern peoples.
He looked and saw a well in a field, where three flocks of sheep lay resting, because the flocks were watered from that well. The stone covering the mouth of the well was large.
When all the flocks gathered there, the shepherds rolled the stone from the mouth of the well, watered the sheep, and then returned the stone to its place.
Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where are you from?" "We are from Haran," they replied.
"Do you know Laban son of Nahor?" he asked. "We know him," they said.
"Is he well?" Jacob asked. "He is well," they replied, "and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
Jacob said, "It is still broad daylight, and it is not yet time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and take them out to pasture."
"We cannot," they said, "until all the flocks have gathered and the stone has been rolled away from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother's brother, together with Laban's sheep, he went up to the well, rolled the stone from its mouth, and watered the flock of Laban, his mother's brother.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
He told her that he was Rebekah's son and a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father.
When Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. Jacob recounted all these things to him.
Laban said to him, "Surely you are my own flesh and blood." Jacob stayed with him for a month.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my relative, should you serve me for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be."
Now Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah, and the younger Rachel.
Leah had soft, delicate eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
Jacob loved Rachel and said, "I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter."
Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than to another man. Stay with me."
Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him only a few days because of his love for her.
Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are complete, so that I may take her as my wife."
Laban gathered all the men of the place and gave a feast.
In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob consummated the marriage with her.
Laban also gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
In the morning, Jacob discovered that it was Leah, and he said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?"
Laban said, "It is not the custom in our country to give the younger daughter before the firstborn.
Complete this bridal week, and we will give you the other as well, provided you serve me another seven years."
Jacob did so and completed her week; then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban also gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob also consummated his marriage with Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He served Laban another seven years.
The LORD saw that Leah was unloved, and He enabled her to conceive, while Rachel remained barren.
Leah conceived and bore a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "Because the LORD has seen my affliction; surely now my husband will love me."
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son also." So she named him Simeon.
Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." Therefore she named him Levi.
Once more she conceived and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing children.
Rachel saw that she had borne no children to Jacob, and she envied her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die."
Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?"
She said, "Here is my servant Bilhah; go in to her, so that she may bear upon my knees, and I too may have children through her."
So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, "God has vindicated me; He has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she named him Dan.
Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, "With great struggles I have wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed." So she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah said, "What good fortune!" and she named him Gad.
Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "I am happy, because women will call me happy." So she named him Asher.
During the wheat harvest Reuben went out and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."
Leah said, "Is it not enough that you have taken my husband? Would you take my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel said, "Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must come in to me, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he lay with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my reward, because I gave my servant to my husband." So she named him Issachar.
Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son to Jacob.
Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good endowment; now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons." So she named him Zebulun.
Afterward she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son and said, "God has taken away my reproach."
She named him Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son."
As soon as Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, that I may go to my own place and to my country.
Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, that I may go, for you know the service that I have given you."
Laban said to him, "If I have found favor in your sight, please stay, for I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
He said, "Name your wages, and I will give them."
Jacob said, "You yourself know how I have served you, and how your livestock has fared with me.
For you had little before I came, and it has increased abundantly, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I have gone. But now when shall I provide for my own house?"
Laban said, "What shall I give you?" Jacob said, "You shall not give me anything. If you will do this for me, I will again pasture your flock and keep it."

"Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep and every black lamb among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats, and such shall be my wages."

"So my integrity will answer for me later, when you come to inspect my wages: every one among the goats that is not speckled or spotted, and every one among the sheep that is not black, if found with me, shall be counted stolen."
Laban said, "Good; let it be according to your word."

That day Laban removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted, every one that had white on it, and all the black among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.
He set a three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob pastured the rest of Laban's flock.
Then Jacob took fresh rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree, and peeled white streaks in them, exposing the white of the rods.
He set the rods that he had peeled in front of the flocks in the troughs, the watering places, where the flocks came to drink; and they bred when they came to drink.
The flocks bred in front of the rods and brought forth streaked, speckled, and spotted.
Jacob separated the lambs and set the flock to face the streaked and all the black in Laban's flock. He put his own droves apart and did not put them with Laban's flock.
Whenever the stronger animals were breeding, Jacob would put the rods in the troughs before the eyes of the flock, so that they might breed among the rods.
But for the weaker animals he would not put them in, so the weaker became Laban's and the stronger became Jacob's.
Thus the man increased exceedingly and had large flocks, female servants and male servants, camels and donkeys.
Jacob heard that Laban's sons were saying, "Jacob has taken everything our father owned and has gained all this wealth from what belonged to our father."
And Jacob noticed that Laban's attitude toward him was not what it had been.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Go back to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent word to Rachel and Leah to come out to the fields where his flocks were.
He said to them, "I see that your father's attitude toward me is not what it was before, but the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have worked for your father with all my strength,
yet your father has cheated me by changing my wages ten times. However, God has not allowed him to harm me.
If he said, 'The spotted ones will be your wages,' then all the flocks gave birth to spotted young; and if he said, 'The streaked ones will be your wages,' then all the flocks bore streaked young.
So God has taken away your father's livestock and has given them to me.
"In breeding season, I once had a dream in which I looked up and saw that the male goats mating with the flock were streaked, speckled, or spotted.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' And I replied, 'Here I am.'
And he said, 'Look up and see that all the male goats mating with the flock are streaked, speckled, or spotted, for I have seen all that Laban has been doing to you.'
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and where you made a vow to me. Now leave this land at once and go back to your native land.'"
Then Rachel and Leah replied, "Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father's estate?
Does he not regard us as foreigners? Not only has he sold us, but he has used up what was paid for us.
Surely all the wealth that God took away from our father belongs to us and our children. So do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob put his children and his wives on camels,
and he drove all his livestock ahead of him, along with all the goods he had accumulated in Paddan Aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
When Laban had gone to shear his sheep, Rachel stole her father's household gods.
Moreover, Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him he was running away.
So he fled with all he had, crossed the Euphrates River, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
Taking his relatives with him, he pursued Jacob for seven days and caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
Then God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream at night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."
Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country of Gilead when Laban overtook him, and Laban and his relatives camped there too.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have deceived me, and you have carried off my daughters like captives in war.
Why did you run off secretly and deceive me? Why didn't you tell me, so I could send you away with joy and singing to the music of timbrels and harps?
You didn't even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye. You have done a foolish thing.
I have the power to harm you; but the God of your father said to me last night, 'Do not say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.'
Now you have gone off because you longed for your father's household. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid, because I thought you would take your daughters away from me by force.

But if you find anyone who has your gods, that person shall not live. In the presence of our relatives, identify whatever is yours and take it." Now Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the gods.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two female servants, but he found nothing. After he came out of Leah's tent, he entered Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the household gods and put them inside her camel's saddle and was sitting on them. Laban searched through everything in the tent but found nothing.
Rachel said to her father, "Don't be angry, my lord. I cannot stand up in your presence; I am having my period." So he searched but could not find the household gods.
Jacob was angry and took Laban to task. "What is my crime?" he asked. "What sin have I committed that you hunt me down?
Now that you have searched through all my belongings, what have you found that belongs to your household? Put it here in front of our relatives and yours, and let them decide between the two of us.
I have been with you for twenty years now. Your sheep and goats have not miscarried, nor have I eaten rams from your flocks.
"I did not bring you animals torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself. You demanded payment from me for whatever was stolen by day or night.
This was my situation: The heat consumed me in the daytime and the cold at night, and sleep fled from my eyes.
It was like this for the twenty years I was in your household. I worked for you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flocks, and you changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, you would surely have sent me away empty-handed. But God has seen my hardship and the toil of my hands, and last night He rebuked you."

Laban answered Jacob, "The women are my daughters, the children are my children, and the flocks are my flocks. All you see is mine. Yet what can I do today about my daughters or about the children they have borne?
Come now, let's make a covenant, you and I, and let it serve as a witness between us."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
He said to his relatives, "Gather some stones." So they took stones and piled them in a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
Laban called it Jegar Sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between us today." That is why it was named Galeed.
He said, "May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are away from each other.
If you mistreat my daughters or if you take any other women besides my daughters, even though no one is with us to see, remember that God is a witness between you and me."
Laban also said, "Here is this heap, and here is this pillar, which I have set up between you and me.
This heap is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not go past this heap to your side to harm you and that you will not go past this heap and this pillar to my side to harm me."
"May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob took an oath in the name of the Fear of his father Isaac.
He offered a sacrifice there in the hill country and invited his relatives to a meal. They ate and spent the night there.
Early the next morning Laban kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then he left and returned home.
Jacob went on his way, and God's angels met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's camp," and he named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, in the territory of Edom.
He commanded them, "Tell my lord Esau that your servant Jacob has been staying with Laban and has only now set out.
I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants, and I am sending this word to my lord so that I may find favor in your eyes."
The messengers returned to Jacob and said, "We reached your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you with four hundred men."
Jacob was deeply afraid and distressed, so he divided the people with him, along with the flocks, herds, and camels, into two camps.
He thought, "If Esau comes to one camp and attacks it, the other camp may escape."
Jacob prayed, "God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, the LORD, who told me, 'Return to your land and your kindred, and I will deal well with you,'
I am unworthy of all the steadfast love and faithfulness You have shown Your servant; with only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.
Please rescue me from my brother's hand, from Esau's hand, for I fear he will attack me and slaughter mothers and children alike.
Yet You said, 'I will surely do you good and make your offspring as numerous as the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted.'"
He spent that night there, and from what he had with him he took a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He put them into the hands of his servants, each herd by itself, and told them, "Go on ahead of me and leave space between one herd and the next."
He instructed the first servant, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks who you are, where you are going, and whose animals are ahead of you,
say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. This is a gift sent to my lord Esau, and he himself is coming behind us.'"
He gave the same instructions to the second and third servants and to all who followed the herds, telling them to speak to Esau in the same way when they met him.
They were to say that your servant Jacob was coming behind them, for Jacob reasoned, "I will appease him with the gift that goes before me, and afterward I will face him; perhaps he will accept me."
So the gift passed on ahead of him, while he spent that night in the camp.
That night Jacob arose, took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, along with everything he owned.
Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he touched the socket of Jacob's hip, and the hip socket was dislocated as they wrestled.
Then the man said, "Let me go, for dawn is breaking." But Jacob replied, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
The man asked him, "What is your name?" "Jacob," he answered.
Then he said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men and have prevailed."
Jacob asked, "Please tell me your name." But the man said, "Why do you ask my name?" And he blessed Jacob there.
Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was preserved."
The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip.
Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because the man touched the socket of Jacob's thigh at the tendon.
Upon lifting his eyes, Jacob beheld Esau approaching with four hundred men; consequently, he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants.
He stationed the maidservants and their children foremost, Leah and her children next, and Rachel with Joseph in the rear.
He himself passed on before them, prostrating himself to the ground seven times until he reached his brother.
Yet Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell upon his neck, kissed him, and they wept together.
When Esau raised his eyes and perceived the women and children, he inquired, "Who are these with you?" Jacob replied, "They are the children whom God has graciously bestowed upon your servant."
Then the maidservants approached with their children and bowed low.
Leah and her children likewise drew near and prostrated themselves, and afterward Joseph and Rachel approached and did the same.
Esau inquired, "What do you intend by all this company I encountered?" Jacob answered, "To find favor in the sight of my lord."
Esau said, "I have abundance, my brother; keep what you have."
Jacob said, "No, please—if I have found favor in your sight, accept this gift from my hand. I have seen your face, and it is as though I had seen the face of God, and you have received me graciously.
Please accept my blessing, which has been brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and I have all I need." So he urged him, and Esau accepted it.
Then Esau said, "Let us journey on together, and I will go ahead of you."
Jacob replied, "My lord knows that the children are frail and that the flocks and herds are nursing; if they are driven hard for even one day, the whole flock will perish.
Let my lord pass on ahead of his servant, and I will proceed at a leisurely pace, according to the pace of the livestock ahead of me and the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir."
So Esau said, "Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me." But Jacob said, "Why should I find favor in the sight of my lord?"
So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
But Jacob journeyed to Succoth and built a house for himself, and he made shelters for his livestock; therefore the place was named Succoth.
Jacob arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, on his way from Paddan-aram, and he camped before the city.
From the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, he purchased for a hundred pieces of money the parcel of land where he had pitched his tent.
There he erected an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the young women of the land.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of that region, saw her, seized her, lay with her, and violated her.
Yet his soul clung to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter; he loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her.
Then Shechem said to his father Hamor, “Get me this young woman for a wife.”
Now Jacob had heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but because his sons were with the livestock in the field, Jacob remained silent until they returned.
Meanwhile, Hamor, Shechem’s father, went out to speak with Jacob.

When Jacob’s sons returned from the field and heard what had happened, they were grieved and deeply angered, for Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter—a thing that should never be done.
Hamor spoke with them and said, “My son Shechem’s heart is set on your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife.
Intermarry with us: give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You may settle among us, and the land will be open before you; live in it, trade in it, and acquire holdings in it.”
Shechem also said to her father and brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and I will give whatever you ask.
Set the bride-price and gift as high as you wish; I will pay whatever you say. Only give me the young woman as my wife.”
Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, speaking as they did because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said to them, “We cannot do this thing—give our sister to a man who is uncircumcised—for that would be a disgrace to us.”
“Only on this condition will we consent to you: if every male among you is circumcised, as we are.
Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves, and we will live among you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our daughter and leave.”
Their proposal pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man did not delay in carrying out the agreement, for he delighted in Jacob’s daughter, and he was the most honored member of his father’s household.
Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of the city:
“These men are at peace with us. Let them settle in the land and trade in it, for the land is spacious enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives and give our daughters to them.”
“But only on this condition will these men consent to live with us and become one people: every male among us must be circumcised, as they are.
Will not their livestock, their property, and all their animals become ours? Let us only agree, and they will settle among us.”
All who went out through the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised—all who went out through the city gate.
On the third day, when the men were still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons—Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers—took their swords, came upon the city unawares, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem’s house, and departed.
Jacob’s sons came upon the slain and plundered the city because Shechem had defiled their sister.
They took their sheep, oxen, and donkeys—everything in the city and in the fields.
They carried off all their wealth, their little ones, and their wives, plundering everything in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble on me by bringing me into disrepute among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number; they will gather themselves together against me and attack me, and I shall be destroyed, I and my household.”
They said, “Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?”
God said to Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there, and erect an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, “Remove the foreign gods that are among you, sanctify yourselves, and change your garments.
Let us arise and go up to Bethel, and I will build an altar there to the God who answered me in the day of my distress and has accompanied me wherever I have traveled.”
So they surrendered to Jacob all the foreign gods in their possession and the rings in their ears, and Jacob concealed them beneath the oak near Shechem.
As they journeyed, the terror of God fell upon the surrounding cities, so that none pursued Jacob’s sons.
Jacob and all the people with him arrived at Luz—that is, Bethel—in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar and named the place El Bethel, because God had revealed Himself to him there when he fled from his brother.
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried beneath the oak below Bethel, and he called it Allon-bacuth.
After Jacob returned from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
God said to him, “Your name is Jacob, but you will no longer be called Jacob; your name will be Israel.” So He called him Israel.
God also said, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and an assembly of nations will come from you, and kings will descend from your line.
The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give it to your descendants after you.”
Then God ascended from him in the place where He had spoken with him.
Jacob erected a stone pillar in the place where God had spoken with him; he poured out a drink offering upon it and anointed it with oil.
Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They departed from Bethel, and while they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and her labor was arduous.
During her difficult labor, the midwife said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you have this son as well.”
As her soul was departing—for she was dying—she named him Ben-oni, but his father named him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem.
Jacob erected a pillar over her tomb; it remains the pillar of Rachel’s tomb to this day.
Israel traveled onward and pitched his tent beyond Migdal-eder.
While Israel was residing in that land, Reuben went in and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel learned of it. Now Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah were Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These were the sons born to Jacob in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba—that is, Hebron—where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.
Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years.
He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his ancestors; he was old and full of years, and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
These are the descendants of Esau, who is Edom.
Esau married women from Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite.
He also married Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel.
Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These were the sons of Esau born to him in Canaan.

Esau took his wives, sons, daughters, all the members of his household, his livestock, all his animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan, and he moved to a land away from his brother Jacob.
Their combined possessions were too great for them to remain together, and the land where they were staying could not support them because of their livestock.
So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the descendants of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau by his wife Adah; and Reuel, son of Esau by his wife Basemath.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These were the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.
The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These were the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.
These were the sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah to Esau.
These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, were chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, and chief Kenaz.
Chief Korah, chief Gatam, and chief Amalek were also chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; they were the sons of Adah.
The sons of Reuel, son of Esau, were chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, and chief Mizzah. These were the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; they were the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.
The sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife, were chief Jeush, chief Jalam, and chief Korah. These were the chiefs descended from Esau through Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
These were the sons of Esau—that is, Edom—and these were their chiefs.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah.
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan followed. These were the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Timna was Lotan's sister.
These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. He is the Anah who discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
These are the sons of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, and chief Anah.
Chief Dishon, chief Ezer, and chief Dishan were also chiefs. These were the chiefs of the Horites, listed according to their chiefs, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites:
Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
When Jobab died, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad reigned in his place; he defeated Midian in the field of Moab. The name of his city was Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
When Samlah died, Shaul of Rehoboth on the River reigned in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and regions, by their names: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth.
Chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon.
Chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar.
Chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their settlements in the land they possessed. He is Esau, the father of the Edomites.
Now Jacob lived in the land where his father had sojourned, in the land of Canaan.

These are the generations of Jacob: Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers; and, as a youth, he served with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives. And Joseph brought a damaging report about them to their father.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had been born to him in his old age; and he made him an ornate robe.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and were unable to speak peaceably to him.
Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him all the more.
He said to them, “Please hear this dream that I have dreamed:
Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright; and behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf.”
Then his brothers said to him, “Will you indeed reign over us? Or will you indeed rule us?” So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.
Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers, saying, “Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”

He told it to his father and to his brothers; and his father rebuked him and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?”
And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
Now his brothers went to pasture their father’s flock near Shechem.
And Israel said to Joseph, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them.” And he said, “Here I am.”
Then he said to him, “Go now, see whether it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word.” So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the field; and the man asked him, “What are you seeking?”
He said, “I am seeking my brothers. Please tell me where they are pasturing the flock.”
The man said, “They have moved on from here, for I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him.
They said to one another, “Here comes the dreamer.
Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say, ‘A wild beast has devoured him.’ And we will see what will become of his dreams.”
But when Reuben heard it, he delivered him from their hands, saying, “Let us not take his life.”
And Reuben said to them, “Do not shed blood; cast him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not harm him”—intending to rescue him from them and restore him to his father.
So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his robe, the ornate robe he was wearing.
And they took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.

Then they sat down to eat a meal. They lifted up their eyes and looked, and behold, a caravan of Ishmaelites was coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, going down to Egypt.
Then Judah said to his brothers, “What do we gain by killing our brother and concealing his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let us not lay hands on him, for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And his brothers agreed.
Then Midianite traders passed by; and they drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They brought Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes.
He returned to his brothers and said, “The boy is gone, and I—where am I to go?”
Then they took Joseph’s robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood.
They sent the ornate robe and brought it to their father, and said, “We found this. Please see whether this is your son’s robe or not.”
He recognized it and said, “It is my son’s robe. A wild beast has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces.”
Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and all his daughters rose to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted and said, “I shall go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” So his father wept for him.
Meanwhile the Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
At that time, Judah left his brothers and went down to stay with a certain Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua; he married her and went in to her.
She conceived and bore a son, whom he named Er.
She conceived again and bore another son, whom she named Onan.
She bore yet a third son and named him Shelah; he was born in Chezib.
Judah arranged a wife for his firstborn, Er; her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother's wife and fulfill your duty as a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew, however, that the offspring would not be his; so whenever he went in to his brother's wife, he spilled his semen on the ground, so that he would not produce offspring for his brother.
The thing he did was evil in the sight of the LORD, and He put him to death as well.

Then Judah told his daughter-in-law Tamar, “Remain a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he feared that Shelah too might die, as his brothers had. So Tamar went and lived in her father's house.
After a long time, Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up with his friend Hirah the Adullamite to Timnah, where his sheep were being sheared.
Tamar was told, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

So she removed her widow's garments, covered herself with a veil, wrapped herself, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, on the road to Timnah; for she saw that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.
When Judah saw her, he took her for a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
He turned aside to her by the road and said, “Come now, let me come in to you.” He did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She replied, “What will you give me, that you may come in to me?”
He said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge until you send it?”
He asked, “What pledge shall I give you?” She answered, “Your signet, your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” He gave them to her, came in to her, and she conceived by him.
Then she arose, went away, removed her veil, and put on her widow's garments again.
Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite, to recover the pledge from the woman, but he could not find her.
He asked the men of that place, “Where is the prostitute who was by the roadside at Enaim?” They replied, “There has been no prostitute here.”
He returned to Judah and said, “I could not find her, and the men of the place also said that no prostitute had been there.”
Judah said, “Let her keep them, lest we be held in contempt. I sent this young goat, and you did not find her.”

About three months later, Judah was told, “Tamar your daughter-in-law has engaged in prostitution, and moreover she is pregnant by her prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.”

As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law: “By the man to whom these belong I am pregnant.” She also said, “Please identify whose these are—the signet, the cord, and the staff.”
Judah recognized them and said, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” And he did not have sexual relations with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
As she was giving birth, one of them put out a hand; the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his hand, saying, “This one came out first.”
But as he drew back his hand, his brother came out; and she said, “How have you broken out!” So he was named Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he was named Zerah.
Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, where Potiphar—an Egyptian official of Pharaoh and captain of the guard—purchased him from the Ishmaelites who had transported him there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a prosperous man, residing in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master perceived that the LORD was with him and that the LORD brought prosperity to everything he undertook.
Joseph won his master’s favor and served him; his master appointed him steward of the household and entrusted to him all his possessions.

From the moment he placed Joseph in charge of his household and all that he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake, and the LORD’s blessing rested upon everything he had, both indoors and in the fields.
Consequently, he relinquished oversight of all his property to Joseph and concerned himself with nothing except the food he consumed. Now Joseph was strikingly handsome and well proportioned.
After these events, his master’s wife looked at Joseph and said, “Have sexual relations with me.”
But he refused and said to his master’s wife, “Look, my master does not know what is in the house with me, and he has entrusted everything he owns to my care.
No one in this household is greater than I am, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I commit this great wickedness and sin against God?”
Although she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, nor would he lie beside her or be with her.
One day, however, he entered the house to perform his duties, and none of the household servants was present.
She caught him by his cloak and said, “Have sexual relations with me,” but he left his cloak in her hand and ran outside.
As soon as she saw that he had left his cloak in her hand and had fled outside,
she summoned the men of her household and said, “See, he has brought a Hebrew into our house to mock us. He came in to me to have sexual relations with me, but I cried out in a loud voice.
When he heard me raise my voice and cry out, he left his cloak beside me and ran outside.”
She kept his cloak beside her until his master came home.
Then she said to him, “The Hebrew servant whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me.
But when I raised my voice and cried out, he left his cloak beside me and ran outside.”
When his master heard the words his wife had spoken to him—“This is what your servant did to me”—his anger burned.
Joseph’s master took him and confined him in prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were held, and he remained there.
But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love, and He gave him favor in the sight of the prison keeper.
The prison keeper entrusted to Joseph all the prisoners in the prison, and whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.
The prison keeper paid no attention to anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with him, and the LORD made everything he did prosper.
After these events, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt transgressed against their master, Pharaoh.
Pharaoh grew furious with two of his officials—the chief cupbearer and the chief baker—
and delivered them into custody in the residence of the captain of the guard, the very prison where Joseph was bound.
The captain of the guard entrusted Joseph with their care, and he attended them; consequently, they remained incarcerated for an extended period.
Subsequently, both men—the cupbearer and the baker of Egypt's king, imprisoned in the dungeon—dreamed a dream during the same night, each dream possessing a distinctive interpretation.
When Joseph entered their presence in the morning, he perceived their despondency.
So he inquired of Pharaoh's officials confined with him in his master's house, "Why do your faces appear so downcast today?"
They answered, "We have dreamed a dream, but no one can interpret it." Joseph replied, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Pray recount the dreams to me."
Thereupon the chief cupbearer related his dream to Joseph: "In my dream, behold, a vine stood before me.
The vine bore three branches; as it budded, its blossoms emerged, and its clusters matured into grapes.
Pharaoh's cup rested in my hand; I gathered the grapes, extracted their juice into Pharaoh's cup, and presented the cup to Pharaoh."
Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation: the three branches signify three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will restore you to favor and reinstate you in your position; then you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand, as you did before when you were his cupbearer."
"But when things go well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, so that he may bring me out of this house.
For I was indeed abducted from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have committed no offense warranting my confinement in this pit."
When the chief baker perceived that the interpretation was propitious, he said to Joseph, "I too dreamed, and behold, three baskets of fine bread rested upon my head.
In the uppermost basket were all manner of baked delicacies for Pharaoh, the product of a baker's artistry, while birds devoured them from the basket atop my head."
Joseph answered, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets represent three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will condemn you and have you hanged on a tree, and the birds will eat your flesh from you."
On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he hosted a banquet for all his servants; in their presence he rendered judgment upon the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He reinstated the chief cupbearer in his office, and the cup was restored to Pharaoh's hand.
But the chief baker he hanged, precisely as Joseph had interpreted for them.
Nevertheless, the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him.
Two full years later, Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing beside the Nile.
He saw seven cows, beautiful and well fed, come up out of the river and graze among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows—ugly and gaunt—came up from the Nile and stood beside the first cows on the riverbank.
The ugly, gaunt cows devoured the seven beautiful, fat cows, whereupon Pharaoh awoke.
He fell asleep again and dreamed a second time: seven heads of grain, plump and good, grew on a single stalk.
After them, seven heads of grain, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouted up.
The thin heads swallowed the seven plump, full heads. Pharaoh awoke and realized it had been a dream.
In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he sent for all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dream, but none could interpret it for him.
Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "Today I remember my offenses.
When Pharaoh was angry with his servants, he imprisoned me and the chief baker in the house of the captain of the guard.
One night we both dreamed—each of us a dream with its own meaning.
A young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he interpreted each one according to its meaning.
It happened just as he said: I was restored to my position, and the baker was hanged."
Pharaoh then sent for Joseph, and they hurried him out of the prison. He shaved, changed his clothes, and went in to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have dreamed a dream, and no one can interpret it. I have heard that you can understand a dream and interpret it."
Joseph answered Pharaoh, "I cannot do that on my own; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile.
Seven cows, fat and beautiful, came up out of the river and grazed among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up—scrawny, very ugly, and lean. I have never seen such miserable cattle in all Egypt.
The lean, ugly cows devoured the first seven fat cows.
Yet after swallowing them, they looked just as thin and ugly as before. Then I awoke.
In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, full and good, growing on one stalk.
After them, seven heads of grain, withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind, sprouted up.
The thin heads swallowed the seven good heads. I told this to the magicians, but no one could explain it to me."
Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's dream is one dream. God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years; it is the same dream.
The seven lean, ugly cows that came up afterward are seven years, and the seven empty heads scorched by the east wind will be seven years of famine.
This is what I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do.
Seven years of great abundance are coming throughout all Egypt.
After them will come seven years of famine, and all the abundance will be forgotten in Egypt; the famine will ravage the land.
The abundance will not be remembered because the famine that follows will be so severe.
The dream was repeated to Pharaoh twice because God has established the matter, and He will bring it about soon."
Joseph continued, "Now let Pharaoh look for a discerning and wise man and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh appoint officials over the land and collect a fifth of Egypt's harvest during the seven years of abundance.
Let them gather all the food of those good years and store grain under Pharaoh's authority, keeping it in the cities.
That food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine in Egypt, so that the country will not be destroyed by famine."
The plan pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find anyone like this man, in whom is the Spirit of God?"
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is no one so discerning and wise as you.
You are to be over my house, and all my people will be governed by your word. Only the throne will I keep higher than you."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have placed you over all the land of Egypt."
Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand; he dressed him in fine linen and placed a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in his second chariot, and men cried out before him, "Bow the knee!" Thus he put him in charge of all Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, and without you no one in all Egypt will lift a hand or a foot."
Pharaoh named him Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On, as his wife. Joseph then went out over all the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. He left Pharaoh's presence and traveled throughout Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty, the land produced abundantly.
Joseph gathered all the food of those seven years in Egypt and stored it in the cities; in each city he stored the produce of the surrounding fields.
Joseph stored up grain in such abundance—like the sand of the sea—that he stopped keeping count, because it was beyond measure.
Before the years of famine came, Joseph had two sons by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On.
He named his firstborn Manasseh, saying, "God has made me forget all my hardship and my father's household."
He named the second Ephraim, saying, "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
The seven years of plenty in Egypt came to an end.
Then the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but throughout Egypt there was bread.
When all Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for food. Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you."
The famine was over all the face of the earth. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, as the famine grew severe in Egypt.
All the earth came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was severe everywhere.
When Jacob perceived that grain was available in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you merely gaze at one another?
I have heard that grain is to be had in Egypt. Descend there and procure grain for us, that we may survive and not perish."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to Egypt to purchase grain.
Yet Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, along with them, reasoning, "Lest some calamity befall him."
Thus the sons of Israel came to buy grain among the throngs who came, for the famine had gripped the land of Canaan.
Now Joseph was the governor of the land, the one who dispensed grain to all its inhabitants. When Joseph's brothers arrived, they prostrated themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

Joseph recognized his brothers the moment he saw them, yet he concealed his identity and addressed them harshly. "Where do you come from?" he demanded. "From the land of Canaan," they replied, "to purchase food."
Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him.
Joseph recalled the dreams he had dreamed concerning them, and he accused them: "You are spies! You have come to observe the vulnerability of the land."
"No, my lord," they protested. "Your servants have come merely to buy food.
We are all sons of a single father. We are honest men; your servants are not spies."
"On the contrary," he retorted, "you have come to spy out the land's vulnerability."
"Your servants," they explained, "are twelve brothers, sons of one man in Canaan. The youngest remains with our father today, and one is no longer living."
Joseph declared, "As I have stated, you are spies.
Here is how you will be tested: as surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not depart from this place until your youngest brother arrives.
Dispatch one of you to retrieve your brother, while the rest remain confined, so that your claims may be verified. Otherwise, as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are indeed spies."
He then confined them all for three days.
On the third day, Joseph addressed them: "Do this and live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain imprisoned while the rest carry grain to relieve the famine in your households.
Bring your youngest brother to me, so your words may be confirmed and you may live." They consented.
They said to one another, "Surely we are guilty concerning our brother. We witnessed his anguish when he pleaded with us, yet we refused to listen. That is why this calamity has befallen us."
Reuben replied, "Did I not warn you, 'Do not sin against the boy'? You refused to listen, and now his blood is demanded of us."
They were unaware that Joseph comprehended their words, since an interpreter mediated between them.
He turned aside from them and wept. Then he returned and spoke to them, and he seized Simeon and bound him in their presence.
Joseph commanded that their containers be filled with grain, that each man's money be returned in his sack, and that provisions be given them for the journey. So it was done.
They loaded their grain onto their donkeys and departed.
At the lodging place, one opened his sack to feed his donkey and discovered his money at the mouth of his sack.
He cried to his brothers, "My money has been returned—indeed, it is in my sack!" They were gripped by dread, and trembling, they turned to one another, asking, "What has God done to us?"
They returned to their father Jacob in Canaan and recounted all that had befallen them, saying,
"The man, the lord of the land, spoke harshly to us and treated us as spies.
We told him, 'We are honest men, not spies.'
We are twelve brothers, sons of one father. One is no more, and the youngest remains with our father in Canaan.
The man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I will know you are honest men: leave one brother with me, take grain for your households, and depart.'
'Bring your youngest brother to me, and then I will know you are not spies but honest men. I will release your brother to you, and you may trade freely in the land.'"
As they emptied their sacks, each man's bundle of money appeared in his sack. When they and their father saw the money, they were terrified.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You have bereaved me of my children! Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and now you would take Benjamin. Everything is against me."
Reuben said to his father, "You may put my two sons to death if I do not return him to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will bring him back to you."

He replied, "My son will not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he alone remains. If any harm befalls him on the journey you are taking, you will bring my gray head down to Sheol in grief."
Now the famine had grown severe throughout the land.
When they had eaten the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, “Go back and buy us a little more food.”
Judah said to him, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.’
If you send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you.
But if you do not send him, we will not go down, for the man said to us, ‘You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.’”
Israel said, “Why have you dealt so cruelly with me by telling the man that you had another brother?”

They answered, “The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family, asking, ‘Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?’ We answered him according to these words. How could we have known he would say, ‘Bring your brother down’?”
Judah said to his father Israel, “Send the boy with me, and let us arise and go, so that we may live and not die—both we and you and our little ones.
I will be surety for him; you may hold me accountable for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame before you for the rest of my life.
For if we had not delayed, we could have returned twice by now.”

Their father Israel said to them, “If it must be so, then do this: take some of the best products of the land in your bags and carry down a gift to the man—a little balm and a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios, and almonds.
Take double the money with you, and carry back the money that was returned in the mouths of your sacks; perhaps it was an error.
Take your brother as well, and go back to the man.
May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, so that he will release your other brother along with Benjamin. As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.”
So the men took the gift, and they took double money with them, along with Benjamin. They set out and went down to Egypt, and they stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, “Bring the men into the house, slaughter an animal, and prepare it, for these men are to dine with me at noon.”
The man did as Joseph had commanded and brought the men to Joseph’s house.

The men were afraid because they were brought into Joseph’s house, and they said, “We have been brought here because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time, so that he may attack us, seize us, and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys.”
They approached the steward of Joseph’s house and spoke to him at the entrance to the house,
saying, “Please, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food,
and when we reached the lodging place and opened our sacks, each man’s money was in the mouth of his sack—our money in its full amount. We have brought it back with us.
We have also brought down other money to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks.”
He replied, “Peace be with you; do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has given you treasure in your sacks. I received your money.” Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The man brought the men into Joseph’s house and gave them water; they washed their feet, and he gave their donkeys fodder.
They prepared the gift for Joseph’s arrival at noon, for they had heard that they were to eat there.
When Joseph came home, they brought into the house to him the gift they had with them, and they bowed down to him to the ground.
He asked them how they were and said, “Is your father well—the old man you told me about? Is he still alive?”
They said, “Your servant our father is well; he is still alive.” Then they bowed down and prostrated themselves.
He looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother’s son, and said, “Is this your younger brother, the one you told me about?” Then he said, “God be gracious to you, my son.”
Joseph hurried out, because he was deeply moved with compassion for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. He entered his private room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out. Regaining his composure, he said, “Serve the food.”

They served him by himself, them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.
They sat before him in order of age, from the firstborn to the youngest, and the men looked at one another in astonishment.
He sent portions to them from his own table, but Benjamin’s portion was five times as large as any of theirs. They drank and were merry with him.
Joseph commanded the steward of his house, “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s silver in the mouth of his sack.
Put my silver cup in the mouth of the youngest man’s sack, along with the silver for his grain.” And he did according to the word Joseph had spoken.
When morning dawned, the men were sent away, they and their donkeys.
They had not gone far from the city when Joseph said to his steward, “Rise, pursue the men; overtake them, and say to them, ‘Why have you repaid good with evil?’”
“Is this not the cup my lord drinks from, and by which he practices divination? You have done evil in doing this.”
He overtook them and spoke these words to them.
They said to him, “Why does my lord speak such words? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing.
Behold, we brought back to your lord’s house from the land of Canaan the silver that we found in the mouths of our sacks. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord’s house?
Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also shall be my lord’s slaves.”
He said, “Now let it be according to your words: he with whom it is found shall be my slave, but you shall be blameless.”
Then each man hurried and lowered his sack to the ground, and each opened his sack.
He searched them, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest; and the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack.
They tore their clothes, and each man loaded his donkey and returned to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph’s house, for he was still there, and they fell before him to the ground.
Joseph said to them, “What deed is this that you have done? Do you not know that a man such as I practices divination?”

Judah said, “What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? How shall we justify ourselves? God has found out the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are my lord’s slaves, both we and he in whose hand the cup was found.”
He said, “Far be it from me to do this. The man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my slave; but you, go up in peace to your father.”
Then Judah approached him and said, “Please, my lord, let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears, and do not let your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh.
My lord asked his servants, ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’
And we said to my lord, ‘We have an old father, and a child of his old age, a little one; his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loves him.’
Then you said to your servants, ‘Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.’
And we said to my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father, for if he leaves his father, he will die.’
But you said to your servants, ‘Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you shall not see my face again.’ “
And it happened when we went up to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.
And our father said, ‘Go back, buy us a little food.’
But we said, ‘We cannot go down. If our youngest brother is with us, then we will go down; for we cannot see the man’s face unless our youngest brother is with us.’
And your servant my father said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons.
The one went out from me, and I said, “Surely he has been torn to pieces,” and I have not seen him since.
And if you take this one also from me, and harm befalls him, you will bring down my gray hair with sorrow to Sheol.’ “
Now therefore, when I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us, since his life is bound up with his life,
it will happen that when he sees that the boy is not there, he will die; and your servants will bring down the gray hair of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol.
