And Manoah said, “Now when your words come to pass, what will be the boy’s way of life and his work?”
So the Angel of the LORD said to Manoah, “Let the woman heed everything I told her.
She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. She must observe all that I commanded her.”
Then Manoah said to the Angel of the LORD, “Please let us detain you, so that we may prepare a young goat for you.”

And the Angel of the LORD said to Manoah, “If you detain me, I will not eat your bread. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” (For Manoah did not know that he was the Angel of the LORD.)
Then Manoah said to the Angel of the LORD, “What is your name, so that when your words come to pass, we may honor you?”
And the Angel of the LORD said to him, “Why do you ask my name? It is beyond understanding.”
So Manoah took a young goat with the grain offering and offered them on the rock to the LORD. And as Manoah and his wife looked on, the LORD did a wondrous thing.
For when the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the Angel of the LORD ascended in the flame of the altar. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell on their faces to the ground.
Now the Angel of the LORD did not appear to Manoah or his wife again. Then Manoah knew that he was the Angel of the LORD.
And Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God!”

But his wife said to him, “If the LORD had desired to kill us, He would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things, nor would He have told us such things as these at this time.”
So the woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson; and the child grew up, and the LORD blessed him.
And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah, where he saw a woman among the daughters of the Philistines.
When he returned, he told his father and mother, “I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah; get her for me as a wife.”

His father and mother asked him, “Is there no woman among your brothers’ daughters or among all our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to take a wife?” But Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.”
His father and mother did not know that this matter was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother, and as they came to the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion came roaring toward him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one tears a young goat. He did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
He went down and spoke to the woman, and she was pleasing in Samson’s eyes.
After some days he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion. In it was a swarm of bees and honey.

He scooped the honey into his hands and ate it as he walked. When he came to his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate it; but he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s carcass.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson made a feast there, for young men used to do so.
When the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.
Samson said to them, “Let me now propound a riddle to you. If you can fully explain it to me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.
But if you cannot explain it to me, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.” They said to him, “Propound your riddle, that we may hear it.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they could not explain the riddle.
On the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s household with fire. Have you invited us here to rob us?”

Samson’s wife wept before him and said, “You only hate me; You do not love me. You have propounded a riddle to the sons of my people, and You have not explained it to me.” He said to her, “Behold, I have not explained it to my father or my mother, and shall I explain it to you?”
She wept before him during the seven days while their feast lasted. On the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him; and she explained the riddle to the sons of her people.

Before the sun went down on the seventh day, the men of the city said to him, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He said to them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.”

Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty of their men. He took their garments and gave them as the changes of clothes to those who had explained the riddle. His anger burned, and he went up to his father’s house.
But Samson’s wife was given to his companion who had been his attendant.
After some days, during the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, bringing a young goat. He said, "I will go in to my wife in her chamber." But her father would not let him enter.
Her father said, "I was certain you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please let her be yours instead."
Samson said to them, "This time I am justified in bringing harm upon the Philistines."
So Samson went and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches, turned the animals tail to tail, and placed one torch between each pair of tails.
Then he set fire to the torches and released the foxes into the Philistines' standing grain. The fire consumed the shocks, the standing grain, and even the olive orchards.

When the Philistines asked, "Who did this?" they were answered, "Samson, the Timnite's son-in-law, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion." So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, "If you do this, I will not rest until I have avenged myself on you."
He struck them down in a devastating slaughter, and then went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock at Etam.
The Philistines went up, encamped in Judah, and spread out at Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come up against us?" They answered, "We have come to bind Samson and do to him as he did to us."

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock at Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?" He replied, "As they did to me, so I have done to them."
They said to him, "We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."
They answered, "No; we will only bind you and hand you over to them. We will not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

When he reached Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they met him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes on his arms became like flax scorched by fire; his bindings melted from his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand, took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.
Samson said, "With a donkey's jawbone I have piled them into heaps. With a donkey's jawbone I have slain a thousand men."
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand and named that place Ramath-lehi.
He was very thirsty, so he called to the LORD and said, "You gave this great deliverance through Your servant, and now must I die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"
Then God split the hollow place at Lehi, and water came out of it. Samson drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore he named it En-hakkore; it is in Lehi to this day.
He judged Israel twenty years during the days of the Philistines.
Samson traveled to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and had sexual relations with her.

When the people of Gaza learned that Samson had arrived, they encircled the city and lay in wait for him all night at the gate; they remained silent throughout the night, saying, "We will wait until morning, and then we will kill him."

Samson lay there until midnight, but at midnight he arose, seized the doors of the city gate together with the two posts, tore them loose with the bar, laid them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the hill facing Hebron.
Afterward he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah.

The Philistine lords came to her and said, "Entice him, and discover where his great strength lies and how we may overpower him, so that we may bind him and afflict him; each of us will give you 1,100 pieces of silver."
Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies and how you may be bound so that you may be afflicted."
Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I will become weak and be like any other man."
So the Philistine lords brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.

Meanwhile, men were lying in wait in an inner room. She said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings as a strand of tow snaps when it touches fire, so his strength remained undiscovered.
Delilah said to Samson, "You have mocked me and told me lies. Now please tell me how you may be bound."
He said to her, "If they bind me securely with new ropes that have never been used, then I will become weak and be like any other man."

So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them. Then she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" The men lying in wait were in an inner room, but he broke the ropes from his arms like a thread.
Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you may be bound." He said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head into the web."
So she fastened it with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.
Then she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times and have not told me where your great strength lies."
Because she pressed him daily with her words and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.

So he told her all his heart and said, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If I am shaven, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like any other man."

When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent for the Philistine lords, saying, "Come up once more, for he has told me all his heart." So the Philistine lords came up to her and brought the money in their hand.
She made him sleep on her knees; then she called for a man and had the seven locks of his head shaved off. She began to afflict him, and his strength left him.
She said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as before and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, bound him with bronze shackles, and made him grind grain in the prison house.
However, the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
Now the Philistine lords gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to celebrate. They said, "Our god has delivered Samson, our enemy, into our hand."
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, "Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy, the destroyer of our country, who slew many of us."
When their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison house, and he entertained them; then they made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."
The house was full of men and women; all the Philistine lords were there, and on the roof were about three thousand men and women who looked on while Samson was made a spectacle.
Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "Lord, the LORD, please remember me and strengthen me just this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."
Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested and braced himself against them, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he pushed with all his might, and the house fell on the lords and on all the people in it. So the dead whom he killed in his death were more than those he had killed during his life.
His brothers and all his father's household came down, took him up, carried him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
A man named Micah resided in the hill country of Ephraim.

He said to his mother, "The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from you, and concerning which you pronounced a curse—even declaring within my hearing, 'Look, the silver is with me; I took it'—well, I have the silver; it is here." His mother responded, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."

He restored the eleven hundred shekels to his mother, whereupon she declared, "I had solemnly dedicated this silver to the LORD from my own hand for my son, to fashion a carved image and a molten image; therefore, I now restore it to you."

Accordingly, he returned the silver to his mother. She took two hundred shekels from it and gave them to a silversmith, who fashioned a carved image and a molten image; these were then installed in Micah's house.
Now this man Micah possessed a house of gods. He fashioned an ephod and teraphim, and he consecrated one of his sons, who served as his priest.
In those days Israel lacked a king, so each man did what was right in his own eyes.
A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, belonging to the clan of Judah, was sojourning there.
The man departed from Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn wherever he might secure a livelihood, and he journeyed as far as the hill country of Ephraim, reaching Micah's house.
Micah inquired, "Where do you come from?" The Levite answered, "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am traveling to sojourn wherever I may find opportunity."
Micah said, "Remain with me and serve as father and priest to me, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per annum, a suit of garments, and your sustenance." Thus the Levite accompanied him.
The Levite consented to dwell with the man, and the young man became as one of his sons.
Micah consecrated the Levite; the young man became his priest and remained in Micah's household.
Then Micah declared, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite serving as my priest."

In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance for itself in which to dwell, for until that day they had not received an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.

So the Danites sent five men from their clans, from the borders of their territory—men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol—to spy out the land and explore it. The Danites said to them, “Go and search the land.” So they went up into the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.

While they were staying at Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They turned aside and said to him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What do you have here?”
He said to them, “Micah has done this and that for me, and he hired me, and I became his priest.”
They said to him, “Please inquire of God for us, so that we may know whether the journey we are undertaking will succeed.”
The priest said to them, “Go in peace; the LORD is favorable to your journey.”

So the five men departed and came to Laish, where they saw the people living securely, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and secure. There was no ruler in the land to put them to shame in any way, and they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
When they returned to Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers asked them, “What do you have to report?”
They said, “Arise, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. Will you sit still? Do not be slack in going to enter and possess the land.
When you go, you will come to a secure people and a spacious land, for God has given it into your hand—a place where there is no lack of anything on earth.”
So six hundred men of the Danite clan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol.
They went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. Therefore that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it lies behind Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed through the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their brothers, “Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now consider what you should do.”
They turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, the house of Micah, and greeted him.
The six hundred Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood at the entrance of the gate.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land went in and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men.
When these men entered Micah’s house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”

They said to him, “Be silent. Put your hand over your mouth and come with us, and be a father and priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?”
The priest’s heart was glad. He took the ephod, the household gods, and the carved image, and went in the midst of the people.
They turned and departed, putting the little ones, the livestock, and the valuables ahead of them.
When they had gone far from Micah’s house, the men who lived in the houses near Micah’s house were called together and overtook the Danites.
They called to the Danites, who turned around and said to Micah, “What is wrong with you, that you have gathered a company?”
He said, “You have taken my gods that I made, and the priest, and have gone away. What do I have left? How can you say to me, ‘What is wrong with you?’”
The Danites said to him, “Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest bitter men attack you, and you lose your life and the lives of your household.”
So the Danites went on their way, and Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, and he turned and went back to his house.
They took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and came to Laish, to a quiet and secure people. They struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.
There was no deliverer, because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It lay in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and dwelt in it.
They named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city formerly was Laish.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land.
They set up for themselves the carved image that Micah had made, all the time the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days Israel had no king, and a Levite was sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim. He took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
But his concubine was unfaithful to him; she left him and returned to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah, where she remained for four months.

Her husband then set out after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back, taking with him a servant and a pair of donkeys. When he reached her father's house, the girl's father saw him and rejoiced at his coming.
His father-in-law, the young woman's father, detained him, and he stayed with him three days; they ate, drank, and lodged there.
On the fourth day they rose early in the morning, and he prepared to depart; but the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Refresh yourself with a morsel of bread, and afterward you may go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the girl's father said to the man, "Please be content and stay the night, and be cheerful."
When the man rose to go, his father-in-law urged him, so he stayed there another night.
On the fifth day he rose early to depart, and the girl's father said, "Refresh yourself, please, and tarry until the day declines." So the two of them ate.

Then the man rose to go, he and his concubine and his servant; but his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Look, the day is fading toward evening. Please stay the night; the day is drawing to a close. Stay here, that you may be cheerful, and tomorrow rise early for your journey, and go to your home."
Yet the man was unwilling to stay the night, so he arose and departed. He came as far as opposite Jebus—that is, Jerusalem—and with him were two saddled donkeys and his concubine.
When they were near Jebus, the day had declined greatly, and the servant said to his master, "Come, let us turn aside into this city of the Jebusites and lodge in it."
But his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into a foreign city that does not belong to the Israelites; we will pass on to Gibeah."
He said to his servant, "Come, let us draw near to one of these places and lodge in Gibeah or in Ramah."
So they passed on and traveled, and the sun set as they came near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to lodge in Gibeah, and when they entered the city they sat down in the open square, but no one took them into his house to spend the night.
Then in the evening an old man came in from his work in the field; he was from the hill country of Ephraim and was sojourning in Gibeah, though the men of the place were Benjamites.
He lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the city square, and the old man said, "Where are you going, and from where have you come?"

He answered him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there, and I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has received me into his house.
Yet there is both straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, for your maidservant, and for the young man with us; we lack nothing."
The old man said, "Peace be to you; let me attend to all your needs; only do not spend the night in the square."
So he brought him into his house and gave fodder to the donkeys; they washed their feet, ate, and drank.

While they were making their hearts merry, behold, the worthless men of the city, Benjamites, surrounded the house, beating on the door. They said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may sexually assault him."
The master of the house went out to them and said, "No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not do this disgraceful thing.
Behold, here is my daughter, a virgin, and his concubine. I will bring them out now, and you may humble them and do to them what seems good in your eyes; but to this man do not do this vile thing."
But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and brought her out to them, and they raped her and abused her all night until morning; at dawn they sent her away.
As morning was breaking, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, and she lay there until it was light.
When her master rose in the morning and opened the doors of the house and went out to continue his journey, behold, his concubine was lying at the door of the house with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up, and let us go." But there was no answer. So he took her up on the donkey, and the man arose and went to his place.
When he came to his house, he took a knife, seized his concubine, and cut her into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, "Such a thing has never been seen or done from the day the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt until this day. Consider it, take counsel, and speak."
All the Israelites, from Dan to Beersheba and throughout the land of Gilead, went out, and the whole congregation assembled as one man before the LORD at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people—all the tribes of Israel—took their stand in the assembly of God: four hundred thousand foot soldiers, each armed with a sword.
The Benjaminites learned that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, "Tell us, how did this wickedness come about?"
The Levite, husband of the murdered woman, answered, "I came to Gibeah in Benjamin with my concubine to spend the night.
During the night the men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house; they meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine until she died.
So I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent her throughout the territory of Israel, because they had committed an outrage and a disgraceful act in Israel.
Behold, all you men of Israel, give your counsel and advice here."
Then all the people rose as one man and said, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house."
"Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men from every hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, a hundred from every thousand, and a thousand from every ten thousand, to procure provisions for the people, so that when they come to Geba of Benjamin they may deal with all the disgraceful thing that has been done in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this wickedness that has occurred among you?"

"Now therefore deliver up the men, the worthless fellows who are in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gathered from their cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites mustered from their cities twenty-six thousand men armed with swords, besides seven hundred chosen men from the inhabitants of Gibeah.
Among all this people were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone so accurately that he would not miss by a hair's breadth.
The Israelites, apart from Benjamin, mustered four hundred thousand men armed with swords, all of them men of war.
The Israelites arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, saying, "Which of us shall go up first to battle against the Benjaminites?" And the LORD said, "Judah first."
The Israelites rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up in battle array against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and struck down twenty-two thousand Israelites on that day.
But the people, the men of Israel, encouraged themselves and again drew up for battle in the place where they had drawn up on the first day.

The Israelites went up and wept before the LORD until evening, and they inquired of the LORD, saying, "Shall we again approach to battle against our brothers the Benjaminites?" And the LORD said, "Go up against them."
The Israelites drew near to the Benjaminites on the second day.
Benjamin came out against them from Gibeah on the second day and struck down eighteen thousand more Israelites, all of them swordsmen.

Then all the Israelites and all the people went up and came to Bethel and wept; they sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
The Israelites inquired of the LORD—for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days—

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, stood before it in those days, saying, "Shall I go out once more to battle against my brothers the Benjaminites, or shall I cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand."
So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.
The Israelites went up against the Benjaminites on the third day and drew up against Gibeah as at other times.

The Benjaminites went out against the people and were drawn away from the city; they began to strike down the people as before, about thirty men of Israel, on the highways—one leading up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah—and in the open country.
The Benjaminites said, "They are defeated before us, as before." But the Israelites said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."
Then all the men of Israel rose from their place and drew up at Baal-tamar, and the ambush of Israel burst forth from its place at Maareh-geba.
Ten thousand chosen men from all Israel came opposite Gibeah, and the battle was fierce; but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was upon them.
The LORD struck Benjamin before Israel, and the Israelites destroyed twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin that day, all of them swordsmen.
The Benjaminites saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the ambush that they had set against Gibeah.
The ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the ambush moved out and put the whole city to the sword.
The appointed signal between the men of Israel and the ambush was that they should make a great column of smoke rise from the city.
The men of Israel turned in battle, and Benjamin began to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel, for the Benjaminites said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle."
But when the column of smoke began to rise from the city, Benjamin looked behind them, and behold, the whole city was going up in smoke to heaven.
Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster had come upon them.
So they turned their backs before the men of Israel toward the way of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and those who came out of the cities destroyed them in their midst.
They surrounded the Benjaminites, pursued them, and trampled them down with ease as far as a point opposite Gibeah toward the east.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor.
They turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and the Israelites cut down five thousand men along the highways and pursued them as far as Gidom, striking down two thousand more.
So all who fell of Benjamin that day were twenty-five thousand men armed with swords, all of them men of valor.
But six hundred men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

The men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and struck them with the edge of the sword, both the inhabitants of every city and the beasts and all that was found; they also set on fire all the cities that were found.
Now the Israelites had sworn at Mizpah, “No one among us shall give his daughter to Benjamin in marriage.”
The people went to Bethel and sat there before God until evening, lifting up their voices and weeping bitterly.
They said, “O the LORD, God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe is lacking in Israel?”
The next day the people rose early, built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

Then the Israelites asked, “Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the assembly to the the LORD?” For a solemn oath had been taken against anyone who did not come up to the the LORD at Mizpah: “He shall surely be put to death.”
And the Israelites had compassion on Benjamin their brother and said, “Today one tribe has been wiped out in Israel.
What shall we do for wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by the the LORD not to give them any of our daughters in marriage?”
So they asked, “Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come up to the the LORD at Mizpah?” And behold, no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp to the assembly.
For when the people were mustered, behold, none of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there.
So the congregation sent twelve thousand of their most valiant warriors there and commanded them, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the sword, including the women and children.
This is what you shall do: you shall utterly destroy every male and every woman who has had sexual relations with a man.”

And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young women who were virgins, who had never had sexual relations with a man; and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole congregation sent word and spoke to the Benjamites who were at the rock of Rimmon, and offered them peace.
And Benjamin returned at that time, and they gave them the women whom they had kept alive from the women of Jabesh-gilead; but they were not enough for them.
And the people grieved for Benjamin, because the the LORD had caused a rift among the tribes of Israel.
Then the elders of the congregation said, “What shall we do for wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been destroyed?”
And they said, “There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe may not be wiped out from Israel.”
“But we cannot give them wives from our daughters, for the Israelites have sworn, saying, ‘Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin.’”
So they said, “Behold, there is the annual feast of the the LORD in Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east side of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.”
And they commanded the Benjamites, saying, “Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards.

Keep watch; if the daughters of Shiloh come out to take part in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and seize for yourselves each man a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

And when their fathers or brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, ‘Be gracious to them, for we did not take a wife for each man in the war, and you did not give them wives, so you will not now be guilty.’”

And the Benjamites did so, and took wives for themselves from the women who were dancing, whom they carried off, according to their number; and they went and returned to their inheritance, and rebuilt the cities and dwelt in them.
And the Israelites departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and family; and they went out from there, every man to his inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did as he saw fit.
In the days when the judges governed Israel, a severe famine afflicted the land, and a man from Bethlehem in Judah departed with his wife and two sons to sojourn in the territory of Moab.
The man was named Elimelech; his wife was Naomi, and his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They entered Moab and settled there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi’s husband, died, leaving her with her two sons.
Her sons married Moabite women—one named Orpah and the other Ruth—and they resided there for about ten years.
Then both Mahlon and Chilion died as well, and the woman was bereaved of her husband and her two sons.
When Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by granting them food, she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the territory of Moab.
Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law, she left the place where she had been living and set out on the road back to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go, return each to her mother’s house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.
May the LORD grant you security, each in the home of a husband.” Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud.
They said, “We will surely return with you to your people.”
Naomi said, “Return, my daughters; why should you go with me? Do I still have sons in my womb who could become your husbands?
Return, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. Even if I said I still had hope—even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons—
would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from marrying because of them? No, my daughters, for it is far more bitter for me than for you, because the LORD has afflicted me.”
They raised their voices and wept again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.
Naomi said, “See, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods. Return after your sister-in-law.”
Ruth said, “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn back from following you. Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do so to me, and more also, if anything but death separates me from you.”
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she ceased speaking to her.
So the two traveled on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived in Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women asked, “Is this Naomi?”
She said, “Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why do you call me Naomi, when the LORD has brought this suffering upon me and the Almighty has afflicted me?”
So Naomi returned, accompanied by Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, who came back with her from Moab. They reached Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Now Naomi had a kinsman on her husband’s side, a man of considerable standing from the clan of Elimelech, and his name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go into the fields and gather the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi answered, “Go ahead, my daughter.”
So she departed and entered a field, gleaning behind the harvesters. It happened that the portion of the field belonged to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech.
Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, “The LORD be with you!” “The LORD bless you!” they answered.
Boaz asked the overseer of his harvesters, “To whom does this young woman belong?”
The overseer replied, “She is the Moabite woman who returned from Moab with Naomi.
She asked, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.’ She has been here since morning, working steadily, and has rested only briefly in the shelter.”
So Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, listen to me. Do not go to glean in another field, and do not leave this one; stay here with my young women.”

“Keep your eyes on the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the girls. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.”
At this she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, “Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should notice me, though I am a foreigner?”

Boaz answered, “I have been fully informed of all that you have done for your mother-in-law after your husband’s death—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to a people you did not know before.”
“May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a full reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under Whose wings you have come to take refuge.”
Then she said, “May I continue to find favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not even one of your servant girls.”

At mealtime Boaz said to her, “Come over here and eat some bread, dipping your morsel in the wine vinegar.” When she sat down beside the harvesters, he offered her roasted grain. She ate until she was satisfied and had some left over.
When she rose to glean, Boaz commanded his young men, “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not humiliate her.”
“Moreover, pull out some handfuls for her from the bundles and leave them for her to gather, and do not rebuke her.”
So Ruth gleaned in the field until evening. Then she threshed what she had gathered, and it was about an ephah of barley.
She carried it into the town and showed her mother-in-law what she had gleaned. She also brought out and gave her the leftover food from her meal.

Her mother-in-law asked her, “Where did you glean today, and where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you!” Then Ruth told her mother-in-law, “The man I worked with today is named Boaz.”
Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “The LORD bless him! He has not ceased to show kindness to the living and the dead.” She added, “This man is a close relative of ours; he is one of our redeemers.”
Ruth the Moabite added, “He also told me, ‘Stay with my young men until they have finished all my harvest.’”
Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “It will be good for you, my daughter, to go with his young women, because in another field you might be harmed.”
So Ruth stayed close to the young women of Boaz to glean until the barley harvest and the wheat harvest were completed. And she continued to live with her mother-in-law.
Naomi, her mother-in-law, said to Ruth, "My daughter, should I not seek a secure home for you, so that life may go well for you?
Now Boaz, with whose young women you have been working, is he not our relative? Tonight he is winnowing barley at the threshing floor.
Wash yourself, anoint yourself, put on your best clothes, and go down to the threshing floor; but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, notice the place where he lies; then go in, uncover his feet, and lie down. He will tell you what you should do."
Ruth answered, "I will do everything you say."
So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had commanded her.
After Boaz had eaten and drunk and was in good spirits, he went to lie down at the far end of the grain heap. Ruth came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
At midnight the man was startled; he turned over and discovered a woman lying at his feet.
"Who are you?" he asked. She replied, "I am Ruth, your servant. Take me under your protection as your wife, for you are my kinsman-redeemer."
"Blessed are you by the LORD, my daughter. Your last act of kindness is better than the first, because you did not pursue younger men, whether poor or rich.
Now, my daughter, do not be afraid; I will do for you everything you ask, for everyone at the gate knows that you are a woman of noble character.
"It is true that I am a redeemer, yet there is a redeemer closer than I am.
Stay here tonight, and in the morning, if he wishes to redeem you, let him do so; but if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until morning."
So she lay at his feet until morning and rose before anyone could recognize his neighbor. Boaz said, "Let it not be known that a woman came to the threshing floor."
Then he said, "Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out." She held it out, and he measured out six measures of barley and put them on her. Then he returned to the city.
When Ruth came to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked, "Who are you, my daughter?" Ruth told her everything the man had done for her.
Ruth added, "He gave me these six measures of barley and said, 'Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'"
Naomi replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how this matter turns out, for the man will not rest until he has settled it today."

Boaz ascended to the city gate and took his seat; almost immediately, the kinsman-redeemer of whom he had spoken passed by. Boaz called out, "Step aside and sit here, my friend." The man turned aside and sat down.
Boaz then summoned ten of the city's elders and instructed them, "Sit here as well," and they complied.
Boaz said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has returned from the territory of Moab, is offering for sale the parcel of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech.

I felt obliged to disclose this to you and to say that you should purchase it in the presence of those seated here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you are willing to redeem it, redeem it; if not, tell me plainly, for no one else possesses the right of redemption ahead of you, and I stand next in line after you." He answered, "I will redeem it."

Boaz continued, "On the day you acquire the field from Naomi, you must also take Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the deceased, as a wife, so that the dead man's name may be perpetuated upon his inheritance."
The redeemer replied, "I cannot redeem it for myself without jeopardizing my own inheritance. You redeem it yourself; I am unable to do so."
Moreover, in Israel at that time, whenever a man redeemed or exchanged property, he would remove his sandal and give it to the other party; this act served as legal confirmation of the transaction.
The redeemer therefore removed his sandal and said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself."
Boaz then addressed the elders and all the people: "You are witnesses today that I have purchased from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, as well as all that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon.

I have likewise acquired Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's widow, to be my wife, so that the deceased's name may be preserved upon his inheritance and not be erased from his family or from the gate of his community. You are witnesses today."

All the people at the gate, together with the elders, responded, "May the LORD make the woman entering your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and gain renown in Bethlehem.
May your household be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through the offspring the LORD grants you by this young woman."
Accordingly, Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He consummated the marriage, and the LORD granted her conception, so that she bore a son.
The women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be proclaimed in Israel.
He will restore your vitality and sustain you in your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you—who is better to you than seven sons—has borne him."
Naomi took the child, cradled him, and became his nurse.
The neighboring women declared, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed, and he became the father of Jesse, the father of David.
Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,
Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,
Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,
Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives: one was named Hannah, and the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Year after year this man went up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served as priests of the the LORD.
On the day of the sacrifice, Elkanah gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, although the the LORD had closed her womb.
Because the the LORD had closed her womb, her rival provoked her bitterly and vexed her.
This happened year after year: whenever Hannah went up to the house of the the LORD, her rival provoked her, so she wept and would not eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not better to you than ten sons?"
After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the the LORD.
In bitterness of soul she prayed to the the LORD and wept bitterly.

She made a vow, saying, "O the LORD of hosts, if You will indeed look on the affliction of Your servant and remember me, and not forget Your servant, but give Your servant a son, then I will give him to the the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."
As she continued praying before the the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put away your wine from you."
Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman of sorrowful spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the the LORD.
Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for out of my great anxiety and vexation I have been speaking until now."
Eli answered, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to Him."
She said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the the LORD; then they returned and came to their house at Ramah. Elkanah was intimate with his wife Hannah, and the the LORD remembered her.
In due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, saying, "I have asked him of the the LORD."
The man Elkanah and all his household went up to offer the yearly sacrifice to the the LORD and to fulfill his vow.
But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "I will not go up until the child is weaned; then I will bring him, so that he may appear before the the LORD and dwell there forever."
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Do what seems best to you; stay until you have weaned him. Only may the the LORD establish His word." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.
When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the the LORD at Shiloh, and the child was young.
Then they slaughtered a bull and brought the child to Eli.
She said, "As you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here in your presence praying to the the LORD.
For this child I prayed, and the the LORD has granted me my petition.
Therefore I have given him to the the LORD; as long as he lives, he is given to the the LORD." And he worshiped the the LORD there.
Hannah prayed and said, “My heart rejoices in the the LORD; my strength is lifted up in the the LORD. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation.
There is no one holy like the the LORD, for there is none besides You, and there is no rock like our God.
Do not go on speaking so proudly; do not let arrogance come from your mouth, for the the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by Him deeds are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are broken, but those who stumbled are armed with strength.
The well-fed hire themselves out for bread, while the hungry are filled; the barren woman bears seven children, but she who has many sons grows feeble.
The LORD brings death and gives life; He sends down to Sheol and raises up.
The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and He exalts.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to seat them with princes and give them an inheritance of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the the LORD’s, and He has set the world upon them.
He guards the feet of His faithful ones, but the wicked are silenced in darkness, for not by might does a man prevail.
The LORD shatters those who contend with Him; He thunders against them from heaven. The LORD judges the ends of the earth; He gives strength to His king and exalts the power of His anointed.”
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, while the boy ministered to the the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.
Now the sons of Eli were worthless men; they did not know the the LORD.
The custom of the priests with the people was this: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant came while the meat was boiling, carrying a three-pronged fork in his hand.
He would thrust it into the pan, kettle, cauldron, or pot, and whatever the fork brought up the priest took for himself. This is what they did to all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.
Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest’s servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, “Give the priest meat to roast; he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.”
If the man said to him, “Let them burn the fat first, then take as much as you desire,” he would answer, “No, give it now; if not, I will take it by force.”
Thus the sin of the young men was very great before the the LORD, for they treated the the LORD’s offering with contempt.
But Samuel was ministering before the the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod.
Moreover, his mother made him a little robe and brought it to him year by year when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, “May the The LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to the the LORD.” Then they would go home.
Indeed, the The LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the the LORD.
Now Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
So he said to them, “Why do you do such things? I hear from all the people about your evil deeds.
No, my sons; the report that I hear is not good, for you are causing the people of the the LORD to transgress.

If one man sins against another, God may mediate for him; but if a man sins against the the LORD, who can intercede for him?” But they did not listen to their father, because the the LORD had decided to put them to death.
And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the the LORD and with men.
Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him, “Thus says the the LORD: Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh’s rule?

Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest, to go up to My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me? And did I not give to your father’s house all the offerings made by fire by the children of Israel?
Why then do you scorn My sacrifice and My offering that I have commanded for My dwelling, and honor your sons above Me by fattening yourselves on the best of all the offerings of My people Israel?

Therefore the the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: ‘I did indeed say that your house and your father’s house would walk before Me forever.’ But now the the LORD declares: ‘I would never permit that; those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be lightly esteemed.’
Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.
And you will see distress in My dwelling in place of all the good that was done to Israel, and there will never be an old man in your house.
Yet not every man of yours will I cut off from My altar, so that your eyes will fail and your heart will grieve; and all the increase of your house will die in the prime of life.
And this will be a sign to you that will come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: in one day both of them shall die.
Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind. I will build him a sure house, and he shall walk before My anointed forever.

And everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, ‘Please appoint me to one of the priestly offices, that I may eat a piece of bread.’”
Now the youth Samuel was ministering to the LORD in Eli's presence, and in those days revelations from the LORD were scarce; visions were not commonly granted.
By then Eli's eyesight had begun to fail, rendering him unable to see, and he was reclining in his customary place.
The lamp of God had not yet been extinguished, and Samuel was reclining within the sanctuary of the LORD, where the ark of God rested.
Then the LORD summoned Samuel, and he responded, "Here I am!"
He hastened to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you summoned me." But Eli said, "I did not call; lie down again." So Samuel went and lay down.
And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" Samuel arose, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you summoned me." But Eli said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again."
Now Samuel had not yet come to know the LORD, nor had the word of the LORD yet been disclosed to him.
The LORD summoned Samuel a third time. He arose, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you summoned me." Then Eli discerned that the LORD was calling the boy.
Therefore Eli instructed Samuel, "Go, lie down; and should He call you, you are to say, 'Speak, the LORD, for Your servant hears.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
Then the LORD came and stood by him, calling as He had before, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for Your servant hears."
Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to accomplish a deed in Israel that will cause all who hear of it to shudder.
On that day I will execute against Eli every word I have spoken concerning his household, from first to last.
I have declared to him that I will judge his house in perpetuity because of the iniquity he acknowledged: his sons were blaspheming God, and he failed to restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the guilt of Eli's house shall never be expiated by sacrifice or offering."
Samuel remained there until morning, when he opened the doors of the house of the LORD; yet he dreaded disclosing the vision to Eli.
Eli summoned Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." Samuel answered, "Here I am."
Then Eli said, "What is the word that He spoke to you? Do not conceal it from me. May God deal with you, be it ever so severely, if you withhold from me any part of all that He said to you."
Samuel recounted everything and concealed nothing from him. Then Eli said, "It is the LORD; let Him do what seems good in His sight."
Samuel continued to grow, and the LORD was with him, permitting none of his words to go unfulfilled.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, recognized that Samuel had been established as a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for He revealed Himself to Samuel at Shiloh through the word of the LORD.
The word of Samuel reached all Israel. Then Israel marched out to confront the Philistines in battle; they encamped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines encamped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up in formation against Israel, and when the fighting spread, Israel was routed before the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the field of battle.

When the people returned to camp, the elders of Israel asked, "Why has the the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us take the ark of the covenant of the the LORD from Shiloh, that He may come among us and deliver us from the power of our enemies."

So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, accompanied the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the the LORD entered the camp, all Israel shouted so loudly that the earth trembled.
The Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and asked, "What is this tremendous shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?" When they learned that the ark of the the LORD had entered the camp,
the Philistines were terrified, for they said, "God has come into the camp!" And they cried, "Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will rescue us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness."
Then the Philistines urged one another, "Be strong and act like men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they once were to you. Be men, and fight!"
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated; every man fled to his tent. The slaughter was immense—thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell.
The ark of God was captured, and Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
That same day a Benjamite ran from the battle line and reached Shiloh with his clothes torn and dust on his head.

When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat beside the road, watching anxiously, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man entered the city to report the news, the whole city cried out.
Eli heard the outcry and asked, "What is this commotion?" So the man hurried in and reported to Eli.
Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes had grown dim, so that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, "I have just come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." "What happened, my son?" Eli asked.

The messenger answered, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured."
When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward off his seat beside the gate. His neck was broken, and he died, for he was an old man and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.

Now his daughter-in-law, Phinehas's wife, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and husband were dead, she knelt down and gave birth, for her labor pains overwhelmed her.
As she was dying, the women attending her said, "Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!" But she did not respond or pay any attention.
She named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel," because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
Now the Philistines had seized the ark of God and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
They carried the ark of God into the temple of Dagon and set it beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod rose early the next morning, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD. They lifted Dagon and restored him to his place.

But when they rose early again the following morning, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD; his head and both hands were severed at the threshold, and only his torso remained.
Therefore, to this day, neither the priests of Dagon nor anyone who enters Dagon's temple in Ashdod steps on the threshold.
The hand of the LORD was heavy upon the Ashdodites; He devastated them and struck them with tumors, both in Ashdod and throughout its surrounding territory.
When the men of Ashdod saw what had happened, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for His hand is heavy upon us and upon Dagon our god."

So they sent for and gathered all the lords of the Philistines. Then they asked, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" The lords replied, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried to Gath." So they carried the ark of the God of Israel there.
After it had been carried there, the hand of the LORD was against that city, producing great panic; He struck the men of the city, from the youngest to the oldest, and tumors broke out among them.
They then sent the ark of God to Ekron. When the ark of God arrived in Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, "They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to me in order to kill me and my people!"

So they sent for and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send the ark of the God of Israel away; let it return to its own place, so that it will not kill me and my people." For a deadly panic had seized the whole city, and the hand of God was exceedingly heavy there.
The men who did not die were afflicted with tumors, and the outcry of the city ascended to heaven.
The ark of the the LORD remained in Philistine territory for seven months.
The Philistines summoned their priests and diviners and asked, "What should we do with the ark of the the LORD? Tell us how we ought to send it back to its place."

"If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty; rather, you must return a guilt offering to Him. Then you will be healed, and it will become clear to you why His hand has not withdrawn from you.

As for the guilt offering you should return to Him, let it be five gold tumors and five gold mice, corresponding to the number of Philistine rulers, for the same plague has afflicted all of you and your rulers.

Therefore make images of your tumors and of your mice—the very creatures that are ravaging the land—and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps He will lighten His hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.
Why should you harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? When He dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away so that they could go?
"Now then, prepare a new cart and take two milk cows that have never been yoked. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves away and keep them at home.
Take the ark of the the LORD and place it on the cart. Put the gold objects that you are returning as a guilt offering into a chest beside it, and send it off so that it may go on its way.

Then watch: if it goes up the road toward Beth Shemesh, then He has brought this great disaster upon us; but if not, then we will know that His hand did not strike us, and that what happened to us was merely chance."
The men did so. They took two milk cows, hitched them to the cart, and penned their calves at home.
They placed the ark of the the LORD on the cart, along with the chest containing the gold mice and the images of their tumors.

The cows went straight along the road toward Beth Shemesh, keeping to the highway and lowing as they went; they did not turn aside to the right or to the left. The Philistine rulers followed them as far as the border of Beth Shemesh.
The people of Beth Shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark, they rejoiced at the sight.
The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stopped there beside a large stone. They split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the the LORD.

The Levites lowered the ark of the the LORD and the chest beside it, which held the gold objects, and placed them on the large stone. That day the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and presented sacrifices to the the LORD.
When the five Philistine rulers saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold tumors the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

The gold mice corresponded to the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers—fortified cities and unwalled villages alike—even as far as the great stone of Abel, on which they set down the ark of the the LORD. That stone remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.

But He struck down some of the men of Beth Shemesh because they had looked into the ark of the the LORD. He struck down fifty thousand and seventy men, and the people mourned because the the LORD had struck the people with a great slaughter.
The men of Beth Shemesh said, "Who can stand before the the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall He go up from us?"
So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath Jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the the LORD. Come down and take it up to yourselves."
The men of Kiriath-jearim came and took the ark of the LORD, and they carried it to the house of Abinadab on the hill; then they consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD.
A long time passed—twenty years in all—and the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim, while all the house of Israel mourned and sought the LORD.

Then Samuel said to all Israel, “If you return to the LORD with all your heart, remove the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him alone; then He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.”
So the children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD alone.
Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you.”
They assembled at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the LORD. On that day they fasted and said, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Then Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah.

When the Philistines heard that the children of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. The Israelites heard of it and were afraid because of the Philistines.
The children of Israel said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, so that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”
Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel cried out to the LORD on behalf of Israel, and the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to battle Israel. But the LORD thundered with a loud voice against the Philistines that day and threw them into confusion, so that they were defeated before Israel.
The men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down as far as below Beth-car.
Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and he called its name Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.”
So the Philistines were subdued and did not come again into the territory of Israel. The hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel, from Ekron to Gath, were restored to Israel, and Israel delivered its territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
Year by year he went on a circuit from Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all those places.
Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there he judged Israel. He also built an altar to the LORD.
When Samuel had advanced in years, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
His firstborn was named Joel, and his second was Abijah; they administered justice in Beersheba.
Yet his sons did not conduct themselves according to his ways. Instead, they turned aside after dishonest gain, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
All the elders of Israel assembled and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, “Look, you are advanced in years, and your sons do not conduct themselves according to your ways. Therefore, appoint a king to judge us, as all the other nations have.”
The matter displeased Samuel when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” So Samuel prayed to the the LORD.
The The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you; rather, they have rejected Me as their King.
They are doing to you precisely what they have done to Me from the day I brought them up from Egypt until now: they have forsaken Me and served other gods.
Now listen to their voice, but solemnly warn them and explain the manner of the king who will reign over them.”
Samuel communicated all the words of the the LORD to the people who had requested a king.
He said, “This is how the king who will reign over you will treat you: he will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and cavalry, and they will run before his chariot.
He will appoint commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and he will set some to plow his ground, reap his harvest, and manufacture his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to serve as perfumers, cooks, and bakers.
He will seize the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and bestow them upon his servants.
He will exact a tenth of your grain and your vineyards and give it to his officials and servants.
He will take your male and female servants, your finest young men, and your donkeys, and employ them in his service.
He will exact a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his servants.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but the the LORD will not answer you in that day.”
But the people refused to heed Samuel’s voice. They said, “No! We must have a king over us,
so that we may be like all the other nations, and so that our king may judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard all the people’s words and repeated them to the the LORD.
The The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the men of Israel, “Go back, each of you, to his own city.”
There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a valiant warrior.
He had a son named Saul, a choice and handsome young man; among the Israelites, no one surpassed him in handsomeness, and from his shoulders upward he towered above all the people.
The donkeys belonging to Kish, Saul's father, had strayed. Kish said to his son Saul, "Take one of the servants with you, rise, and go search for the donkeys."

So he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. Then they passed through the land of Shaalim, yet they were not there; then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but they did not find them.
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him, "Come, let us return, lest my father stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious about us."

But he said, "Look, there is a man of God in this city, and he is an honored man; everything he says surely comes to pass. Let us go there now; perhaps he will tell us about our journey on which we have set out."
Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what shall we bring the man? The bread in our sacks is gone, and we have no gift to bring to the man of God. What do we have?"
The servant answered Saul, "Look, I have a quarter shekel of silver; I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way."
(Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he would say, "Come, let us go to the seer," for the prophet of today was formerly called a seer.)
Saul said to his servant, "Well said; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God was.
As they were going up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water, and they said to them, "Is the seer here?"
They answered, "He is; look, he is just ahead of you. Hurry now, for he came into the city today, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place.

As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice; afterward the invited guests will eat. Now go up, for at this time you will find him."
So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, look, Samuel was coming out toward them to go up to the high place.
Now the LORD had revealed to Samuel a day before Saul came, saying,

"Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him as prince over My people Israel. He shall save My people from the hand of the Philistines, for I have seen My people, because their cry has come to Me."
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD said to him, "Look, the man of whom I spoke to you! This is he who shall rule over My people."
Then Saul approached Samuel in the midst of the gate and said, "Please tell me where the seer's house is."
Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me; and in the morning I will let you go, and will tell you all that is on your mind.
As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And for whom is all the desire of Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?"
Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjamite, from the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least of all the families of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"
Then Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty men.
Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion that I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'"

So the cook took up the leg with what was on it and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, "Look, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the appointed time, while I said, 'I have invited the people.'" So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
When they came down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.
They rose early, and at dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, saying, "Get up, that I may send you away." So Saul arose, and both of them, he and Samuel, went out into the street.

As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stand here a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."
Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it over Saul's head, kissed him, and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?

When you leave me today, you will meet two men at Rachel's tomb in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys you set out to find have been found. And now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is worried about you, asking, "What should I do about my son?"' "

Then you will go on from there and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there—one carrying three young goats, one carrying three loaves of bread, and one carrying a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands. "

After that you will come to Gibeah of God, where there is a Philistine garrison. As you approach the town, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres, and they will be prophesying.
Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into a different man. "
When these signs have come, do whatever the situation requires, for God is with you.
