Go down ahead of me to Gilgal, and I will surely come down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do."
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed his heart, and all these signs were fulfilled that day.
When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a company of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.
All who had known him previously and saw him prophesying with the prophets asked one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"
And a man from there answered, "And who is their father?" So it became a proverb: "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
When Saul had finished prophesying, he went up to the high place.
Now Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, "Where have you been?" "Looking for the donkeys," Saul replied. "When we could not find them, we went to Samuel."
"Please tell me," said his uncle, "what Samuel said to you."
Saul answered, "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." But he did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship.
Then Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah.

And he said to the Israelites, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from all the kingdoms that oppressed you.'

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions, and you have said, 'No, set a king over us.' Now present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and clans."
So Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
Then he brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of Matri was chosen. And Saul son of Kish was chosen, but when they looked for him, he could not be found.
So they inquired further of the LORD, "Has the man come here yet?" And the LORD said, "Yes, he has hidden himself among the supplies."
So they ran and brought him out, and as he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of the others.
Then Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
Then Samuel explained to the people the rights of kingship, wrote them on a scroll, and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home.
Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him.
But some worthless men said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no gift. But Saul kept silent.
Nahash the Ammonite advanced and encamped against Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite replied, “I will make a treaty with you on this condition: I will gouge out all your right eyes and thereby disgrace all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Grant us seven days so that we may send messengers throughout all the territory of Israel. If no one comes to save us, then we will surrender to you.”
When the messengers reached Gibeah of Saul and reported these words to the people, all the people raised their voices and wept.
Meanwhile, Saul was returning from the fields behind his oxen. Saul asked, “Why are the people weeping?” They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God came powerfully upon him, and his anger blazed.

He took a yoke of oxen, dismembered them, and sent the pieces throughout all the territory of Israel by messengers, proclaiming, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march with Saul and Samuel.” Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they mobilized as one man.
He mustered them at Bezek: three hundred thousand men of Israel and thirty thousand men of Judah.

They said to the messengers who had come, “Thus you shall say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun grows hot, you will be delivered.’” The messengers returned and reported this to the men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.
The men of Jabesh said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may deal with us as you see fit.”

The next day Saul divided the people into three companies. They entered the camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors were scattered so thoroughly that not even two of them remained together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who was it that said, ‘Shall Saul reign over us?’ Bring those men here so that we may put them to death.”
Saul said, “No one is to be put to death today, for today the LORD has brought deliverance to Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the monarchy there.”
So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they installed Saul as king before the LORD. They offered peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced exceedingly.
Samuel said to all Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have set a king over you.
Now look, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until today.

Look, here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His Anointed: Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I taken a bribe to look the other way? I will make restitution to you.”
They said, “You have not defrauded us or oppressed us, and you have taken nothing from anyone’s hand.”
He said to them, “The LORD is witness against you, and His Anointed is witness today, that you have found nothing in my hand.” They said, “He is a witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up from the land of Egypt.
Now then, stand, and I will bring a charge against you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds the LORD performed for you and for your fathers.
When Jacob came to Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD, and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.

But they forgot the LORD their God, and He delivered them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, and they fought against them.
They cried out to the LORD and said, ‘We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. Now deliver us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve You.’
Then the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you from the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.
When you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, came against you, you said to me, ‘No; instead, a king shall reign over us,’ though the LORD your God was your king.
Now then, look—the king you have chosen, whom you asked for—and look, the LORD has set a king over you.
If you fear the LORD and serve Him and listen to His voice and do not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God.
But if you do not listen to the voice of the LORD and rebel against the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you, as it was against your fathers.”
“Now then, stand and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes.

Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call to the LORD, and He will send thunder and rain, so that you may know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king.”
So Samuel called to the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day; and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for your servants, that we may not die; for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil; yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after worthless things, which cannot profit or deliver, for they are worthless.
For the LORD will not forsake His people, because of His great name, for the LORD has been pleased to make you His people.
Moreover, as for me, it would be unthinkable for me to sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you; instead, I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the LORD and serve Him in truth with all your heart, for consider what great things He has done for you.
But if you do wickedly, you will be swept away, both you and your king.”
Saul was a year old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel for two years.

Saul chose three thousand men of Israel for himself: two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, each to his own tent.
Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Saul blew the trumpet throughout the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear!"
All Israel heard the report: "Saul has struck the Philistine garrison, and Israel has also become obnoxious to the Philistines." Then the people were summoned to follow Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines assembled to fight against Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They advanced and encamped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
When the Israelites saw that they were in trouble, because the people were hard pressed, they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, strongholds, and cisterns.
Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people who remained with him trembled.
Saul waited seven days, the appointed time set by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people began to desert him.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.
As soon as he finished offering it, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel said, "What have you done?" Saul replied, "I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come at the appointed time, and that the Philistines were assembling at Michmash.
So I said to myself, 'The Philistines will now come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' Therefore I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering."

Samuel said to Saul, "You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of the LORD your God, which He commanded you. For now the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.

But now your kingdom will not endure. The LORD has sought for Himself a man after His own heart, and the LORD has appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."
Then Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counted the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan, with the people who remained with them, were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines encamped at Michmash.
Raiders came out of the Philistine camp in three companies. One company turned toward Ophrah, in the land of Shual.
Another turned toward Beth-horon, and the third turned toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
Now no blacksmith could be found throughout all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, "Otherwise the Hebrews will make swords or spears for themselves."
So all Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen each man's plowshare, mattock, axe, and sickle.
The charge was two-thirds of a shekel for plowshares and mattocks, and one-third of a shekel for sharpening axes and setting goads.
Thus on the day of battle, neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
And the garrison of the Philistines moved out to the pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan, Saul's son, said to the young man carrying his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine outpost on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying under the pomegranate tree in Migron on the outskirts of Gibeah, and the troops with him numbered about six hundred men.
Ahijah son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas son of Eli, priest of the LORD in Shiloh, was wearing an ephod. The troops did not know that Jonathan had left.
On each side of the pass that Jonathan intended to cross to reach the Philistine outpost stood a cliff; one was called Bozez and the other Seneh.
One cliff rose to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba.

Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come, let us go over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few."
His armor-bearer answered, "Do all that you have in mind. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul."
Jonathan said, "Come on, then; we will cross over toward them and let them see us.
If they say, 'Stay there until we come to you,' we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' we will climb up, because that will be our sign that the LORD has given them into our hands."
So both of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost, and the Philistines said, "Look! Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they were hiding."

The men of the outpost shouted to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, "Come up to us and we'll teach you a lesson." So Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Climb up after me; the LORD has given them into Israel's hands."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer right behind him, and the Philistines fell before Jonathan, while his armor-bearer killed them as he followed.
In that first assault Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed about twenty men in an area of about half an acre.
Then panic struck the camp, the field, and all the people; the outpost and the raiding party also trembled. The ground shook, and a panic from God spread through the land.
Saul's watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin saw the army melting away in all directions.
Saul said to the troops with him, "Muster the men and see who has left us." When they did, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God." (At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.)
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp increased more and more, so Saul said to the priest, "Stop."
Then Saul and all the men with him assembled and went to battle. They found the Philistines in total confusion, striking each other with swords.
The Hebrews who had previously been with the Philistines and had gone up with them into the camp went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
When all the Israelites who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they joined the pursuit.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved beyond Beth Aven.

Now the Israelites were in distress that day, because Saul had bound the people with an oath, saying, "Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening, before I have avenged myself on my enemies." So none of the troops tasted food.
All the army entered the woods, and there was honey on the ground.
They saw the honey flowing, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because the troops feared the oath.
But Jonathan had not heard his father's oath. He reached out the end of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the soldiers told him, "Your father bound the army with a solemn oath: 'Cursed be anyone who eats food today.'" And the troops were exhausted.
Jonathan said, "My father has made trouble for the country. See how my eyes brightened when I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better if the troops had eaten today some of the plunder! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been even greater?"
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and the troops were very weary.
The troops pounced on the plunder and took sheep, cattle, and calves, and slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood.
Then someone told Saul, "Look, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood." Saul said, "You have broken faith. Roll a large stone over here before me."

Then Saul said, "Go among the people and tell them, 'Each of you bring me your ox and your sheep, and slaughter them here and eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood.'" So that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar he built to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn, and not leave one of them." They said, "Do whatever seems best to you." But the priest said, "Let us approach God here."
Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You deliver them into Israel's hand?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and find out how this sin happened today.
As surely as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, even if the guilt lies with my son Jonathan, he must die." But no one said a word.
Saul said to all Israel, "You stand over there; I and my son Jonathan will stand over here." The people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."
Then Saul prayed to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Give a clear answer." Jonathan and Saul were chosen by lot, and the people went free.
Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was chosen.
Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." Jonathan replied, "I tasted a little honey with the end of the staff in my hand. And now I must die?"
Saul said, "May God deal with me, be it ever so severely, if you do not die, Jonathan."

But the people said to Saul, "Should Jonathan die—he who brought about this great deliverance in Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, because he did this with God's help." So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own land.

After Saul had assumed kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he inflicted punishment.
He fought valiantly and defeated the Amalekites, and delivered Israel from the hands of those who had plundered them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malki-Shua. The names of his two daughters were Merab the older and Michal the younger.
Saul's wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner son of Ner, whose father was Saul's uncle.
Saul's father was Kish, and Abner's father Ner was the son of Abiel.
There was fierce war with the Philistines throughout all the days of Saul, and whenever Saul saw any mighty man or warrior, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, "the LORD sent me to anoint you king over His people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD.
Thus says the LORD of hosts: I have noted what Amalek did to Israel, for he opposed them on the way when they came up from Egypt.
Now go and strike Amalek, and devote to destruction all that they have; do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey."
So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley.

Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them; for you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.
He took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted all the people to destruction with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep, the oxen, the fatlings, the lambs, and all that was good, and they were unwilling to devote them to destruction; but everything that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel:
"I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following Me and has not performed My commandments." And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night.
Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning, and it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself, then turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed are you by the LORD! I have performed the commandment of the LORD."
Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?"
Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed."
Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." And he said, "Speak."
Samuel said, "Although you consider yourself insignificant, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.'
Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do what is evil in the sight of the LORD?"
Saul said, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the devoted things, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."
Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has also rejected you from being king."
Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me, that I may bow down to the LORD."
Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you, for you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."
As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the hem of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you.
And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or relent, for He is not a man, that He should relent."
Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow down to the LORD your God."
So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed down to the LORD.
Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. And Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."
Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I have selected one of his sons to be king for Me."
Samuel said, "How can I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me." The LORD answered, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD.'
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I designate."
Samuel did what the the LORD had said and went to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came trembling to meet him and asked, "Do you come in peace?"
"Peace," he replied. "I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice." Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and thought, "Surely the the LORD's anointed stands here before Him."

But the the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look at his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. Man does not see what the the LORD sees; man looks at the outward appearance, but the the LORD looks at the heart."
Then Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel. But Samuel said, "The The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Then Jesse had Shammah pass by, but Samuel said, "The The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel said to Jesse, "The The LORD has not chosen any of these."

Samuel asked Jesse, "Are these all the sons you have?" "There is still the youngest," Jesse answered, "but he is tending the sheep." Samuel said, "Send for him; we will not sit down until he arrives."
So Jesse sent for him and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. Then the the LORD said, "Rise and anoint him, for he is the one."
So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers. From that day on, the Spirit of the the LORD came powerfully upon David. Then Samuel left and went to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of the the LORD had departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the the LORD tormented him.
Saul's servants said to him, "Surely an evil spirit from God is tormenting you.
Let our lord command your servants who are here before you to seek out a man who plays the lyre. Whenever the evil spirit from God comes upon you, he will play, and you will feel better."
Saul said to his servants, "Find me someone who plays well and bring him to me."

One of the servants answered, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the lyre. He is a mighty warrior, valiant in battle, discerning in speech, and handsome. And the the LORD is with him."
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse, saying, "Send me your son David, who is with the sheep."
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them with his son David to Saul.
David came to Saul and entered his service. Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer.
Then Saul sent word to Jesse: "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my eyes."
Whenever the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, David would take his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for war and assembled at Socoh in Judah; they encamped between Socoh and Azekah in Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered and encamped in the Valley of Elah, and they drew up their battle line against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill, Israel stood on the opposite hill, and the valley lay between them.
A champion came out from the Philistine camp. His name was Goliath of Gath, and his height was six cubits and a span.
He wore a bronze helmet and a coat of scale armor weighing five thousand shekels of bronze.
He had bronze greaves on his legs and a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear resembled a weaver's beam, its iron head weighed six hundred shekels, and his shield-bearer walked before him.

He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.
If he is able to fight me and kill me, then we will be your servants; but if I prevail and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us."
The Philistine added, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, and we will fight together."
When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.
Now David was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, who had eight sons. In Saul's days the man was old and advanced in years.
The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the war: Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third.
David was the youngest, while the three oldest followed Saul.
David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine came forward morning and evening and took his stand.
Jesse said to his son David, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this roasted grain and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp for your brothers.
Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See how your brothers are doing, and bring back some token from them."
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines.

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with a keeper, took the supplies, and went as Jesse had commanded him. He reached the camp as the army was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up their battle lines against each other.
David left his baggage with the keeper of supplies, ran to the ranks, and greeted his brothers.
While he was speaking with them, the champion Goliath the Philistine from Gath came up from the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before, and David heard them.
All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were greatly afraid.

The men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man coming up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. The king will enrich with great riches the man who kills him; he will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel."

David said to the men standing by him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"
The people answered him as before, "So shall it be done for the man who kills him."

When Eliab, his oldest brother, heard him speaking to the men, his anger burned against David, and he said, "Why have you come down here? With whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart; you have come down only to see the battle."
David said, "What have I done now? Was it not just a word?"
He turned away from him toward another and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him as they had at first.
When the words that David spoke were heard, they were reported to Saul, and he sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him; your servant will go and fight this Philistine."
Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."
David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. When a lion or a bear came and took a lamb from the flock,
I went out after it and struck it and delivered the lamb from its mouth. If it rose against me, I seized it by its beard, struck it, and killed it.
Your servant has struck down both lion and bear, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God."
David added, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said, "Go, and may the LORD be with you."
Saul clothed David with his own armor: he put a bronze helmet on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail.
David strapped his sword over the armor and tried to walk, for he had not tested them. David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David took them off.
He took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook; he put them in the shepherd's bag he had, with his sling in his hand, and drew near to the Philistine.
The Philistine came on and drew near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him.
When the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth—ruddy and handsome.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."
David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with sword, spear, and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. I will give the carcasses of the Philistine host to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.
And all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear; for the battle is the LORD's, and He will give you into our hands."
When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.
Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with sling and stone; he struck the Philistine and killed him, though there was no sword in David's hand.
David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
The men of Israel and Judah rose up and shouted and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron. The slain Philistines lay along the way to Shaaraim, even as far as Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites returned from chasing the Philistines and plundered their camp.
David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put his weapons in his tent.
When Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Whose son is this youth, Abner?" Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know."
The king said, "Inquire whose son the young man is."
When David returned from striking down the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul with the Philistine's head in his hand.
Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
After David had finished speaking to Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were bound together, and Jonathan loved him as he loved his own life.
Saul took David into his service that day and would not let him return to his father's house.
Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan stripped off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, sword, bow, and belt.
So David went out wherever Saul sent him and succeeded in all he did, and Saul appointed him over the men of war. The appointment pleased all the people and Saul's servants as well.

When the troops returned home after David had killed the Philistine, women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul, singing and dancing with tambourines, joyful songs, and stringed instruments.
As the women danced, they sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."
Saul was very angry, and the saying displeased him. He said, "They have credited David with tens of thousands, but me with only thousands. What more can he have but the kingdom?"
From that day on, Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God came forcefully upon Saul. He prophesied inside the house while David played the harp, as he did each day. Now there was a spear in Saul's hand,
and Saul hurled it, thinking, "I will pin David to the wall." But David eluded him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.
So Saul removed David from his presence and made him commander of a thousand. David led the troops on their military campaigns.
David was successful in all his ways, for the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw that David was highly successful, he was afraid of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he led them on their military campaigns.

Then Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "My hand need not be against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him."
David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should be the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came for Merab, Saul's daughter, to be given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite as wife.
Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David, and when they told Saul, the matter pleased him.

Saul thought, "I will give her to him, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him." So Saul said to David, "For a second time you may become my son-in-law today."
Then Saul ordered his servants, "Speak to David privately and tell him, 'Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now then, become the king's son-in-law.'"
Saul's servants spoke these words to David. David replied, "Does it seem to you a small thing to become the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed."
The servants reported these words to Saul.

Then Saul replied, "Tell David, 'The king desires no dowry except a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take vengeance on the king's enemies.'" Now Saul intended to cause David's death at the hands of the Philistines.
When the servants reported this to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. The appointed time had not yet passed.

David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and presented them as the full number to the king, so that he might become the king's son-in-law. Then Saul gave his daughter Michal to David in marriage.
When Saul realized that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved him,
he became even more afraid of David. And Saul remained David's enemy for the rest of his days.
Then whenever the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul's servants, so that his name was highly esteemed.
Saul communicated to his son Jonathan and to all his courtiers his command that David be put to death; nevertheless, Jonathan, Saul’s son, cherished David with profound affection.
Jonathan warned David, “My father Saul is intent upon killing you. Therefore, exercise vigilance at daybreak: remain in a concealed location and hide yourself.”
He added, “I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will discourse with my father concerning you. Then I will observe the outcome and report it to you.”
Jonathan extolled David to Saul his father, saying, “Let not the king sin against his servant David, for he has committed no sin against you, and his deeds have redounded greatly to your benefit.

He staked his life and struck down the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great deliverance for all Israel. You witnessed it and rejoiced. Why then would you sin by shedding innocent blood and slaying David without cause?”
Saul heeded Jonathan’s counsel and swore by the LORD: “As the LORD lives, David shall not be executed.”
Jonathan summoned David and rehearsed all these words to him. Then Jonathan escorted David into Saul’s presence, and David ministered before him as he had formerly.
Once more war erupted, and David went forth and fought the Philistines. He inflicted upon them a crushing defeat, and they fled before him.
Moreover, an evil spirit from the LORD afflicted Saul while he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David played the lyre.
Saul sought to transfix David against the wall with the spear, but David evaded Saul; the spear struck the wall, and David fled and escaped that night.

Saul dispatched messengers to David’s house to surveil him and to kill him in the morning. Michal, David’s wife, alerted him, “If you do not preserve your life tonight, tomorrow you will be executed.”
Accordingly, Michal lowered David through the window, and he fled and escaped.
Michal took the household idol and laid it in the bed, placed a goat-hair bolster at its head, and covered it with a garment.
When Saul sent messengers to seize David, she claimed, “He is ill.”
Saul then sent messengers to inspect David, commanding, “Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may put him to death.”
When the messengers entered, they found the household idol in the bed, with the goat-hair bolster at its head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me in this manner and released my enemy, so that he has escaped?” Michal answered Saul, “He said to me, ‘Let me go! Why should I kill you?’”
David fled and escaped, and he went to Samuel at Ramah and recounted to him everything Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel departed and took up residence in Naioth.
It was reported to Saul, “David is in Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to apprehend David, but when they observed the band of prophets prophesying, with Samuel presiding over them, the Spirit of God descended upon them, and they too prophesied.
When this was reported to Saul, he dispatched another contingent of messengers, and they likewise prophesied. Saul sent a third contingent of thirty men, and they also prophesied.
Then he himself traveled to Ramah and arrived at the great cistern in Secu. He inquired, “Where are Samuel and David?” Someone replied, “They are in Naioth in Ramah.”
So he proceeded to Naioth in Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him as well. He continued onward, prophesying as he went, until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He likewise stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel, and he lay naked throughout that day and that night. Consequently, people say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came before Jonathan, saying, "What have I done? What is my guilt, and what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?"

Jonathan said to him, "May that never be! You shall not die. Look, my father does nothing, great or small, without disclosing it to me. Why then should my father hide this matter from me? It is not so."

David said, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your sight, and he has said, 'Let Jonathan not know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the the LORD lives and as your soul lives, I am only a step away from death."
Jonathan said to him, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you."
David said to Jonathan, "Look, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit with the king to eat. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field until the third day at evening.
If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem, his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the family.'
If he says, 'It is well,' your servant shall have peace; but if he is very angry, then know that evil is determined by him.

Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the the LORD with you. But if there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself; for why should you bring me to your father?"
Jonathan said, "May that never be! If I knew that evil were determined by my father to come upon you, would I not tell you?"
David said to him, "Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?"
Jonathan said, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, "As the the LORD God of Israel lives, when I have sounded out my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, and look, if there is goodwill toward David, then I will send to you and disclose it to you.

But if my father is determined to harm you, may the the LORD punish Jonathan, and even more, if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in peace. And may the the LORD be with you, as He has been with my father.
And if I am still alive, show me the the LORD's kindness, so that I do not die;
but do not cut off your kindness from my house forever, not even when the the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the the LORD hold David's enemies accountable."
And Jonathan made David swear again, because he loved him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day you shall go down quickly and come to the place where you hid yourself on the day of the incident, and remain by the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to the side, as though I shot at a target.

And look, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you; take them,' then come, for there is peace for you, and no danger, as the the LORD lives.
But if I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the the LORD has sent you away.
And as for the matter which we have spoken of, look, the the LORD is between you and me forever."
So David hid in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food.
The king sat on his seat as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan arose, and Abner sat by Saul, but David's place was empty.
Yet Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him; he is not clean; surely he is unclean."
On the next day, the second day of the month, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem.

He said, 'Let me go, please, for our family has a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me. And now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away, please, that I may see my brothers.' Therefore he has not come to the king's table."

Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he is doomed to die."
Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
Then Saul hurled the spear at him to strike him, so Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.
And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointed time with David, and a little boy was with him.
He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy came to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, Jonathan cried after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?"
Then Jonathan cried after the boy, "Hurry, make haste, do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master.
But the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go, carry them to the city."

As soon as the boy was gone, David arose from the south side and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, until David wept even more.

Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, since we have sworn both of us in the name of the the LORD, saying, 'The The LORD be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he arose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech trembled when he met David and asked him, "Why are you alone, with no one accompanying you?"

David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has commanded me on a matter and told me, 'Let no one know anything about the mission I am sending you on or the orders I have given you.' I have directed the young men to a specified place.
Now, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you can provide."
Ahimelech answered David, "I have no ordinary bread on hand; there is only consecrated bread, provided the young men have kept themselves from women."
David answered the priest, "Women have indeed been kept from us, as is customary when I set out. The young men's bodies are holy even on missions that are not holy, and how much more so today!"

So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, because no bread was there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD to be replaced by hot bread on the day it was taken away.
Now one of Saul's servants was there that day, detained before the LORD; his name was Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul's shepherds.
David said to Ahimelech, "Do you have a spear or sword on hand? I have brought neither my sword nor my equipment, because the king's business was urgent."

The priest replied, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want it, take it, for there is no other here." David said, "There is none like it; give it to me."
David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish, king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Is it not he of whom they sing in the dances, 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"
David took these words to heart and was very afraid of Achish, king of Gath.
So he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness while in their presence; he scribbled on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "Look, you see a man behaving like a madman. Why did you bring him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this one to rave before me? Must this man come into my house?"
David left that place and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and his father’s entire household heard about it, they went down to him there.
Everyone who was in distress, everyone who had a creditor, and everyone who was bitter in soul gathered to him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.
From there David went to Mizpeh in Moab and said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me.”
So he brought them before the king of Moab, and they stayed with him throughout the time David remained in the stronghold.
Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not remain in the stronghold; leave and go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went into the forest of Hereth.
When Saul heard that David and the men with him had been discovered, he was sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, spear in hand, with all his servants standing around him.

Saul said to the servants standing by him, “Listen now, Benjaminites! Will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards? Will he make every one of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?

For all of you have conspired against me, and no one tells me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or tells me that my son has incited my servant to ambush me, as is the case today.”
Then Doeg the Edomite, who was standing among Saul’s servants, answered, “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob.
Ahimelech inquired of the the LORD for him, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
So the king sent for Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and for all his father’s household, the priests of Nob, and they all came to the king.
Saul said, “Listen now, son of Ahitub.” “Here I am, my lord,” Ahimelech replied.
Saul said to him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me by giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God for him, so that he rises against me to lie in wait, as he does today?”
Ahimelech answered the king, “And who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house?

Have I today begun to inquire of God for him? Far be it from me! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all my father’s house, for your servant knew nothing of all this, whether small or great.”
The king said, “You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house.”

The king said to the guards standing by him, “Turn and kill the priests of the the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and because they knew he was fleeing and did not disclose it to me.” But the king’s servants were unwilling to stretch out their hand to strike the priests of the the LORD.
The king said to Doeg, “You turn and strike the priests.” So Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests, and that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
He also put Nob, the city of the priests, to the sword—men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep.
But one son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled to David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the the LORD.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I am responsible for the deaths of all your father’s household.
Stay with me; do not be afraid, for whoever seeks your life seeks mine; you will be safe with me.”
They reported to David, "The Philistines are attacking Keilah and plundering the threshing floors."
David inquired of the LORD, "Should I go and attack these Philistines?" The LORD replied, "Go and attack the Philistines and rescue Keilah."
David's men said to him, "We are already afraid here in Judah. How much more will we be if we go to Keilah against the Philistine forces?"
David again inquired of the LORD. The LORD answered him, "Get up and go down to Keilah, for I am giving the Philistines into your power."
David and his men went to Keilah, fought the Philistines, drove off their livestock, inflicted a heavy defeat on them, and rescued the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he brought an ephod with him.
Saul learned that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, "God has delivered him into my power, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars."
Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David knew that Saul was secretly plotting harm against him. He said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."
David said, "The LORD, God of Israel, Your servant has heard that Saul is coming to Keilah to destroy the city because of me."
David asked, "Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me to him? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? The LORD, God of Israel, please tell Your servant." The LORD said, "He will come down."
David asked, "Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men to Saul?" The LORD said, "They will surrender you."
David and his men, about six hundred, got up and left Keilah, going wherever they could. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he abandoned the campaign.
David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. Saul sought him every day, but God did not deliver him into Saul's power.
David realized that Saul had come out to seek to kill him. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.
Jonathan son of Saul went to David at Horesh and encouraged him in God.
He said to him, "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will not capture you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you. Even my father Saul knows that."
The two made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, while Jonathan went home.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon?
Now, O king, come down whenever you desire; our part is to surrender him into the king's power."
Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me.
Go, make certain, learn, and locate the place where he stays and who has seen him there, for I am told he is very cunning.
See and learn all the hiding places where he hides, then come back to me with a firm report; I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah."
They set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to seek David. When David was told, he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. Saul heard and pursued David into the wilderness of Maon.
Saul was on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other. David was hurrying to get away from Saul, while Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them.
A messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have invaded the land."
Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape.
David went up from there and stayed in the strongholds of En Gedi.
When Saul returned from his pursuit of the Philistines, he was informed, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.”
Saul selected three thousand choice men from all Israel and set out to seek David and his men among the crags of the wild goats.
He came to the sheepfolds along the road; there was a cave there, and Saul entered it to relieve himself. David and his men, meanwhile, were sitting in the innermost recesses of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Behold, this is the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I am giving your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as seems good in your eyes.’” David rose and covertly cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
Afterward David’s conscience smote him because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, or stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
With these words David restrained his men and did not allow them to rise against Saul. Then Saul rose from the cave and went on his way.
Afterward David arose, left the cave, and called after Saul, saying, “My lord the king.” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed his face to the ground and prostrated himself.
David said to Saul, “Why do you heed the words of men who say, ‘David seeks your harm’?

Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD delivered you into my hand in the cave; and though someone urged me to kill you, I spared you and said, ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed.’

And see, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand; for by cutting off the corner of your robe I did not kill you. Know and see that there is no evil or transgression in my hand, and I have not sinned against you, yet you hunt my life to take it.
May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me on you; but my hand shall not be against you.
As the proverb of the ancients says, ‘Out of the wicked comes forth wickedness’; but my hand shall not be against you.
After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog? After a flea?
May the LORD therefore be judge, and judge between me and you, and see and plead my cause, and deliver me out of your hand.”
When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.
He said to David, “You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me with good, whereas I have repaid you with evil.
You have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that when the LORD gave me into your hand you did not kill me.
For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? And may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day.
And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand.
Swear to me now by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants after me and that you will not destroy my name from my father’s house.”
David swore to Saul. Saul went to his house, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Now Samuel died, and all Israel assembled, mourned for him, and buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
A certain man in Maon had property in Carmel. He was very wealthy, with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
His name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was an intelligent and beautiful woman, but her husband was harsh and evil in his dealings; he was a Calebite.
While David was in the wilderness, he heard that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
So David sent ten young men and instructed them, "Go up to Carmel, find Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Say to him: 'Long life to you! Peace be to you and to your house and to all that is yours.'
Now I hear that you are shearing sheep. When your shepherds were with us, we did not mistreat them, and nothing of theirs was missing the whole time they were in Carmel.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a festive day. Please give whatever you have on hand to your servants and to your son David.'"
When David's young men arrived, they said all this to Nabal in David's name and then waited.
Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters.
Should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers and give it to men coming from who knows where?"
So David's men turned around and went back. When they arrived, they reported every word.

David said to his men, "Each of you strap on your sword!" So each man strapped on his sword, and David also strapped on his. About four hundred men went up with David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies.
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he berated them.
Yet these men were very good to us. We were not mistreated, and we did not miss anything the whole time we were out in the fields with them.
They were a wall around us both night and day, the whole time we were with them tending our sheep.
Now consider carefully what you should do, because disaster is about to fall on our master and on his whole household. He is such a worthless man that no one can talk to him."

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
Then she said to her young men, "Go on ahead of me; I will follow you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
As she rode her donkey down a mountain trail, hidden from view, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she met them.
Now David had said, "Surely in vain I have guarded all that this man has in the wilderness, so that nothing of his was missing. He has repaid me evil for good.
May God deal with David's enemies, be it ever so severely, if by morning I leave alive one male of all who belong to him!"
When Abigail saw David, she hurried and dismounted from her donkey, fell facedown before David, and bowed to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, "My lord, let the blame be on me alone. Please let your servant speak to you; hear the words of your servant.

Please do not let my lord pay attention to this worthless man Nabal, for he is just like his name. His name means Fool, and folly is with him. But I, your servant, did not see the young men my lord sent.

Now then, my lord, as surely as the LORD lives and as you live, since the LORD has kept you from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand, may your enemies and those who seek evil against my lord be like Nabal.
Now let this gift your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord.
Please forgive your servant's offense, for the LORD will certainly make my lord a lasting house, because my lord fights the LORD's battles, and no wrongdoing will be found in you as long as you live.

If anyone rises to pursue you and seek your life, then your life will be bound securely in the bundle of the living with the LORD your God, but He will sling out the lives of your enemies as from the pocket of a sling.
When the LORD has done for my lord all the good He has promised, and has appointed you ruler over Israel,
then my lord will not have this stumbling block or a guilty conscience over needless bloodshed or avenging himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, remember your servant."
David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!
Blessed be your discernment, and blessed be you, for today you have kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself with my own hand.

Otherwise, as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from harming you, if you had not come quickly to meet me, then by morning not a single male would have been left to Nabal.
Then David accepted from her hand what she had brought him and said to her, 'Go home in peace. See, I have listened to your voice and granted your request.'"

When Abigail came to Nabal, he was holding a feast in his house like the feast of a king. Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until morning light.
In the morning, when the wine had left Nabal, his wife told him everything. His heart failed within him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has judged the case of Nabal's insult to me and has kept His servant from doing evil. The LORD has brought Nabal's wickedness down on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife.
When David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to take you to him as his wife."
She arose, bowed facedown to the ground, and said, "Here is your servant, ready to wash the feet of my lord's servants."
Then Abigail hurried and rose, mounted a donkey, and followed David's messengers, with her five female servants walking behind her. And she became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, so both of them were his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is David not hiding on the hill of Hachilah, facing the wasteland?”
So Saul rose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to search for David.
Saul camped beside the road on the hill of Hachilah, overlooking the wasteland, while David remained in the wilderness. When David saw that Saul had come after him into the wilderness,
he sent out spies and learned for certain that Saul had indeed come.

Then David rose and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw the spot where Saul lay, along with Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying in the camp, and the troops were camped around him.
David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” Abishai said, “I will go down with you.”
So David and Abishai came to the troops by night. There lay Saul, sleeping in the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head. Abner and the troops were lying around him.
Abishai said to David, “God has delivered your enemy into your hand today. Now let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear; I will not need to strike him twice.”
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him, for who can lay a hand on the the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?
As the the LORD lives, either the the LORD will strike him down, or his day will come and he will die, or he will go down into battle and perish.
The LORD forbid that I should stretch out my hand against the the LORD’s anointed. Now, please take the spear that is at his head and the water jar, and let us go.”
So David took the spear and the water jar from beside Saul’s head, and they went away. No one saw or knew or woke, for they were all asleep; a deep sleep from the the LORD had fallen on them.
David crossed to the other side and stood on top of the hill at a distance; there was a wide space between them.
David called out to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you that calls to the king?”
David said to Abner, “You are a man, and who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not guarded your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord.

This thing that you have done is not good. As the the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not guarded your lord, the the LORD’s anointed. And now see where the king’s spear is and the water jar that was at his head.”
Saul recognized David’s voice and said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” David said, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
David said, “Why does my lord pursue his servant? What have I done? What wrong have I done?”

David said, “Now therefore, please, my lord the king, hear the words of your servant. If the the LORD has stirred you up against me, let Him accept an offering. But if it is men, they are cursed before the the LORD, for they have driven me out today from sharing in the the LORD’s inheritance, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’”
David said, “Now do not let me be killed far from the presence of the the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to hunt a single flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
Saul said, “I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will harm you no more, because my life was precious in your eyes today. Behold, I have acted foolishly and erred greatly.”
David answered, “Here is the king’s spear. Let one of the young men come over and take it.
The The LORD will repay each man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not stretch out my hand against the the LORD’s anointed.”
David said, “And as your life was highly valued in my eyes today, so may my life be highly valued in the eyes of the the LORD, and may He deliver me from all trouble.”
Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son David! You will surely do great things and will surely prevail.” Then David went on his way, and Saul returned to his place.

David said to himself, "Sooner or later Saul will destroy me; I have no prospect here but ruin. If I flee to Philistine territory, Saul will abandon his search for me throughout Israel, and I will slip from his grasp."
So David and the six hundred men with him crossed over to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David and his men settled in Gath with Achish, each man with his household; David brought his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the Carmelite widow of Nabal.
When Saul learned that David had fled to Gath, he ceased searching for him.
David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, grant me a place in one of the rural towns, where I may live. Why should your servant remain in the royal city with you?"
So Achish gave him Ziklag that very day, and from that time Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah.
David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, peoples who had inhabited the land from Shur to Egypt since ancient times.
He devastated the region and left no one alive, neither man nor woman; he carried off sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing, then returned to Achish.
Achish asked, "Where did you raid today?" David replied, "Against the Negev of Judah, against the Negev of the Jerahmeelites, and against the Negev of the Kenites."
David spared no man or woman who might be brought to Gath, lest they report what he had done and the policy he maintained throughout his time in Philistine territory.
Achish trusted David and concluded, "He has made himself utterly detestable to his people Israel; therefore he will serve me forever."
In those days, the Philistines gathered their forces for war against Israel. Achish said to David, "You must understand that you and your men will march out with me in the camp."
David said to Achish, "Then you know what your servant will do." Achish replied, "Then I will make you my bodyguard for life."
Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. Saul had removed the mediums and the spiritists from the land.
The Philistines assembled and camped at Shunem, while Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine camp, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by the Urim, or by the prophets.
Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman who is a medium, so that I may go to her and consult her." His servants said to him, "There is a woman who is a medium at En-dor."
Saul disguised himself, put on other clothes, and went with two men. They came to the woman at night. He said, "Please divine for me by the spirit, and bring up for me whomever I name to you."
The woman said to him, "You know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the spiritists from the land. Why then are you setting a trap for my life, to bring about my death?"
Saul swore to her by the LORD, saying, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing."
The woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. The woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul."
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman said to Saul, "I see a divine being coming up out of the earth."
He said, "What is his appearance?" She said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." Then Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are making war against me, and God has departed from me and no longer answers me, neither by prophets nor by dreams. Therefore I have called you, to tell me what I should do."
Samuel said, "Why do you ask me, when the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?
The LORD has done to you as He spoke through me: the LORD has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your neighbor David.
Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out His fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this to you today.

Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel, along with you, into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will also deliver the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines."
Then Saul quickly fell full length on the ground and was very afraid because of Samuel's words. Moreover, there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no food all day and all night.

The woman came to Saul and saw that he was greatly terrified. She said to him, "Behold, your maidservant has obeyed your voice, and I have put my life in my hand and have listened to your words, which you spoke to me.
Now therefore, please listen to the voice of your maidservant, and let me set a piece of bread before you, and eat, so that you may have strength when you go on your way."
He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants and the woman urged him, and he listened to their voice. He rose from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She hurried and slaughtered it, took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread.
She brought it before Saul and before his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.
The Philistines mustered all their forces at Aphek, while Israel encamped beside the spring in Jezreel.
As the Philistine rulers advanced with their contingents of hundreds and thousands, David and his men brought up the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders asked, “What are these Hebrews doing here?” Achish answered, “Is this not David, servant of Saul, king of Israel? He has been with me for days and years, and I have found no fault in him from the day he defected until now.”

But the Philistine commanders were furious with Achish and said, “Send the man back to the place you assigned him. He must not march with us into battle, or he may turn against us in the fight. What better way could he regain his master's favor than with the heads of our men?
Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

Then Achish summoned David and said, “As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright, and your service with me in the camp has been good in my sight, for I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until now. Nevertheless, the rulers are not pleased with you.
Now turn back and go in peace, so that you do not displease the Philistine rulers.”
David asked, “But what have I done? What have you found against your servant from the day I came to you until now? Why may I not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish replied, “I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, ‘He must not go up with us into battle.’
Now then, rise early in the morning with your master's servants who came with you, and as soon as you are up and it is light, depart.”
So David and his men rose early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines advanced to Jezreel.
