On the third day, David and his men arrived at Ziklag, but the Amalekites had raided the Negev and Ziklag, attacking Ziklag and burning it to the ground.
They had taken captive the women there, young and old alike; they killed no one, but carried them off and went their way.
When David and his men reached the city, they found it burned, and their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
Then David and the people with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
David's two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, had been taken captive.

David was in great distress because the people were embittered and spoke of stoning him, for every man was bitter in soul over his sons and daughters; but David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
Then David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue this raiding band? Shall I overtake them?" And He answered, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives."
So David set out with his six hundred men and came to the Brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed.
Two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook, so David continued the pursuit with four hundred men.
They found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him water to drink and bread to eat,
and they gave him a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. After he had eaten, his strength returned, for he had eaten no bread and drunk no water for three days and three nights.
David asked him, "To whom do you belong, and where are you from?" He replied, "I am an Egyptian, the servant of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me three days ago because I became ill.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites and the territory belonging to Judah and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag."
David asked him, "Will you lead me down to this raiding band?" He answered, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will lead you down to this band."

So he led him down, and there the Amalekites were spread out over the countryside, eating, drinking, and celebrating because of the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from Judah.
David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not one of them escaped, except four hundred young men who fled on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing was missing, small or great, sons or daughters, or any of the plunder; David brought back everything.
David took all the flocks and herds, and his men drove them ahead of the other livestock, saying, "This is David's spoil."

When David reached the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and had been left at the Brook Besor, they came out to meet him and the people with him. David approached them and greeted them.

But all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil we recovered, except each man's wife and children. Let them take them and go."
David replied, "My brothers, you shall not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hand the raiding band that came against us.
Who would listen to you in this matter? The share of the one who goes down to battle shall be the same as the share of the one who stays with the supplies; they shall share alike."
From that day forward, David made this a statute and ordinance for Israel, and it stands to this day.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah, his friends, saying, "Here is a gift for you from the spoil of the LORD's enemies."
He sent it to those in Bethel, Ramoth of the Negev, Jattir,
Racal, the cities of the Jerahmeelites, the cities of the Kenites,
Hebron, and to all the places where David and his men had roamed.
Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the Israelites fled before them, and the men of Israel fell slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines overtook Saul and his sons and killed his sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.
The battle pressed hard against Saul; the archers came upon him, and he was severely wounded by them.

Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised men come, thrust me through, and abuse me.” But his armor-bearer would not do it, because he was greatly afraid; therefore Saul took the sword and fell on it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell on his sword and died with him.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that day.

When the Israelites on the other side of the valley and beyond the Jordan saw that the Israelites had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled; and the Philistines came and occupied them.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They beheaded him, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the Philistine country to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among the people.
They placed his armor in the temple of Ashtoreth and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.
When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all the valiant men rose, marched through the night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. They came to Jabesh and burned them there.
Then they took their bones and buried them beneath the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.
After Saul’s death, David returned from striking down the Amalekites and remained in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man arrived from Saul’s camp with his clothes torn and dust on his head; when he reached David, he fell facedown in homage.
“Where have you come from?” David asked him. “I have escaped from the Israelite camp,” he replied.
“What was the outcome?” David asked. “Please tell me.” “The troops fled from the battle,” he replied. “Many of the people fell and died. And Saul and his son Jonathan are dead.”
Then David asked the young man who brought the report, “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?”
“I happened to be on Mount Gilboa,” the young man answered, “and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and horsemen closing in on him.
When he turned around and saw me, he called out to me, and I answered, ‘Here I am.’
‘Who are you?’ he asked. ‘An Amalekite,’ I answered.
Then he said to me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, but my life still lingers.’

So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that after he had fallen he could not survive. And I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.”
Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and all the men who were with him did the same.
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
Then David asked the young man who had brought him the report, “Where are you from?” “I am the son of a foreigner,” he answered. “I am an Amalekite.”
David asked him, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the the LORD’s anointed?”
Then David called one of his young men and said, “Go, strike him down!” So he struck him down, and he died.
For David had said to him, “Your blood be on your own head, because your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I killed the the LORD’s anointed.’”
Then David took up this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan,
and he ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:
“Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!
Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
O mountains of Gilboa, may you have neither dew nor rain, nor fields that yield offerings. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil.
“From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty.
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and pleasant in life, were not parted in death. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions.
O daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and finery, who decked your necks with gold jewelry.
“How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights.
I am distressed for you, Jonathan my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”
After this, David inquired of the LORD, “Shall I go up to one of the cities of Judah?” The LORD said to him, “Go up.” David asked, “Where shall I go up?” He answered, “To Hebron.”
So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal’s widow from Carmel.
David brought up the men who were with him, each with his household, and they settled in the cities of Hebron.
The men of Judah came and anointed David king over the house of Judah. They also told David, “The men of Jabesh-gilead are the ones who buried Saul.”
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said, “Blessed are you to the LORD, because you have shown this kindness to Saul your lord by burying him.
Now may the LORD show kindness and faithfulness to you; I too will reward you for this good deed, because you have done it.
Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them.”
But Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him across to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David.
David reigned over the house of Judah in Hebron for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s servants went out and met them by the pool of Gibeon; they sat down, these on one side of the pool and those on the other.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men rise and compete before us.” Joab said, “Let them rise.”
Then they rose and crossed over by number: twelve for Benjamin and for Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David’s servants.
Each man seized his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, so they fell together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, in Gibeon.
The battle grew very fierce that day; Abner and the men of Israel were defeated before David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there—Joab, Abishai, and Asahel—and Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.
Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went he did not turn to the right or to the left from following him.
Abner looked behind him and asked, “Are you Asahel?” He answered, “I am.”
Abner said to him, “Turn aside to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his armor.” But Asahel refused to turn aside from following him.
Abner said again to Asahel, “Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to Joab your brother?”

He refused to turn aside, so Abner struck him with the blunt end of his spear beneath the fifth rib; the spear came out behind him, and he fell and died there. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel fell and died stood still.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. The sun was going down when they reached the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites rallied behind Abner, formed a single band, and stood on top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab, “Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you not tell the people to turn back from pursuing their brothers?”
Joab answered, “As God lives, if you had not spoken, the men would have kept pursuing their brothers until morning.”
Then Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people stopped; they no longer pursued Israel, and they ceased from fighting.
Abner and his men marched all night through the Arabah; they crossed the Jordan, went through all Bithron, and came to Mahanaim.
Joab returned from pursuing Abner and gathered all the people. Nineteen of David’s servants were missing, besides Asahel.
But David’s servants had struck down three hundred sixty men of Benjamin and Abner’s forces, and they died.
They took up Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
A long war raged between the house of Saul and the house of David, and while David grew steadily stronger, Saul's house grew steadily weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel;
his second was Chileab, by Abigail, the widow of Nabal the Carmelite; the third was Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur;
the fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital;
and the sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David's wife. All these were born to David in Hebron.
While war continued between the houses of Saul and David, Abner was consolidating his power in Saul's house.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, and Ish-Bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you slept with my father's concubine?"

Abner grew very angry at Ish-Bosheth's words and replied, "Am I some contemptible dog of Judah? To this day I have shown steadfast loyalty to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and I have not handed you over to David; yet today you accuse me over a woman.
May God deal with Abner, and worse, if I do not do for David exactly what the LORD has sworn to him:
to transfer the kingdom from Saul's house and establish David's throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-Bosheth could not answer Abner a single word, for he feared him.
Then Abner sent messengers to David, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and I will use my influence to bring all Israel over to you."
David replied, "Good. I will make a covenant with you, but I require one thing of you: you will not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see me."
David also sent messengers to Ish-Bosheth son of Saul, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred Philistine foreskins."
So Ish-Bosheth sent and took her from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband followed her, weeping all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go back," and he went back.
Abner conferred with the elders of Israel and said, "For some time now you have been seeking David as king over you.
Now then, act on it, for the LORD has said of David, 'By the hand of My servant David I will save My people Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies.'"
Abner also spoke to the Benjaminites, and then he went to Hebron to tell David everything that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin approved.
Abner and twenty men with him came to David at Hebron, and David prepared a feast for Abner and his men.

Abner said to David, "Let me go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so that they may make a covenant with you, and you may reign over all that your heart desires." Then David sent Abner away, and he departed in peace.
Just then David's servants and Joab returned from a raid, bringing much plunder with them. Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, for David had sent him away in peace.
When Joab and all the troops with him arrived, they told him, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away in peace."
Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Look, Abner came to you; why did you send him away so that he could leave in peace?
You know Abner son of Ner: he came to deceive you, to learn your movements and your plans, and to find out everything you are doing."
After Joab left David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, who brought him back from the well of Sirah; David did not know about it.

When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside at the gate, as though to speak with him privately, and there stabbed him in the stomach. So Abner died in revenge for the blood of Asahel, Joab's brother.
When David heard of it later, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

Let the guilt fall on Joab's head and on all his father's house, and may Joab's house never be without one who has a discharge, or is a leper, or leans on a staff, or falls by the sword, or lacks bread."
Joab and his brother Abishai had killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle.
David said to Joab and to all the people with him, "Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn for Abner." And King David himself walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron, and the king wept aloud at Abner's tomb; all the people wept as well.
The king sang a lament over Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not fettered; you fell as a man falls before wicked men." Then all the people wept over him again.
All the people urged David to eat something while it was still day, but David took an oath, saying, "May God do to me, and more, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down."
All the people noticed this, and it pleased them; everything the king did pleased all the people.
So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put Abner son of Ner to death.
The king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel?
I am weak today, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. The LORD will repay the evildoer according to his wickedness."
When Saul's son heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was thrown into consternation.
Now Saul's son had two men who were commanders of raiding parties—Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the Benjaminites—for Beeroth was counted as belonging to Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as resident aliens to this day.

Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who was lame in both feet; he was five years old when the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse lifted him and fled, but as she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, set out and came to the house of Ish-bosheth at the heat of the day, at noon, while he lay taking his midday rest.
They made their way into the inner room of the house, as if to fetch wheat, and struck him in the abdomen; then Rechab and his brother Baanah slipped away.
When they entered the house, he was lying on his bed in his bedroom; they struck him, killed him, beheaded him, took his head, and traveled all night by way of the Arabah.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. Today the LORD has given my lord the king vengeance on Saul and his line."
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As the LORD lives, who redeemed my soul from all distress,
when someone told me that Saul was dead, thinking he was bringing good news, I seized him and put him to death at Ziklag—that was the reward I gave him for his tidings.
How much more, then, when wicked men have murdered a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now demand his blood from your hand and purge you from the earth?"

Then David commanded his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hanged them beside the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner's tomb at Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "We are your own flesh and blood.
In the past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And the LORD said to you, 'You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will become their ruler.'"
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them before the LORD. Then they anointed David king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years:
seven years and six months in Hebron over Judah, and thirty-three years in Jerusalem over all Israel and Judah.

The king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, who lived there. The Jebusites said to David, "You will not get in here; even the blind and the lame can keep you out." They thought, "David cannot get in here."
Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion—the City of David.

On that day David said, "Whoever attacks the Jebusites must reach them through the water shaft to strike down the lame and blind who are David's enemies." That is why people say, "The blind and the lame will not enter the house."
So David lived in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built up the surrounding area, from the terraces inward.
David grew greater and greater, because the LORD God of Hosts was with him.
Then Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David.
David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.
After arriving from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went up to seek him out. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.
Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will You hand them over to me?" The LORD replied, "Go up, for I will surely hand the Philistines over to you."
So David went to Baal-perazim and defeated them there. He said, "As waters break out, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me." Therefore he named that place Baal-perazim.
The Philistines abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them off.
Once more the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD, and He said, "Do not march straight up, but circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees.
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out, because then the LORD has gone out before you to strike the Philistine army."
So David did as the LORD had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines from Gibeon all the way to Gezer.
David again assembled all the select men of Israel, thirty thousand strong.

Then David and all the people with him set out from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the Name, the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim.
They set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab on the hill; Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart,
with the ark of God, while Ahio walked ahead of it.
David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all kinds of wooden instruments, harps, lyres, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen had stumbled.
Then the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his irreverence, so he died there beside the ark of God.
David became angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah, and he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day.
David was afraid of the LORD that day and said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"
So David was unwilling to move the ark of the LORD to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
Thus the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.

When King David was told, "The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him because of the ark of God," he went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the City of David with rejoicing.
When those carrying the ark of the LORD had taken six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf.
David, wearing a linen ephod, danced with all his might before the LORD.
So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sound of the trumpet.
As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul's daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the LORD and set it in its place inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
When David had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts.
Then he distributed to every man and woman in the whole multitude of Israel a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. Then all the people departed, each to his own home.

As David returned to bless his household, Saul's daughter Michal came out to meet him and said, "How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today, uncovering himself in the sight of the maidservants of his subjects, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"
David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me over your father and all his house when He appointed me ruler over the LORD's people Israel—I will celebrate before the LORD.
I will become even more undignified than this, and I will be humiliated in my own eyes. But by these maidservants you spoke of, I will be held in honor."
And Michal daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death.
After the king was settled in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,
he said to Nathan the prophet, "Look, I am living in a house of cedar, but the ark of God remains in a tent."
Nathan replied to the king, "Go and do everything that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."
That night the word of the LORD came to Nathan:
"Go and say to My servant David, 'Will you build Me a house in which to dwell?
From the day I brought the Israelites up from Egypt until now, I have not lived in a house; rather, I have moved with them in a tent and a tabernacle.
Wherever I traveled with all Israel, did I ever ask any of the tribes I commanded to shepherd My people Israel why they had not built Me a cedar house?'"
"Now then, say this to My servant David: 'This is what the LORD of hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over My people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies before you. I will make your name great, like the names of the greatest on earth.

I will provide a place for My people Israel and plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. Wicked people will no longer oppress them, as they did at the beginning,
from the time I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD also declares to you that He will make a house for you.'"
"When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to Me. When he sins, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men.
But My steadfast love will not depart from him, as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
Your house and your kingdom will endure forever before you; your throne will be established forever."
Nathan told David all these words and this entire vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, Lord, the LORD, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
And yet this was a small thing in your sight, Lord, the LORD; you have also spoken about the future of your servant's house. Is this how you deal with mankind, Lord, the LORD?
What more can David say to you? You know your servant, Lord, the LORD.
For your word's sake and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness to make your servant know it.
"Therefore you are great, Lord, the LORD; for there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem for Himself as a people, to make a name for Himself, and to do for them great and awesome things by driving out nations and their gods before your people, whom you redeemed from Egypt?
You established your people Israel for yourself forever, and you, the LORD, became their God.
"Now, the LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and his house, and do as you have spoken.
Let your name be magnified forever, saying, 'The the LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and let the house of your servant David be established before you.
For you, the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you.
"And now, Lord, the LORD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.

Now therefore be pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, Lord, the LORD, have spoken, and with your blessing the house of your servant will be blessed forever."
After this, David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took the Philistines’ principal stronghold from their control.

David also defeated Moab. He forced its people to lie on the ground and measured them with a cord: two lengths he condemned to death, and one length he spared. Thus Moab became subject to David and paid him tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as Hadadezer was going to restore his authority at the Euphrates River.
David captured from him 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the chariot horses, sparing only a hundred for chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to assist Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 of them.
David then stationed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David also took the gold shields that had belonged to Hadadezer’s officers and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a great quantity of bronze.
When King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated Hadadezer’s entire army,

he sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and bless him, because David had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him. Hadadezer had been at war with Toi. Joram brought articles of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued:
Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and the spoil of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became subject to David. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
Thus David reigned over all Israel, administering justice and righteousness to all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar served as priests; Seraiah was scribe.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priests.
David asked, "Is there anyone still left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for Jonathan's sake?"
Now there was a servant of Saul's household whose name was Ziba, and they brought him to David. The king asked him, "Are you Ziba?" "I am your servant," Ziba replied.
The king said, "Is there no one still remaining from Saul's house to whom I can show God's kindness?" Ziba answered the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan, and he is lame in both feet."
"Where is he?" the king asked. Ziba said, "He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar."
So King David sent for him and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar.
When Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, he fell facedown and paid homage. David said, "Mephibosheth!" "Here is your servant," he replied.

David said to him, "Do not be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table."
Mephibosheth bowed low and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard to a dead dog like me?"
Then the king summoned Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "I have given to your master's son everything that belonged to Saul and to all his household."

"You and your sons and your servants are to farm the land for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master's son will have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master's son, will always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "Your servant will do everything my lord the king commands." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and everyone in Ziba's household became servants to Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table; he was lame in both feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent his servants to comfort him concerning his father, and they came to the land of the Ammonites.

But the Ammonite leaders said to Hanun their lord, “Do you really think David honors your father by sending comforters? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to spy out the city, scout it, and overthrow it?”
So Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments in half at the buttocks, and sent them away.
When this was reported to David, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were deeply humiliated. The king said, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back; then return.”

When the Ammonites realized they had made themselves contemptible to David, they sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob and Zobah—twenty thousand foot soldiers—as well as the king of Maacah with one thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
When David heard of it, he sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men.
The Ammonites came out and drew up in battle formation at the entrance of the gate, while the Syrians of Zobah and Rehob, and the men of Tob and Maacah, were by themselves in the open country.
When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and behind, he chose some of the best men in Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.
He put the rest of the troops under his brother Abishai and arrayed them against the Ammonites.
Joab said, “If the Syrians overpower me, come and help me; but if the Ammonites overpower you, I will come and help you.
Be strong! Let us be strong for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good in His eyes.”
So Joab and the people with him advanced to fight the Syrians, and they fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians had fled, they also fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the River, and they came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them.
When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought him.
But the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen. He also struck down Shobach, the commander of their army, and he died there.
When all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. So the Ammonites no longer received help from them.
In the spring, when kings march out to war, David sent Joab with his officers and all Israel. They ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem.
One evening David rose from his bed and walked on the roof of the royal palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and she was exceedingly beautiful.
David sent someone to inquire about her, and he was told, "Is this not Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite?"
David sent messengers to bring her; when she came to him, he slept with her. She had purified herself from her uncleanness, and then she returned home.
The woman conceived and sent word to David: "I am pregnant."
David sent word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." So Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah arrived, David asked how Joab was faring, how the troops were faring, and how the war was progressing.
Then David said to Uriah, "Go home and refresh yourself." Uriah left the palace, and a gift from the king followed him.
But Uriah slept at the entrance of the royal palace with all the king's servants; he did not go down to his house.
When David learned that Uriah had not gone down to his house, he asked Uriah, "Have you not just come from a campaign? Why did you not go home?"

Uriah answered David, "The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in shelters, my lord Joab and your servants are camping in the open field, and should I then go to my house to eat and drink and lie with my wife? As surely as you live and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing."
David said to Uriah, "Stay here today, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink in his presence and made him drunk. In the evening Uriah went out to lie on his bed among the king's servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Station Uriah in the front line where the fighting is fiercest, then fall back so that he may be struck down and die."
While Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were.
The men of the city came out and fought Joab; some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died as well.
Joab sent a messenger to report to David everything that had happened in the battle.
He instructed the messenger, "When you have finished reporting to the king all the details of the battle,
if the king grows angry and asks, 'Why did you approach the city so closely to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from the wall?'

then remind him, 'Who struck down Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Was it not a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go near the wall?' and then say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"
The messenger departed, came to David, and reported everything Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men overpowered us and came out against us in the open country, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.
The archers shot at your servants from the wall, and some of the king's servants died; your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."
David said to the messenger, "Tell Joab, 'Do not be distressed by this matter, for the sword devours one as well as another. Press the attack against the city and destroy it.' Encourage him."
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him.
After the mourning ended, David sent for her and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing David had done displeased the LORD.
The LORD sent Nathan to David, and when he came to him, he said, “In a single city there were two men, one rich and the other impoverished.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb, which he had bought. He nourished it, and it grew up with him and his children. It ate from his food, drank from his cup, lay in his bosom, and became like a daughter to him.

Now a traveler came to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take from his own flock or herd to prepare a meal for the guest who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
Then David’s anger burned greatly against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die.
And he must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and had no compassion.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul.
I gave you your master’s household and your master’s wives into your care; I gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have given you much more.

Why have you despised the word of the LORD, doing what is evil in His sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, taken his wife as your own, and killed him by the sword of the Ammonites.
Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.

This is what the LORD says: Behold, I will bring calamity upon you from your own household. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in broad daylight.
For you acted in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and in the light of day.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan replied, “The LORD has put away your sin; you will not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have given the enemies of the LORD great occasion to blaspheme, the child born to you will surely die.”
Then Nathan went to his house, and the LORD struck the child whom Uriah’s wife had borne to David, so that he became ill.
David therefore sought God on behalf of the child; he fasted, went in, and lay all night on the ground.
The elders of his house stood beside him to raise him from the ground, but he would not rise, and he would not eat with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “While the child was still alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How can we now say to him, ‘The child is dead’? He may harm himself.”
But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, he understood that the child was dead. So David asked his servants, “Is the child dead?” They answered, “He is dead.”

Then David arose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes. He went into the house of the LORD and worshiped; then he went to his own house. When he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child died, you arose and ate.”
He said, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, so that the child may live?’
But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba; he went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him.
He sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
He sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the city’s water supply.
Now therefore gather the rest of the people, encamp against the city, and take it, lest I take the city and it be named after me.”
So David gathered all the people and went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.

He took the crown from the head of their king; its weight was a talent of gold, and it was set with a precious stone. It was placed on David’s head, and he brought out a very great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them pass through the brick kilns. He did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After these events, Absalom son of David had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon, another son of David, loved her.
Amnon grew so obsessed with his sister Tamar that he fell ill; since she was a virgin, it seemed impossible for him to have his way with her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of Shimeah, David's brother, and Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He asked him, "Why are you, the king's son, so haggard every morning? Will you not confide in me?" Amnon replied, "I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and feign illness. When your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and prepare food before my eyes, so that I may eat what she prepares.'"

So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make two cakes in my sight, so that I may eat what she prepares."
David sent word to Tamar at the palace: "Go to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare food for him."
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked them.
She took the pan and served them before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, "Send everyone out of the room." So everyone left.
Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the bedroom so that I may eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.
As she brought them to him to eat, he seized her and said, "Come to bed with me, my sister."
"No, my brother!" she cried. "Do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not commit this disgraceful act."
"Where would I go with my shame? And as for you, you would be counted among the fools in Israel. Now please speak to the king, for he will not refuse to give me to you."
But he refused to listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up and go."
"No," she said, "for sending me away now would be a greater wrong than the one you have already done to me." But he would not listen to her.
He called his young servant and said, "Get this woman out of here and bolt the door behind her."
Now his servant had on a robe with long sleeves, for this is what the king's virgin daughters wore. So his servant put her out and bolted the door behind her.
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore the long-sleeved robe she was wearing, placed her hand on her head, and went away crying aloud.

Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now keep quiet, my sister; he is your brother. Do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom.
When King David heard all this, he was very angry.
Absalom never spoke to Amnon either good or bad, because he hated Amnon for having violated his sister Tamar.
After two full years, Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant is shearing sheep. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."
The king said to Absalom, "No, my son, we should not all go, lest we be a burden to you." Although Absalom urged him, he refused to go, but he gave him his blessing.
"Then please let my brother Amnon go with us." "Why should he go with you?" the king asked.
But Absalom urged him so strongly that he sent Amnon and all the king's sons with him.
Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Watch Amnon until he is merry with wine, and when I tell you, 'Strike Amnon and kill him,' do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous."
So Absalom's servants did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons mounted their mules and fled.
While they were on the way, the report reached David: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons; not one of them survives."
Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground, and all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother, spoke up: "Do not let my lord the king think that all the young men, the king's sons, are dead. Only Amnon is dead, for Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.
So now, my lord the king, do not take this to heart and think that all the king's sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."
Meanwhile Absalom fled. The young man on watch looked up and saw many people coming along the road from the side of the hill behind him.
Jonadab said to the king, "Look, the king's sons are coming. It is just as your servant said."
As soon as he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived and wept aloud; the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day.
Absalom fled and stayed in Geshur for three years.
King David longed to go to Absalom, for he was comforted concerning Amnon, who had died.
Joab son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart was fixed upon Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought back a wise woman, and he said to her, “Please mourn; put on mourning garments, and do not anoint yourself with oil. Be like a woman who has mourned the dead for many days.”
“Then go to the king and speak to him in this manner,” Joab said, putting these words in her mouth.
The woman from Tekoa went to the king, fell on her face to the ground, bowed down, and cried, “Help me, O king!”
The king asked her, “What troubles you?” She answered, “Truly I am a widow, and my husband is dead.”
“Your maidservant had two sons, and they quarreled in the field. With no one to intervene, one struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole clan has risen against your maidservant and says, ‘Surrender the man who struck his brother, so that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed and destroy the heir as well.’ Thus they would extinguish the last ember of my husband’s lineage, leaving my husband neither name nor remnant on the earth.”
The king said to the woman, “Go to your home, and I will issue an order concerning you.”
The woman said to the king, “My lord the king, let the guilt rest upon me and upon my father’s house, while the king and his throne remain innocent.”
The king said, “If anyone speaks to you, bring him to me, and he will not trouble you again.”

She said, “Please let my lord the king remember the LORD your God, so that the avenger of blood does not destroy my son.” The king replied, “As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”
Then the woman said, “Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king.” “Speak,” he said.
The woman said, “Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in pronouncing this judgment, the king condemns himself, since he has not restored his own banished son.

For we will surely die and are like water spilled upon the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; yet God does not take life away, but He devises means so that the banished one is not cast out from Him.”
“Now I have come to speak this word to my lord the king because the people have intimidated me. Your servant said, ‘I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will grant his maidservant’s request.’”
“For the king will hear and deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from God’s inheritance.”
“Your servant said, ‘May the word of my lord the king bring me rest,’ for my lord the king is like the angel of God in discerning good and evil. May the LORD your God be with you.”
The king answered the woman, “Please do not conceal from me anything I ask you.” “Let my lord the king speak,” the woman said.

The king said, “Is Joab’s hand in all this?” The woman answered, “As your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can deviate from anything my lord the king has spoken. Yes, your servant Joab commanded me; he put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
To bring about this change of affairs, your servant Joab has done this thing. But my lord is wise, with the wisdom of the angel of God, to know everything that happens in the land.”
The king said to Joab, “Very well, I have done this. Go and bring back the young man Absalom.”

Joab fell on his face to the ground, bowed down, and blessed the king. Then Joab said, “Today your servant knows that he has found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has granted his servant’s request.”
Joab rose, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him go to his own house, but he must not see my face.” So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king’s face.
In all Israel there was no man so handsome as Absalom; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head he was without blemish.
When he cut the hair of his head—and he cut it at the end of each year because its weight burdened him—he would weigh it out at two hundred shekels by the king’s standard.
Three sons and a daughter were born to Absalom. His daughter’s name was Tamar, and she was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king’s face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come. He sent a second time, but Joab would not come.
So Absalom said to his servants, “Look, Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it ablaze.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.
Joab got up, went to Absalom’s house, and said, “Why have your servants set my field ablaze?”

Absalom answered Joab, “Look, I sent to you and said, ‘Come here, so that I may send you to the king to ask why I came from Geshur. It would have been better for me to remain there.’ Now let me see the king’s face, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.”
Joab went and told the king. Then the king summoned Absalom, and he came to the king and bowed with his face to the ground before him. The king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom procured a chariot and horses for himself, together with fifty men to run ahead of him.

Moreover, Absalom would rise early and station himself beside the road at the gate. Whenever a man had a dispute and came to the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him and ask, "From what city are you?" The man would reply, "Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel."
Then Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are sound and just, but no one from the king's court listens to you."
Absalom would add, "If only someone would appoint me judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or a case would come to me, and I would render him justice."
Whenever a man approached to bow before him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.
In this way Absalom treated all Israel who came to the king for judgment, and so he won the allegiance of the Israelites.
At the end of four years, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron and pay the vow I have made to the LORD.
For your servant vowed a vow while I was living at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will serve the LORD.'"
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron.
But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, you are to say, 'Absalom is king in Hebron!'"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom; they had been invited and went in good faith, knowing nothing of the plot.
While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city of Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
Then a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, for otherwise we will have no escape from Absalom. Hurry and go, lest he overtake us quickly, bring disaster upon us, and strike the city with the sword."
The king's servants said to the king, "Look, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides."
So the king went out, and all his household followed him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.
The king went out, and all the people followed him, and they halted at the last house.
All his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had come with him from Gath passed on before the king.
Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and an exile from your home.

You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you."
But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in whatever place my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be."
David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.
All the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron. All the people passed on toward the wilderness.
Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also, with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until all the people had passed out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place.
But if He says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am; let Him do to me as seems good to Him."
The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Return to the city in peace with your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar. You and Abiathar take your two sons with you.
See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me."
So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there.

But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, with his head covered, and he walked barefoot. And all the people who were with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.
And one told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." David said, "O the LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."
When David came to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head.
David said to him, "If you pass on with me, you will be a burden to me.
But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant from then until now, so now I will be your servant.'
Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? And everything that you hear from the king's house, you shall tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
Look, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son; and by their hand you shall send to me everything that you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city just as Absalom was entering the city.

David had gone only a little beyond the summit when Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, met him with a pair of saddled donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

The king asked Ziba, “What are these?” Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those exhausted in the wilderness to drink.”
The king asked, “Where is your master?” Ziba answered, “He is staying in Jerusalem, because he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will give me back my father’s kingdom.’”
The king said to Ziba, “Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours.” Ziba bowed and said, “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king.”
When King David reached Bahurim, a man from the family of Saul’s house named Shimei son of Gera came out, cursing as he came.
He pelted David and all the king’s servants, as well as all the people and warriors on his right and left, with stones.
As he cursed, Shimei said, “Get out, get out, you bloodthirsty man, you worthless scoundrel!

The LORD has brought back on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. Now you are caught in your own wickedness, because you are a man of blood.”
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head.”
The king replied, “What do you and I have in common, sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD told him to curse David, who can ask, ‘Why are you doing this?’”

David said to Abishai and all his servants, “Look, my own son, who came from my body, is seeking my life; how much more, then, this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
“Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and the LORD will repay me with good for the cursing heaped on me today.”
So David and his men continued along the road, while Shimei kept pace on the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went, hurling stones and flinging dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and there they refreshed themselves.
Meanwhile, Absalom and all the men of Israel entered Jerusalem, with Ahithophel among them.
When David’s friend Hushai the Archite came to Absalom, Hushai said, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why didn’t you go with your friend?”
Hushai replied, “No; rather, I will belong to the one whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, and I will remain with him.
Besides, whom should I serve? Is it not his son? Just as I served your father, so I will serve you.”
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give us your counsel. What should we do?”

Ahithophel answered, “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he has left to keep the house. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself utterly repugnant to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.”
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days, Ahithophel’s counsel was regarded as if one were inquiring of the word of God; such was the counsel of Ahithophel, both to David and to Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out tonight and pursue David.
I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged, terrify him, and make all the people with him flee; then I will strike down the king alone.
I will bring all the people back to you; the man you seek is as though all had returned, and all the people will be at peace.”
The proposal pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he too has to say.”
Hushai came to Absalom, and Absalom said to him, “Ahithophel has spoken thus. Shall we carry out his plan? If not, you speak.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.

You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and they are bitter in spirit, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field; and your father is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops.
Even now he has hidden himself in some pit or some other place. If some of them fall at first, whoever hears it will say, ‘A slaughter has occurred among the people who follow Absalom.’
Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will melt in fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man and that those with him are valiant.
But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand on the seashore in number, and that you go into battle.
Then we will come upon him in whatever place he is found, and we will fall on him as dew falls on the ground; not one man will be left of him and all his men.
If he retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it into the river until not a trace remains.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For the LORD had ordained that the good counsel of Ahithophel be frustrated, so that the LORD might bring disaster upon Absalom.
Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “Thus and thus Ahithophel counseled Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and thus I have counseled.”
Hushai said, “Now therefore send quickly and tell David, ‘Do not spend the night in the plains of the wilderness, but cross over at once, lest the king and all the people with him be overwhelmed.’”
Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were standing at En-rogel, and a maidservant went and told them; they went and told King David, for they could not be seen entering the city.
But a young man saw them and told Absalom; so the two hurried away and came to the house of a man in Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The woman took a covering and spread it over the well’s mouth, and scattered crushed grain on it, so that nothing was known.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house and said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” The woman said to them, “They have crossed over the brook of water.” After they searched and did not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the two came up out of the well and went and told King David. They said to David, “Arise and cross the water quickly, for thus Ahithophel has counseled against you.”
Then David and all the people with him arose and crossed the Jordan; by daybreak not one of them was left behind.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, arose, and went home to his city. He put his affairs in order and hanged himself; he died and was buried in his father’s tomb.
Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.
Absalom had set Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man whose name was Ithra the Israelite, who had married Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins, and pottery, and wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, and parched peas,
honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat; for they said, “The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.”
David mustered the troops who were with him and appointed commanders over thousands and commanders over hundreds.

He dispatched a third of the forces under Joab's command, a third under Abishai son of Zeruiah—Joab's brother—and a third under Ittai the Gittite. Then the king told the people, "I myself will certainly march out with you."

But the people answered, "You must not go out. If we flee, they will not care about us; even if half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us, so it is better for you to support us from the city."
The king replied, "I will do whatever seems best to you." Then the king stood beside the gate, and all the people marched out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king ordered Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, "Deal gently with the young man Absalom, for my sake." All the troops heard the king give this order concerning Absalom.
So the army marched into the field against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
There the Israelites were defeated by David's servants, and the slaughter that day was staggering—twenty thousand men.
The fighting spread across the whole countryside, and the forest claimed more lives that day than the sword did.

Absalom happened to meet David's servants while riding his mule. The mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and Absalom's head caught in the tree; he was left hanging between heaven and earth while the mule kept going.
When one of the men saw this, he reported to Joab, "I have just seen Absalom hanging from an oak."
Joab said to the man who had reported it, "What! You saw him, and you did not strike him to the ground right there? I would have given you ten shekels of silver and a belt."

The man replied, "Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed into my hand, I would not raise my hand against the king's son, because we all heard the king command you, Abishai, and Ittai, 'Protect the young man Absalom.'"
"Otherwise I would have betrayed my own life, for nothing is hidden from the king, and you would have turned against me."
Joab said, "I will not waste time arguing with you." He took three javelins in his hand and drove them into Absalom's heart while Absalom was still alive in the oak.
Then ten of Joab's young armor-bearers surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops stopped pursuing Israel, because Joab restrained them.
They took Absalom's body, threw it into a large pit in the forest, and piled a huge heap of stones over it. Meanwhile all Israel fled, each to his own home.

During his lifetime Absalom had taken a pillar and erected it for himself in the King's Valley, saying, "I have no son to preserve my name." He named the pillar after himself, and it is still called Absalom's Monument.
Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and bring the king the news that the LORD has vindicated him against his enemies."
Joab replied, "You are not the man to carry news today. You may do so another time, but not today, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go and tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran off.

Ahimaaz son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Whatever happens, please let me run after the Cushite." Joab asked, "Why do you want to run, my son? You will gain no reward for this news." "But I want to run," Ahimaaz said. So Joab said, "Run."
Then Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite.
David was sitting between the inner and outer gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, looked out, and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and reported to the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he brings good news." The runner kept coming closer.
The watchman saw another man running and called to the gatekeeper, "Look, another man running alone!" The king said, "He too brings good news."
The watchman said, "I recognize the first runner's stride; it is like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news."

Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hands against my lord the king."
The king asked, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent your servant off, I saw a great commotion, but I did not know what it was."
The king said, "Step aside and stand here." So Ahimaaz stepped aside and stood still.
Then the Cushite arrived and said, "Good news for my lord the king! Today the LORD has vindicated you against all who rose up against you."
The king asked, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The Cushite replied, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise against you to harm you, become like that young man."

The king was deeply shaken. He went up to the room above the gate and wept. As he walked, he cried out, "O my son Absalom—my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was informed that the king was weeping and mourning over Absalom.
The triumph of that day was turned into mourning for the whole nation, because the troops heard that the king was grieving over his son.
The soldiers slipped into the city that day like men ashamed, stealing away as though they had fled from battle.
The king veiled his face and cried out, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!”

Joab entered the house and said to the king, “Today you have disgraced every servant who preserved your life today, along with the lives of your sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, because you have favored those who hate you and scorned those who love you.

You love your enemies and hate your friends; for today you have declared that commanders and servants mean nothing to you, since today I perceive that if Absalom were alive and all of us dead, it would seem right in your eyes.

Now arise, go out, and speak kindly to your servants; for I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not one man will remain with you tonight, and that would be worse for you than all the calamity that has befallen you from your youth until now.”
Then the king arose and sat in the gate. When the people were told, “The king is sitting in the gate,” all the people came before the king, while Israel had fled, each man to his home.
All the people were arguing throughout the tribes of Israel, saying, “The king delivered us from our enemies and saved us from the Philistines, yet now he has fled the land because of Absalom.
Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now why are you silent about bringing the king back?”

King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: “Speak to the elders of Judah and ask, ‘Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when all Israel is already calling for his return?
You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?’
And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my own flesh and blood? May God punish me severely if I do not appoint you commander of the army in Joab’s place from this day forward.’”
So David won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent this message to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.”
The king returned and came as far as the Jordan, while Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and escort him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin were with him, along with Ziba, the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and twenty servants; they rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king.
They crossed the ford to bring the king’s household over and to do whatever seemed good to him, and Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he crossed the Jordan.
He said to the king, “Let not my lord hold me guilty, and do not remember what your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem; let the king not take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned, and therefore I have come today, the first of all the house of Joseph, to go down and meet my lord the king.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, “Should not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the the LORD’s anointed?”

David replied, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should be adversaries to me today? Shall any man be put to death in Israel today? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?”
Then the king swore to him, “You shall not die.”
Mephibosheth son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet, nor trimmed his mustache, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until the day he returned in peace.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king asked, “Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?”
He answered, “My lord the king, my servant deceived me; for your servant said, ‘I will saddle a donkey for myself, ride on it, and go with the king,’ because your servant is lame.
He has slandered your servant to my lord the king; but my lord the king is like the angel of God. Do therefore what is good in your eyes.
For all my father’s house were but dead men before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right have I still to cry out to the king?”
The king said, “Why do you speak any more of your matters? I have decided that you and Ziba shall divide the field.”
Mephibosheth replied, “Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king to see him on his way.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age, and he had provided for the king during his stay at Mahanaim; he was a man of great wealth.
The king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai answered, “How many more days have I to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
