I am eighty years old today. Can I discern between good and evil? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voices of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham; let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you.”
The king said, “Chimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you; indeed, I will do for you whatever you choose for me.”
All the people crossed over the Jordan, and the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his place.
The king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed with him. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel brought the king over.
All the men of Israel came to the king and said, “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, along with all David’s men?”
All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “The king is our close relative. Why are you angry over this? Have we eaten at the king’s expense, or has any gift been given to us?”

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, “We have ten shares in the king, and we have more right to David than you do. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?” Then the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

Now a worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, happened to be there. He blew a trumpet and shouted, “We have no share in David, and no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man of Israel, return home!”
So all the men of Israel withdrew from following David and followed Sheba son of Bichri, while the men of Judah remained loyal to their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

When David returned to his house in Jerusalem, the king took the ten concubines he had left to keep the house, placed them in a guarded residence, provided for them, but did not sleep with them. They remained confined until the day they died, living as widows.
The king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah for me within three days, and you be present here.”
Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the appointed time.
David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba son of Bichri will harm us more than Absalom did. Take your lord’s servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and escape from us.”
Joab’s men went out after him, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty warriors. They left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

They were at the great stone in Gibeon when Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his military tunic, with a belt and a sword in its sheath fastened at his waist; as he stepped forward, the sword slipped out.
Joab said to Amasa, “Are you well, my brother?” Then Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab’s hand. Joab struck him in the abdomen, and his entrails spilled onto the ground; he died without a second blow. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab’s young men stood beside Amasa and cried, “Whoever is for Joab, and whoever is for David, follow Joab!”
Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that everyone who passed by stopped, he dragged Amasa from the road into a field and threw a garment over him.
Once he had been removed from the road, all the men passed on after Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel Beth-maachah and to all the Berites; they assembled and followed him as well.
They came and besieged him in Abel Beth-maachah. They built a siege ramp against the city, and it reached the outer wall; all the troops with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down.
A wise woman called out from the city, “Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so I can speak with you.”
Joab approached her, and the woman asked, “Are you Joab?” “I am,” he replied. “Listen to the words of your maidservant,” she said. “I am listening,” he answered.
Then she said, “In former times people would say, ‘Let them seek counsel at Abel,’ and that settled the matter.”
“I am one of the peaceful and faithful in Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?”
Joab answered, “Far be it from me! Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy!”

“The matter is not so. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba son of Bichri, has rebelled against King David. Hand him over alone, and I will withdraw from the city.” “Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall,” the woman replied.

The woman went to all the people with her wisdom, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, each to his own home. Then Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.
Now Joab was over all the army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
Adoram was over the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Sheva was the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
Ira the Jairite was also David’s priest.

During the reign of David there was a famine for three successive years, and David sought the the LORD's guidance. And the the LORD said, "It is because of Saul and his bloodstained house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

So the king summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (Now the Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had sworn an oath to them, but Saul had sought to kill them in his zeal for the Israelites and Judah.)
So David asked the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? How can I make restitution so that you may bless the inheritance of the the LORD?"
The Gibeonites said to him, "We do not seek silver or gold from Saul or his house, nor do we demand that any man in Israel be put to death." "Whatever you say, I will do for you," David replied.
"The man who devastated us and plotted against us to exterminate us from existing within any border of Israel—
"let seven of his male descendants be given to us so that we may hang them before the the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the the LORD." "I will give them to you," said the king.
Now the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of the oath before the the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

But the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons whom Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, along with the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, who hanged them on the hill before the the LORD. So the seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

And Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock from the beginning of the harvest until the rain poured down from heaven upon them. She did not allow the birds of the air to settle on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.
When David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done,

he went and took the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them the day the Philistines struck down Saul at Gilboa.
So David brought up the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from there, and they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged.

And they buried the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan in Zela in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Kish his father. After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered prayers for the land.
Once again war broke out between the Philistines and Israel. David and his men went down and fought against the Philistines, and David became exhausted.
Then Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who was carrying a new sword, resolved to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his rescue, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You will never again go out with us to battle, so that Israel's guiding light will not be extinguished."
After this, there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of Rapha.
Once again there was a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.
And there was still another battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—twenty-four in all. He too was descended from Rapha.
And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down.
So these four were born to Rapha in Gath, and they were struck down by David and his men.
David composed this song to the the LORD on the day the the LORD delivered him from the grasp of all his enemies and from Saul’s hand.
He said: The the LORD is my Rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.
God is my Rock, in whom I take refuge; my shield, the horn of my salvation, my stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior: You rescue me from violence.
I call upon the the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
For the breakers of death encircled me; torrents of ruin overwhelmed me.
The cords of Sheol coiled around me; the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called to the the LORD; I cried to my God. From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry reached His ears.
Then the earth shook and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and were shaken, because He was angry.
Smoke ascended from His nostrils, and consuming fire issued from His mouth; burning coals were kindled by Him.
He bowed the heavens and descended, with thick darkness beneath His feet.
He rode upon a cherub and flew; He was seen upon the wings of the wind.
He made darkness His covering around Him—dark waters and thick clouds of the skies.
Out of the brightness before Him, coals of fire burned.
The the LORD thundered from heaven; the Most High uttered His voice.
He sent out arrows and scattered them; He flashed forth lightning and routed them.
The channels of the sea were exposed, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of the the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils.
He reached down from on high and seized me; He drew me out of many waters.
He rescued me from my fierce enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me.
They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the the LORD was my support.
He brought me out into a broad place; He rescued me because He delighted in me.
The the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands He has repaid me.
For I have kept the ways of the the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.
For all His ordinances are before me, and I have not turned aside from His statutes.
I have been blameless before Him, and I have kept myself from iniquity.
Therefore the the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my purity in His sight.
To the faithful You show Yourself faithful; to the blameless You show Yourself blameless.
To the pure You show Yourself pure; to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.
You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are upon the proud, that You may bring them down.
For You are my lamp, O the LORD; the the LORD illumines my darkness.
For by You I can run through a troop; by my God I can leap over a wall.
As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.
For who is God besides the the LORD? And who is a Rock except our God?
God is my strength and power; He makes my way perfect.
He makes my feet like the feet of deer and sets me on my high places.
He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.
You have given me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me.
You enlarge my steps beneath me, so my feet have not slipped.
I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed.
I consumed and crushed them, so that they could not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
For You girded me with strength for battle; You subdued under me those who rose against me.
You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and I annihilated those who hated me.
They cried for help, but there was no one to save; they cried to the the LORD, but He did not answer them.
I beat them as fine as the dust of the earth; I trampled them like mud in the streets.
You delivered me from the strife of my people; You kept me as head of the nations. A people I did not know serves me.
Foreigners cringe before me; at the mere report of me they obey.
Foreigners lose heart and come trembling out of their strongholds.
The the LORD lives! Blessed be my Rock, and exalted be God, the Rock of my salvation.
God, who gives me vengeance and subdues peoples under me—
He delivers me from my enemies; You exalt me above my adversaries; You rescue me from violent men.
Therefore I will give thanks to You among the nations, O the LORD, and I will sing praises to Your name.
He gives great salvation to His king and shows steadfast love to His anointed, to David and to his descendants forever.
These constitute David's final words: the oracle of David son of Jesse, the utterance of the man exalted on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, Israel's sweet psalmist.
"The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me, and His word rested upon my tongue.

The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: 'When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he is like the light of morning at sunrise on a cloudless day, like the brightness after rain that brings forth grass from the earth.'
Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every particular.
Will He not bring to fruition my salvation and every desire?
But the worthless are all like thorns raked aside, for they cannot be gathered by hand.
Whoever touches them must be armed with iron and the shaft of a spear; they are utterly consumed in fire."
These are the names of David's mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahkemonite was chief of the Three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred men and slew them in a single encounter.

Next to him stood Eleazar son of Dodai the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men. He remained with David when the Israelites taunted the Philistines who had gathered for battle and the rest of the army withdrew.
Yet Eleazar held his ground and struck down the Philistines until his hand grew weary and clung to his sword.

The LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the troops returned to him, though only to strip the slain. After him came Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines had gathered into a troop where there was a field full of lentils, and the people fled from them.
But Shammah took his stand in the midst of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines. So the LORD brought about a great victory.
At harvest time, three of the thirty chief warriors went down to David at the cave of Adullam, while a Philistine force was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and the Philistine garrison held Bethlehem.
David longed for water and said, "I wish someone would bring me a drink from the well by the gate of Bethlehem."

So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem, and carried it to David. But he refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out as an offering to the LORD.
He said, "I could never do such a thing before the LORD! Is it not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" So he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three mighty men.
Now Abishai, the brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three. He wielded his spear against three hundred men, killed them, and won a name among the Three.
Was he not more honored than the Three? He became their commander, even though he was not reckoned among the Three.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a valiant warrior from Kabzeel, a man of many exploits. He struck down two champions of Moab, and on a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion.

He also struck down an Egyptian, a man of imposing stature. Although the Egyptian wielded a spear, Benaiah went against him with a staff, snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand, and killed him with his own spear.
These were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who won a name among the three mighty men.
He was more honored than the Thirty, but he did not attain to the Three. David appointed him over his bodyguard.
Among the Thirty were Asahel, brother of Joab; Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem;
Shammah the Harodite; Elika the Harodite;
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite;
Abiezer the Anathothite; Mebunnai the Hushathite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Maharai the Netophathite;
Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite; Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjamites;
Benaiah the Pirathonite; Hiddai from the brooks of Gaash;
Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth the Barhumite;
Eliahba the Shaalbonite; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan;
Shammah the Hararite; Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite;
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite;
Hezro the Carmelite; Paarai the Arbite;
Igal son of Nathan of Zobah; Bani the Gadite;
Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah;
Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Ithrite;
and Uriah the Hittite. In all there were thirty-seven.
Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He incited David against them, saying, "Go and take a census of Israel and Judah."
So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, "Go throughout all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I may know their number."

But Joab replied to the king, "May the LORD your God multiply the people a hundredfold beyond what they are, while my lord the king still sees it; but why does my lord the king delight in this matter?"
Nevertheless, the king's word prevailed over Joab and the army commanders. So Joab and the commanders went out from the king's presence to register the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, on the right side of the city that lies in the middle of the valley of Gad, toward Jazer.
Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and they came to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon.
They came to the stronghold of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they went out to the south of Judah at Beersheba.
After they had gone through all the land, they returned to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab reported the total registration to the king: Israel had eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and Judah had five hundred thousand men.

Afterward David's conscience struck him because he had numbered the people, and he said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O the LORD, please take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
When David arose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to Gad the prophet, David's seer, saying,
"Go and tell David, 'Thus says the LORD: I am offering you three things; choose one of them for yourself, and I will do it to you.'"

So Gad came to David and told him, and he said to him, "Shall seven years of famine come upon you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your enemies while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days of pestilence in your land? Now consider and decide what answer I shall return to Him who sent me."
David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us now fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hand of man."
So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the destroying angel, "It is enough; now withdraw your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel striking the people, he said to the LORD, "I have sinned, and I have acted wickedly; but these sheep—what have they done? Please let Your hand be against me and against my father's house."
That day Gad came to David and said to him, "Go up and erect an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
So David went up, as Gad had spoken, according to the LORD's command.
Araunah looked down and saw the king and his servants crossing toward him; then Araunah went out and bowed with his face to the ground before the king.

Araunah asked, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David replied, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague may be stayed from the people."

Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up whatever seems good to him. Look, here are the oxen for the burnt offering, the threshing sledges, and the yokes of the oxen for the wood."
"All these things, O king, Araunah gives to the king. May the LORD your God accept you."

But the king said to Araunah, "No, I will buy it from you at a price; I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
David built an altar to the LORD there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayer for the land, and the plague was stayed from Israel.
Now King David was old and advanced in years, and although they covered him with garments, he could not get warm.
So his servants said to him, “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king. She will stand before the king, serve as his nurse, and lie beside him so that my lord the king may be warm.”
They searched throughout all the territory of Israel for a beautiful young woman and found Abishag the Shunammite, whom they brought to the king.
The young woman was exceedingly beautiful. She became the king’s nurse and served him, but the king did not have sexual relations with her.
Now Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” He prepared chariots and horsemen, with fifty men to run before him.
His father had never rebuked him or said, “Why have you done this?” Adonijah was also very handsome; he had been born after Absalom.
He conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they supported Adonijah.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s mighty men were not with Adonijah.
Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the stone of Zoheleth near En Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah who served the king.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon.
Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, “Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, while our lord David does not know it?
Now please come, let me give you counsel so that you may save your life and the life of your son Solomon.

Go at once to King David and say to him, ‘My lord the king, did you not swear to your servant, saying, “Surely your son Solomon shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne”? Why then has Adonijah become king?’
While you are still there speaking with the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words.”
So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was ministering to him.
Bathsheba bowed and prostrated herself before the king, and the king said, “What do you want?”
She said to him, “My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, ‘Surely your son Solomon shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.’
And now, my lord, Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, do not know it.

He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance. He has invited all the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but he has not invited your servant Solomon. “
My lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
Otherwise, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon will be counted as offenders.”
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
They told the king, “Nathan the prophet is here.” He came in before the king and bowed with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, “My lord the king, have you said, ‘Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne’?

For today he has gone down and sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance. He has invited all the king’s sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. They are eating and drinking before him, and they are saying, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
But he did not invite me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, or Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Has this thing been done by my lord the king, and you have not let your servants know who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”
Then King David answered, “Call Bathsheba to me.” So she came into the king’s presence and stood before the king.
The king swore an oath: “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress,
just as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Your son Solomon shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,’ so I will surely do this today.”
Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and prostrated herself before the king, and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”
King David said, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada.” So they came before the king.
The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and have my son Solomon ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet shall anoint him king over Israel. Blow the trumpet and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’
Then you shall go up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and Judah.”
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, “Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so too.
As the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may He be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.”
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David’s mule, and they brought him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, “Long live King Solomon!”
All the people went up after him, playing on flutes and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth shook with their noise.
Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, “Why is the city in such an uproar?”
While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest came. Adonijah said, “Come in, for you are a valiant man and bring good news.”
Jonathan answered Adonijah, “No! Our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king has sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites with him, and they have had him ride on the king’s mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon. They have gone up from there rejoicing, and the city rings with it. That is the noise you heard.” “
Moreover, Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne.

The king’s servants also came to bless our lord King David, saying, ‘May God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne.’ Then the king bowed in worship on his bed.
The king also said, ‘Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted me to see with my own eyes my son sitting on my throne today.’”
Then all of Adonijah’s guests arose in alarm and went their separate ways.
Adonijah, fearing Solomon, arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.

It was reported to Solomon: “Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, and behold, he has taken hold of the horns of the altar, saying, ‘Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he proves to be a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.”
So King Solomon sent and had him brought down from the altar. He came and bowed before King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, “Go to your house.”
As David's death drew near, he commanded his son Solomon,
"I am about to die, as all people do. Be strong and act like a man.

"Keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in His ways and keeping His statutes, His commandments, His ordinances, and His testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in everything you do and wherever you turn,

so that the LORD may establish His word that He spoke concerning me: 'If your sons keep their way, walking before Me in truth with all their heart and all their soul, then you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'

"Moreover, you know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me—what he did to Abner son of Ner and to Amasa son of Jether, the two commanders of Israel's armies. He killed them, shedding the blood of war in peacetime, and stained his belt and sandals with their blood.
"So act according to your wisdom, and do not let him die peacefully in old age.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them eat at your table, because they came to me when I fled from your brother Absalom.

Also, look—Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, is with you. He cursed me with a grievous curse on the day I went to Mahanaim. Yet he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death by the sword.'
Now do not let him go unpunished, for you are a wise man and you will know what you should do to him. Bring him to the grave in blood."
Then David died and was buried in the City of David.
The days David reigned over Israel were forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Then Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. She asked, "Do you come in peace?" "Peace," he answered.
Then he said, "I have a word for you." She replied, "Speak."
He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine and all Israel looked to me to reign. But the kingdom passed to my brother, for the LORD gave it to him.
Now I ask one request of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."
He said, "Please speak to King Solomon, for he will not refuse you, that he may give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife."
Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak to the king for you."
Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak for Adonijah. The king rose to meet her, bowed to her, and sat on his throne; then he had a throne set for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand.
She said, "I am asking one small request; do not refuse me." The king said to her, "Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you."
She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife."
King Solomon answered his mother, "Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom as well—for he is my older brother—and for Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah."
Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "May God do so to me and more if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life.
"Now therefore, as the LORD lives, who established me and set me on the throne of David my father and made me a house as He promised, surely Adonijah shall be put to death today."
King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your field, for you are a man worthy of death. But I will not put you to death today, because you carried the ark of Lord the LORD before David my father and because you shared in all my father suffered."
So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, to fulfill the word of the LORD that He had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.
The news reached Joab, for Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he had not turned after Absalom. Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar.
It was told to King Solomon that Joab had fled to the tent of the LORD and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."

Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "Thus says the king: 'Come out.'" He replied, "No; I will die here." Benaiah brought back word to the king, saying, "Thus spoke Joab, and thus he answered me."
The king said to him, "Do as he said, and strike him down and bury him, so that you may remove from me and from my father's house the innocent blood that Joab shed.

"The LORD will hold him accountable for that blood, because he fell upon two men more righteous and better than he and killed them with the sword—Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army—without my father David knowing.
"That bloodguilt will rest on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever; but for David and his descendants and his house and his throne, there shall be peace forever from the LORD."
Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and killed him, and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.
The king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada in his place over the army, and Zadok the priest the king appointed in place of Abiathar.
The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there, and do not go out from there anywhere.
"On the day you go out and cross the Brook Kidron, know for certain that you will die; you will bear responsibility for your own death."
Shimei said to the king, "The word is good. As my lord the king has spoken, so your servant will do." Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.
But after three years, two of Shimei's servants fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. They told Shimei, saying, "Behold, your servants are in Gath."
Shimei rose and saddled his donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath.
It was told to Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned.

The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and warn you, saying, 'On the day you go out and walk anywhere, know for certain that you shall surely die'? And you said to me, 'The word I have heard is good.'
Why then have you not kept the oath of the LORD and the commandment that I commanded you?"
The king said to Shimei, "You know in your heart all the evil that you did to David my father. The LORD will hold you accountable for your evil.
But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever."
The king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.

Solomon allied himself with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, by marrying Pharaoh's daughter, and he brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his palace, the house of the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people, however, were still sacrificing on the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.
Now Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of his father David, though he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place; Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, “Ask what I shall give you.”

Solomon said, “You have shown great and faithful love to Your servant David my father, because he walked before You in truth, righteousness, and uprightness of heart toward You. You have kept for him this great and faithful love, and You have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day.
And now, O the LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in place of David my father, though I am but a little child and do not know how to go out or come in.
Your servant is in the midst of Your people whom You have chosen, a great people, too numerous to be numbered or counted.
Give Your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge Your people, to discern between good and evil, for who is able to judge this great people of Yours?”
The request pleased the Lord, because Solomon had asked for this.

God said to him, “Because you have asked for this thing and have not asked for yourself long life, nor riches for yourself, nor the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice,
behold, I have done according to your words. Behold, I have given you a wise and discerning heart, so that there has been none like you before you, nor shall any like you arise after you.
I have also given you what you did not ask—both riches and honor—so that there shall not be any among the kings like you all your days.
And if you walk in My ways, keeping My statutes and My commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days.”

Then Solomon awoke; it had been a dream. He came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
The one woman said, “Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was in the house.
On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. We were alone; no one else was in the house with us—only the two of us.
During the night this woman's son died, because she lay on him.
She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while your maidservant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast.
When I rose in the morning to nurse my son, he was dead; but when I examined him in the morning, he was not the son I had borne.”

The other woman said, “No! My son is the living one, and your son is the dead one.” But the first woman said, “No! Your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.” Thus they argued before the king.
The king said, “The one says, ‘This is my son who lives, and your son is dead,’ and the other says, ‘No, your son is dead, and my son is the living one.’”
The king said, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought a sword before the king.
The king said, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other.”

Then the woman whose son was alive spoke to the king, for her compassion was aroused for her son, and she said, “Please, my lord, give her the living child, and do not kill him.” But the other woman said, “He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him.”
The king answered, “Give the living child to the first woman, and do not kill him; she is his mother.”
When all Israel heard the judgment that the king had rendered, they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.
King Solomon reigned over all Israel.

These were his officials: Azariah son of Zadok served as priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were scribes; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the army; Zadok and Abiathar served as priests; Azariah son of Nathan supervised the officers; Zabud son of Nathan, also a priest, was the king’s trusted friend; Ahishar directed the household; and Adoniram son of Abda oversaw the forced labor.
Solomon appointed twelve officers over all Israel to supply food for the king and his household, each responsible for one month of the year. Their names and districts were as follows:
Ben-hur in the hill country of Ephraim;
Ben-deker in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon Beth-hanan;
Ben-hesed in Arubboth, with Socoh and all the land of Hepher under his jurisdiction;
Ben-abinadab in all Naphath-dor, who had married Taphath, Solomon’s daughter;
Baana son of Ahilud in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean near Zaretan below Jezreel, extending from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and beyond Jokneam;
Ben-geber in Ramoth-gilead, including the towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan—sixty great cities fortified with walls and bronze bars;
Ahinadab son of Iddo in Mahanaim;
Ahimaaz in Naphtali, who had married Basemath, another daughter of Solomon;
Baana son of Hushai in Asher and Bealoth;
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah in Issachar;
Shimei son of Ela in Benjamin; and
Geber son of Uri in the land of Gilead—the territory once ruled by Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan—with one officer assigned to that land.
Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore; they ate, drank, and rejoiced.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. Those nations brought tribute and served Solomon throughout his life.
Solomon’s provision for a single day amounted to thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal,
together with ten fattened oxen, twenty oxen from the pasture, one hundred sheep, and additional game—deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.
He held dominion over all the territory beyond the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all its kings; and he enjoyed peace on every side.
Thus Judah and Israel lived in security, each man enjoying the tranquil prosperity of his own inheritance, from Dan to Beersheba, throughout Solomon’s reign.
Solomon maintained forty thousand stalls for the horses of his chariots and twelve thousand horsemen.
The officers supplied food for King Solomon and for everyone who dined at his table, ensuring that nothing was lacking.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds to the appropriate place, each according to his assignment.
God gave Solomon wisdom and exceedingly great understanding, with a mind as expansive as the sand on the seashore.
Solomon’s wisdom surpassed that of all the sons of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than any man—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol—and his renown spread among all the surrounding nations.
He composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered one thousand five.
He discoursed on trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that springs from the wall; he also discoursed on beasts, birds, creeping things, and fish.
People from every nation came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, including envoys from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
Hiram, king of Tyre, heard that Solomon had been anointed king in place of his father, and Hiram had always been a loyal friend to David.
Solomon sent messengers to Hiram with this message: “
You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the the LORD his God because wars surrounded him, until the the LORD placed his enemies under the soles of his feet.
Now the the LORD my God has granted me rest on every side; I have no adversary and no calamity.

So I intend to build a house for the name of the the LORD my God, just as the the LORD promised my father David: ‘Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, will build the house for My name.’

Therefore command that cedar be cut for me from Lebanon. My servants will work alongside your servants, and I will pay your servants whatever wages you set, because you know that none of us can cut timber like the Sidonians.”
When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he rejoiced greatly and said, “Blessed be the the LORD today, for He has given David a wise son to rule over this great people.”
Hiram sent word to Solomon: “I have heard what you sent to me; I will do all your desire concerning cedar and cypress timber.

My servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will lash them into rafts and float them to whatever place you designate. There I will break them apart, and you can take them away. In return, you will provide food for my household, as I desire.”
So Hiram gave Solomon all the cedar and cypress timber he desired.
In return, Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household and 20 cors of pressed olive oil; Solomon provided this to Hiram year after year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, just as He had promised him, and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon; the two of them made a covenant.
King Solomon conscripted a forced labor of 30,000 men from all Israel.
He sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts: 10,000 men worked in Lebanon each month, and they spent two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon also had 70,000 men who carried burdens and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains.
Besides Solomon’s chief officials who supervised the work, there were 3,300 foremen who ruled over the people doing the work.
At the king’s command, they quarried large, costly stones—dressed stones—to lay the foundation of the temple.
Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders, along with the Gebalites, cut and prepared the timber and stones for building the temple.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv—the second month—Solomon began to build the house of the the LORD.
The house that King Solomon built for the the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
The portico in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.
He also made for the house windows with recessed frames.
Against the wall of the house he built a structure around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary, and he made side chambers all around.

The lowest story was five cubits wide, the middle six cubits, and the third seven cubits; for he made offsets in the wall around the outside of the house, so that the beams would not be fastened into the walls of the house.
The house was built of stone finished at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.
The entrance to the middle story was on the south side of the house; one ascended by winding stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.
So he built the house and finished it; he roofed the house with beams and boards of cedar.
He built the side chambers all along the house, each five cubits high, and they were joined to the house with timbers of cedar.
The word of the the LORD came to Solomon:

“As for this house that you are building, if you walk in My statutes, observe My ordinances, and keep all My commandments by walking in them, then I will establish My word with you, which I spoke to your father David.
And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake My people Israel.”
So Solomon built the house and finished it.
He paneled the walls of the house from floor to ceiling with cedar boards and overlaid the floor of the house with cypress boards.
He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with cedar boards from floor to ceiling and made it within an inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place.
The house—that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary—was forty cubits long.
The interior of the house was carved cedar, adorned with gourds and open flowers; everything was cedar, and no stone was visible.
He prepared an inner sanctuary within the house to place there the ark of the covenant of the the LORD.
The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold; he also overlaid the altar of cedar.
Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold and drew chains of gold across the front of the inner sanctuary, overlaying it with gold.
He overlaid the whole house with gold until the whole house was finished; he also overlaid with gold the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary.
In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
One wing of the first cherub was five cubits, and the other wing five cubits; from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits.
The second cherub was also ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measurement and the same form.
The height of the one cherub was ten cubits, and so was the other.

He set the cherubim in the innermost part of the house; their wings were spread out so that the wing of one touched the wall, the wing of the other touched the opposite wall, and their wings touched one another in the middle of the house.
He overlaid the cherubim with gold.
He carved all the walls of the house around, both inner and outer sanctuaries, with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
He overlaid the floor of the house with gold, both inner and outer.
For the entrance of the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood; the lintel and doorposts were a fifth part of the wall.
The two doors were of olive wood, and he carved on them carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, overlaying them with gold; he spread the gold upon the cherubim and upon the palm trees.
So also he made for the entrance of the nave doorposts of olive wood, a fourth part of the wall.
The two doors were of cypress wood, each with two folding leaves.
He carved on them cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, evenly applied over the carved work.
He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams.
In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts and according to all its specifications; so he was seven years in building it.
It required thirteen years for Solomon to complete the construction of his palace.
He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon one hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height; it rested upon four rows of cedar columns that supported cedar beams.
Cedar paneling covered the structure above the beams resting on the columns—forty-five beams, fifteen in each row.
Three rows of high windows faced one another in three tiers.
Every doorway and rectangular window had stone frames, with the windows aligned opposite one another in three tiers.
He constructed the colonnade fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide, with a portico in front, together with a canopy and pillars before them.
He also built the hall for the throne—the Hall of Justice—where he would judge; it was paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling.
The palace in which he would reside, set farther back, was built in the same manner. Solomon likewise made a palace for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married, comparable to this hall.
All these buildings were constructed from costly stones, cut to size and trimmed with saws, both inside and outside, from the foundation to the coping, including the great courtyard.
The foundations were laid with large, costly stones, some ten cubits long and others eight cubits long.
Above them were high-grade stones, cut to size, together with cedar beams.
The great courtyard was surrounded by a wall of three courses of dressed stone and one course of trimmed cedar beams, as were the inner courtyard and the portico of the house of the LORD.
Now King Solomon sent to bring Hiram from Tyre.

He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a craftsman in bronze. Hiram was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill for every kind of bronze work, so he came to King Solomon and performed all his work.
He cast two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits in circumference.
He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set upon the tops of the pillars, each five cubits high.
For the capitals on top of the pillars he fashioned a network of lattice work and wreaths of chain work, seven for each capital.
He made the pillars with two rows of pomegranates around each network to cover the capitals atop the pillars; he did the same for the second capital.
The capitals atop the pillars in the portico were shaped like lilies and were four cubits high.
The capitals on the two pillars also had pomegranates on the upper part, beside the rounded projection next to the network; two hundred pomegranates were arranged in rows around both capitals.
Thus he erected the pillars at the portico of the temple. He named the right pillar Jachin and the left pillar Boaz.
The capitals on top were shaped like lilies, so the work on the pillars was completed.
He also made the Sea of cast bronze—ten cubits from brim to brim, circular in shape, and five cubits high. A line of thirty cubits measured around it.
Below the rim, ornamental gourds encircled it, ten per cubit, encircling the Sea all around; the gourds were cast in two rows as part of the Sea.
It stood on twelve oxen—three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east—with all their hindquarters toward the center.
It was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was like the rim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It held two thousand baths.
In addition, he made ten bronze stands; each was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
This was the design of the stands: they had side panels, and the panels were between the crossbars.
On the panels between the crossbars were lions, oxen, and cherubim; on the crossbars above and below the lions and oxen were wreathlike decorations.
Each stand had four bronze wheels and bronze axles, and its four corners had supports. Under the basin were cast supports, each bearing wreaths on either side.
The opening inside each stand’s rim was one cubit deep, with a round opening like a pedestal one and a half cubits wide. The rim bore carvings, and its frames were square, not round.
The four wheels were under the panels, and the axles of the wheels were attached to the stand; each wheel was one and a half cubits in diameter.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels: their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all cast metal.
Each stand had four handles, one on each corner, projecting from the stand.
At the top of each stand was a circular band half a cubit high, with supports and panels cast as part of the stand.
He engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the surfaces of the supports and panels wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.
This is how he made the ten stands, each cast from the same mold, of the same size and shape.
He also made ten bronze basins, each holding forty baths; each basin was four cubits across and was placed on one of the ten stands.
He set five stands on the south side of the temple and five on the north, and he set the Sea on the southeast corner of the temple.

Additionally, Hiram made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. So Hiram completed all the work he had undertaken for King Solomon in the house of the LORD: the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars; the two sets of network to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars; the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks—two rows of pomegranates for each network to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars; the ten stands; the ten basins on the stands; the Sea; the twelve oxen under the Sea; and the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. All these articles that Hiram made for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon left all these vessels unweighed, because there were so many; the weight of the bronze could not be measured.
Solomon also made all the furnishings for the house of the LORD: the golden altar; the golden table for the Bread of the Presence;
the lampstands of pure gold—five on the right side and five on the left before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold;
the basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and censers of pure gold; and the gold hinges for the doors of the inner sanctuary and for the doors of the main hall.

So all the work that King Solomon had done for the house of the LORD was completed. Then Solomon brought in the things his father David had dedicated—the silver, gold, and furnishings—and he put them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, together with all the heads of the tribes and the leaders of the ancestral houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, so that they might bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the city of David, which is Zion.
And all the men of Israel assembled before King Solomon at the feast in the month of Ethanim, which is the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had come, the priests took up the ark.
They brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.
King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, stood with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and oxen in such abundance that they could not be counted or numbered.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, into the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside; and they remain there to this day.
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses had placed there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel when they came out of the land of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD,
so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.
Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that He would dwell in thick darkness.
I have indeed built You a house, an exalted dwelling for You to inhabit forever."
Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel while the whole assembly stood.
He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with His hand has fulfilled what He promised with His mouth to David my father, saying,

'Since the day that I brought My people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel in which to build a house, that My name might be there; but I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.'
Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to David my father, 'Because it was in your heart to build a house for My name, you did well that it was in your heart.
Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for My name.'

Now the LORD has fulfilled His word that He spoke, for I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
And there I have set a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that He made with our fathers, when He brought them out of the land of Egypt."
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven,

and said, "O the LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to Your servants who walk before You with all their heart.
You who have kept with Your servant David my father what You promised him; You spoke with Your mouth and with Your hand You have fulfilled it, as it is this day.

Now therefore, O the LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant David my father what You promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before Me as you have walked before Me.'
And now, O God of Israel, let Your word be confirmed, which You have spoken to Your servant David my father.
"But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain You; how much less this house that I have built!
Yet have regard to the prayer of Your servant and to his plea, O the LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that Your servant prays before You this day,
that Your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which You have said, 'My name shall be there,' that You may hear the prayer that Your servant shall pray toward this place.
And listen to the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And hear in heaven Your dwelling place, and when You hear, forgive.
"If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath, and comes and swears before Your altar in this house,
then hear in heaven and act and judge Your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his way upon his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.
"When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they turn again to You and acknowledge Your name and pray and plead with You in this house,
then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel and bring them again to the land that You gave to their fathers.
"When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against You, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge Your name and turn from their sin, when You afflict them,

then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants, Your people Israel, when You teach them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain upon Your land, which You have given to Your people for an inheritance.

"If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is,
whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all Your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and spreading out his hands toward this house,
then hear in heaven Your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each man according to all his ways, as You know his heart, for You alone know the hearts of all the children of mankind,
that they may fear You all the days that they live in the land that You gave to our fathers.
"Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of Your people Israel, comes from a far country for Your name's sake
(for they shall hear of Your great name and Your mighty hand and Your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house,

hear in heaven Your dwelling place and do according to all that the foreigner calls to You, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by Your name.

"If Your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way You shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that You have chosen and the house that I have built for Your name,
then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.
"If they sin against You—for there is no one who does not sin—and You are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near,

yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with You in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely; we have committed wickedness,'

and if they return to You with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to You toward their land, which You gave to their fathers, the city that You have chosen, and the house that I have built for Your name,
then hear in heaven Your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause

and forgive Your people who have sinned against You, and all their transgressions that they have committed against You, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them
(for they are Your people, and Your heritage, which You brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace).
Let Your eyes be open to the plea of Your servant and to the plea of Your people Israel, giving attention to them whenever they call to You.
For You separated them to Yourself from among all the peoples of the earth to be Your heritage, as You spoke through Moses Your servant, when You brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord, the LORD."
Now when Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven.
And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying,
"Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to His people Israel, according to all that He promised. Not one word has failed of all His good promise, which He promised by Moses His servant.
The LORD our God be with us, as He was with our fathers. May He not leave us or forsake us,
that He may incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways and to keep His commandments, His statutes, and His rules, which He commanded our fathers.

Let these words of mine, which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, that He may maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day requires,
that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other.
Let your hearts therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in His statutes and keeping His commandments, as at this day."
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifice before the LORD.
Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD.

The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to hold the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the fat of the peace offerings.
So Solomon and all Israel with him held the feast for seven days and seven more days, fourteen days in all, before the LORD our God, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt.

On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David His servant and to Israel His people.
When Solomon finished building the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and had accomplished everything he desired,
The LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, just as He had appeared to him at Gibeon.

The LORD said to him, “I have heard your prayer and your supplication, which you made before Me. I have consecrated this house that you built, to put My name there forever, and My eyes and My heart will be there for all time.
As for you, if you walk before Me as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and if you keep My statutes and My judgments,
then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, just as I promised David your father, saying, ‘You shall never lack a man on the throne of Israel.’
“But if you and your sons turn away from following Me and do not keep My commandments and My statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,
then I will cut off Israel from the land that I gave them, and the house that I consecrated for My name I will cast out of My sight. Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.

And this house, though now exalted, will become a heap of ruins; everyone who passes by it will be appalled and will hiss, and they will say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this house?’

Then people will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and embraced other gods, worshiping and serving them; therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster upon them.’”
At the end of twenty years, during which Solomon built the two houses—the house of the LORD and the royal palace—
King Hiram of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired. Then King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.
But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities Solomon had given him, they did not please him.
He said, “What are these cities that you have given me, my brother?” Hiram called them the land of Cabul to this day.
Hiram sent to the king one hundred twenty talents of gold.
This is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon conscripted to build the house of the LORD, his own palace, the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer; he burned it with fire and killed the Canaanites who lived in the city. Then he gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife.
So Solomon rebuilt Gezer and Lower Beth-horon,
as well as Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness of the land,
and all the storage cities that Solomon had, the cities for his chariots, the cities for his cavalry, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout his entire realm.
All the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—those who were not Israelites—
their descendants who remained in the land after them, whom the Israelites had not been able to devote to destruction, Solomon conscripted as forced laborers to this day.
But Solomon did not enslave any of the Israelites, for they were the men of war, his servants, his officials, his commanders, his chariot officers, and his cavalry.
These were the chief officers over Solomon’s work: five hundred fifty who ruled over the people doing the work.
But Pharaoh’s daughter moved up from the City of David to the house that Solomon had built for her; then he built the Millo.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he had built to the LORD, and he burned incense before the LORD. So he finished the house.
King Solomon also built a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.
Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, sailors who knew the sea, together with Solomon’s servants.
They sailed to Ophir and took from there four hundred twenty talents of gold, and brought it to King Solomon.
Now when the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions.
She arrived in Jerusalem with a very great caravan—camels bearing spices, an abundance of gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and spoke with him about everything on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was hidden from the king that he did not explain to her.
When the queen of Sheba saw all the wisdom of Solomon, the palace he had built,

the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance and apparel of his ministers, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented at the house of the LORD, she was left breathless.
She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom was true.
I did not believe those reports until I came and saw with my own eyes; indeed, not even half had been told me. You have surpassed the report I heard in both wisdom and prosperity.”
“How blessed are your men! How blessed are these servants of yours who stand continually before you, hearing your wisdom!
Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD has loved Israel forever, He has made you king to execute justice and righteousness.”
She gave the king 120 talents of gold, a vast quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again did such an abundance of spices arrive as that which the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
Hiram’s fleet also brought gold from Ophir, and from Ophir it brought a great deal of almug wood and precious stones.

The king made the almug wood into supports for the house of the LORD and for the royal palace, and into lyres and harps for the singers. Never before had such almug wood been brought, nor has the like been seen to this day.
King Solomon gave the queen everything she desired and asked for, besides what he gave her from his royal bounty. Then she departed and returned to her own country, she and her servants.
The weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents,
besides that from the merchants and traders, and from all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of gold went into each shield.
He also made three hundred shields of hammered gold, with three minas of gold in each shield, and he placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, and its back was rounded at the top. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with two lions standing beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood there, one at each end of the six steps. Nothing like it had ever been made for any kingdom.
All King Solomon’s drinking vessels were gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. In Solomon’s days silver was considered of little value.
For the king had a fleet of Tarshish ships at sea with Hiram. Once every three years the fleet returned, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
The whole world sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart.
Year after year, each visitor brought his tribute: articles of silver and gold, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon accumulated chariots and horsemen: he had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, which he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees in the foothills.
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s merchants purchased them from Kue at the prevailing price.
A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty. They were then exported to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram.
Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter—Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women.

They came from the nations about which the LORD had said to the Israelites, “You shall not intermarry with them, nor shall they intermarry with you, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” Yet Solomon clung to them in love.
He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned his heart aside.
For when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not fully devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father had been.
Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
Thus Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not follow the LORD wholeheartedly, as his father David had.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, on the hill east of Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the Ammonites.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
Now the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
He had commanded Solomon concerning this very matter, that he should not follow other gods; yet Solomon did not keep what the LORD had commanded.

So the LORD said to Solomon, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.
Nevertheless, I will not do it during your lifetime, for the sake of David your father; I will tear it from the hand of your son.
Yet I will not tear away the whole kingdom; I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David My servant and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”
Then the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon—Hadad the Edomite, who was of the royal line in Edom.
For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army had gone up to bury the slain, he had struck down every male in Edom.
(Joab and all Israel had remained there six months, until every male in Edom had been cut off.)
But Hadad, still a young boy, fled to Egypt with some Edomites among his father’s servants.
They set out from Midian and came to Paran; then they took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave Hadad a house, assigned him food, and gave him land.
Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so Pharaoh gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, Queen Tahpenes.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s palace; and Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s palace among the sons of Pharaoh.
But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David had died and that Joab, the commander of the army, was dead, he said to Pharaoh, “Send me away, that I may go to my own country.”
Pharaoh said to him, “But what have you lacked while with me, that you now seek to go to your own country?” And Hadad answered, “Nothing; nevertheless, you must surely let me go.”
