Naaman said, "Please, take two talents." And he urged him. He tied up two talents of silver in two bags, along with two sets of clothing, and gave them to two of his servants, who carried them ahead of Gehazi.
When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the gifts from their hands and stored them in the house. Then he dismissed the men, and they left.
He went in and stood before his master. Elisha said to him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" "Your servant went nowhere," he replied.

Then he said to him, "Did not my heart go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants?"
"Therefore the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever." And he went out from his presence a leper, as white as snow.
The company of prophets said to Elisha, “Behold, the place where we dwell before you is too cramped for us.”
“Please let us go to the Jordan, and each of us take a beam from there, so that we may make a place for ourselves to dwell.” He said, “Go.”
Then one of them said, “Please be willing to go with your servants.” And he said, “I will go.”
So he went with them; and when they came to the Jordan, they cut down trees.
But as one of them was felling a beam, the iron axe head fell into the water, and he cried out, “Alas, my lord! It was borrowed.”
The man of God said, “Where did it fall?” And when he showed him the place, he cut off a stick and threw it in there, and the iron floated.
Then he said, “Lift it out for yourself.” So he reached out his hand and took it.
Now the king of Aram was at war with Israel, and he took counsel with his servants, saying, “I will camp at such and such a place.”
But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, saying, “Beware that you do not pass this place, for the Arameans are coming down there.”
So the king of Israel sent to the place that the man of God had told him about; he warned him, and he kept watch there more than once or twice.
This troubled the heart of the king of Aram, so he called his servants and said to them, “Will you not tell me which of us is for the king of Israel?”
And one of his servants said, “No, my lord the king; but Elisha the prophet, who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom.”
So he said, “Go and see where he is, that I may send and take him.” And they told him, “Behold, he is in Dothan.”
Therefore he sent horses and chariots and a heavy force there; they came by night and surrounded the city.
When the servant of the man of God rose early and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was surrounding the city. He said to his master, “Alas, my lord! What shall we do?”
He said, “Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”

Then Elisha prayed to the LORD, “Please open his eyes that he may see.” And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw; and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
And when they came down to him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, “Strike this people with blindness, please.” And He struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.
Then Elisha said to them, “This is not the way, and this is not the city; follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek.” And he led them to Samaria.
When they had entered Samaria, Elisha said to the LORD, “Open the eyes of these, that they may see.” And the LORD opened their eyes, and they saw; and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, “My father, shall I strike them? Shall I strike them?”

He said, “You shall not strike them. Would you strike those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master.”
So he prepared a great feast for them; and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the bands of Arameans did not come again into the land of Israel.
Afterward Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered all his army and went up and besieged Samaria.
And there was a great famine in Samaria; and behold, they besieged it until a donkey’s head was sold for eighty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a kab of dove dung for five shekels.
As the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, “Help, my lord the king!”
He said, “If the LORD does not help you, how can I help you? From the threshing floor or from the winepress?”
And the king said to her, “What is your trouble?” She said, “This woman said to me, ‘Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.’
So we boiled my son and ate him. And the next day I said to her, ‘Give your son, that we may eat him,’ but she hid her son.”
When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes; and as he was passing along on the wall, the people saw that he had sackcloth beneath on his flesh.
Then he said, “May God do so to me, and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on him today.”

Now Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. The king sent a messenger to him; but before the messenger came to him, Elisha said to the elders, “Do you see how this son of a murderer has sent to take away my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold him fast at the door. Is not the sound of his master’s feet behind him?”
While he was still speaking with them, behold, the messenger came down to him; and he said, “Behold, this evil is from the LORD; why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”

Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD. This is what the LORD says: 'Tomorrow at this time, at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel.'"

The officer on whose arm the king leaned said to the man of God, "Look—even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could this happen?" Then Elisha replied, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
Four leprous men were at the entrance of the gate. They said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die?"

One of them said, "If we go into the city, the famine is there and we will die; if we stay here, we die as well. Come, let us surrender to the Aramean camp. If they spare us, we live; if they kill us, we die."
At twilight they set out for the Aramean camp. When they reached its edge, there was no one there.

For the Lord had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots and horses—a great army. They said to one another, "Look, the king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us."
They rose and fled at twilight, abandoning their tents, horses, and donkeys. They left the camp exactly as it was and ran for their lives.

When those lepers reached the edge of the camp, they entered a tent, ate and drank, and carried off silver, gold, and clothing, which they hid. Then they went to another tent, took more, and hid that too.

They said to one another, "We are not doing right. Today is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent. If we wait until morning, guilt will catch up with us. Come now, let us go and report to the king."
They went and called to the gatekeepers, saying, "We went to the Aramean camp, and there is not a soul there—only horses and donkeys tied up, and tents just as they were."
The gatekeepers shouted the news and relayed it to the royal household.

The king got up at night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Arameans are doing to us. They know we are starving, so they have withdrawn from the camp to hide in the countryside, thinking that when the Israelites leave the city, they can capture them alive and take the city."

One of his servants replied, "Let a few men take five of the horses still left in the city. They are in the same condition as the rest of Israel—indeed, as those who have already perished. Let us send them out and see what happens."
So the king sent two chariots with horses after the Aramean army, ordering, "Go and investigate."
They followed the trail as far as the Jordan and found the whole road strewn with clothing and equipment the Arameans had discarded in their panic. The messengers returned and reported to the king.
The people went out and plundered the camp, and prices fell exactly as the the LORD had promised: a seah of fine flour for a shekel and two seahs of barley for a shekel.

The king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him there as they rushed through, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold when the king came to him.
For the man of God had told the king, "Tomorrow at this time, at the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel."
The officer had replied, "Look—even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could this happen?" And Elisha had answered, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
And so it happened: the people trampled him at the gate, and he died.

Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and go—you and your household—and dwell wherever you can dwell, for the LORD has decreed a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years."
The woman arose and did as the man of God had said; she went with her household and dwelt in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
When the seven years had ended, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines and went to the king to appeal for her house and her field.
The king was speaking with Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, and said, "Please tell me all the great things that Elisha has done."

While Gehazi was recounting to the king how Elisha had restored a dead man to life, the woman whose son he had restored to life came to appeal to the king for her house and her field. Gehazi said, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha restored to life."

The king asked the woman about it, and she told him. Then the king appointed an official for her and said, "Restore to her everything that was hers, together with all the produce of the field from the day she left the land until now."
Elisha came to Damascus while Ben-hadad, king of Aram, was ill. When it was reported to him, "The man of God has come here,"
the king said to Hazael, "Take a gift in your hand and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this illness?'"

So Hazael went to meet him, taking with him a gift of every good thing of Damascus, forty camel loads. He came and stood before Elisha and said, "Your son Ben-hadad, king of Aram, has sent me to you to ask, 'Shall I recover from this illness?'"
Elisha said to him, "Go and say to him, 'You will certainly recover.' Yet the LORD has shown me that he will certainly die."
Elisha fixed his gaze on him and stared until Hazael felt ashamed; then the man of God wept.

Hazael asked, "Why does my lord weep?" Elisha answered, "Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites: you will set their fortresses on fire, you will kill their young men with the sword, you will dash their little ones to pieces, and you will rip open their pregnant women."
Hazael said, "What is your servant, a dog, that he should do so great a thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram."
Hazael left Elisha and returned to his master. When Ben-hadad asked, "What did Elisha say to you?" he answered, "He told me that you would certainly live."
But the next day Hazael took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king's face, so that he died. Then Hazael reigned in his place.
In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah.
He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for Ahab's daughter was his wife; and he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.
Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah, for the sake of His servant David, because He had promised to preserve a lasting royal line for him and his descendants forever.
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah and set up a king over themselves.
Then Joram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots. He rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders, but his troops fled to their tents.
So Edom has been in revolt against Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.
The rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
In the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri, king of Israel.
He walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, because he was related by marriage to the house of Ahab.
He went with Joram son of Ahab to war against Hazael, king of Aram, at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram.

King Joram returned to Jezreel to be healed of the wounds that the Arameans had inflicted on him at Ramah when he fought against Hazael, king of Aram. And Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to see Joram son of Ahab, because Joram was sick.
Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Prepare yourself and take this flask of oil in your hand, then go to Ramoth-gilead.
When you arrive there, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Then go in, get him away from his companions, and take him into an inner room.
Then take the flask of oil, pour it on his head, and say, 'This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee without lingering.
So the young prophet went to Ramoth-gilead.
When he arrived, the commanders of the army were sitting there. He said, "I have a message for you, commander." Jehu asked, "For which of us?" He replied, "For you, commander."

Then Jehu got up and went into the house. The prophet poured the oil on his head and declared, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel.'"
He continued, "You are to strike down the house of Ahab, your master, so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and of all the LORD's servants shed by Jezebel.
The whole house of Ahab will perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, both slave and free, in Israel.
I will make the house of Ahab like the houses of Jeroboam son of Nebat and Baasha son of Ahijah.
And the dogs will devour Jezebel in the plot of ground at Jezreel, and no one will bury her." Then he opened the door and fled.
When Jehu went out to his master's servants, they asked him, "Is everything all right? Why did this madman come to you?" He said to them, "You know the man and his talk."
"That's a lie," they said. "Tell us now." So Jehu said, "He told me, 'This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel.'"
Then each man quickly took his garment and put it under Jehu on the bare steps, blew the trumpet, and proclaimed, "Jehu is king!"
Thus Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, conspired against Joram. Now Joram and all Israel had been defending Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Aram.

But King Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans had inflicted on him in his battle with Hazael king of Aram. So Jehu said, "If you are willing, let no fugitive leave the city to go and report in Jezreel."
Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, because Joram was lying there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see Joram.

When the watchman standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu's troops approaching, he called out, "I see a company!" Joram said, "Take a horseman and send him to meet them, and have him ask, 'Is it peace?'"

So a horseman rode off to meet Jehu and said, "This is what the king says: 'Is it peace?'" Jehu replied, "What do you have to do with peace? Fall in behind me." The watchman reported, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."
Then the king sent a second horseman, who went to them and said, "This is what the king says: 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Fall in behind me."
Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu son of Nimshi—he drives like a madman."

Then Joram said, "Hitch up my chariot." So they hitched it up, and Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah rode out, each in his own chariot, to meet Jehu. They met him in the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.
When Joram saw Jehu, he asked, "Is it peace, Jehu?" Jehu replied, "How can there be peace as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?"
Joram turned his chariot and fled, calling to Ahaziah, "Treachery, Ahaziah!"
Then Jehu drew his bow and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow pierced his heart, and he collapsed in his chariot.

Then Jehu said to Bidkar his officer, "Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. Remember that when you and I were riding side by side behind his father Ahab, the LORD lifted up this prophecy against him:

'As surely as I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons yesterday,' declares the LORD, 'I will repay you in this very field,' declares the LORD. Now, therefore, pick him up and throw him into the field, in accordance with the word of the LORD."

When Ahaziah king of Judah saw this, he fled by the road to Beth-haggan. Jehu pursued him, shouting, "Shoot him too!" So they shot him in his chariot on the ascent to Gur, near Ibleam, and he fled to Megiddo and died there.
Then his servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David.
In the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab, Ahaziah had become king over Judah.
When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. She painted her eyes, arranged her hair, and looked out of a window.
As Jehu entered the gate, she called out, "Is it peace, Zimri, you murderer of your master?"
He looked up at the window and called, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked down at him.
"Throw her down!" he said. So they threw her down, and some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and Jehu trampled her underfoot.
Then Jehu went in and ate and drank. Afterward he said, "Attend to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter."
But when they went to bury her, they found nothing but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.

They returned and told Jehu, who said, "This is the word of the LORD that He spoke through His servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour the flesh of Jezebel.
Jezebel's corpse will be like dung on the surface of the field in the plot at Jezreel, so that no one will say, "This is Jezebel."'"
Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria—to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of Ahab's sons—saying,
“Now, then, when this letter reaches you, you have your master's sons with you, together with chariots, horses, fortified cities, and weapons.
Choose the best and most capable of your master's sons, set him on his father's throne, and fight for your master's house.”
But they were terrified and said, “Look—the two kings could not withstand him. How, then, can we stand?”

So the palace administrator, the city governor, the elders, and the guardians sent word to Jehu: “We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say. We will not proclaim anyone king. Do whatever seems right in your eyes.”

Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, “If you are for me and will obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and bring them to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” Now the king's sons—seventy men—were with the leading men of the city, who were raising them.
As soon as the letter reached them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered all seventy, placed their heads in baskets, and sent them to him at Jezreel.
When the messenger arrived and reported, “They have brought the heads of the king's sons,” Jehu said, “Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until morning.”
Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood before all the people and said, “You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these?
Know, then, that not one word of the LORD concerning the house of Ahab will fail to come to pass, for the LORD has accomplished what He spoke through His servant Elijah.”
So Jehu struck down everyone left of Ahab's house in Jezreel—his chief men, his close friends, and his priests—until no survivor remained.
Then he set out for Samaria. While he was on the way, at Beth-eked of the Shepherds,

Jehu met the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah and asked, “Who are you?” They replied, “We are the brothers of Ahaziah, and we have come down to greet the sons of the king and the sons of the queen mother.”
He ordered, “Seize them alive.” So they seized them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked—forty-two men—and spared none of them.

When he left there, he met Jehonadab son of Rechab coming to meet him. He greeted him and asked, “Is your heart as true to mine as mine is to yours?” Jehonadab answered, “It is.” Jehu said, “If so, give me your hand.” So he gave him his hand, and Jehu drew him up into the chariot beside him.
And he said, “Come with me and witness my zeal for the LORD.” So he had him ride in his chariot.
When he reached Samaria, he struck down everyone remaining to Ahab in Samaria until he had destroyed them, according to the word of the LORD that He had spoken to Elijah.
Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, “Ahab served Baal only a little, but Jehu will serve him much more.

Now summon to me all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests; let no one be absent, for I intend to offer a great sacrifice to Baal. Anyone who is absent shall not live.” But Jehu acted deceitfully, intending to destroy the worshipers of Baal.
Jehu ordered, “Consecrate a solemn assembly for Baal.” So they proclaimed it.
Jehu sent word throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that not a man was left who did not come. They entered the house of Baal, and it was filled from end to end.
He said to the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for all the worshipers of Baal.” So he brought out robes for them.

Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab son of Rechab and said to the worshipers of Baal, “Search carefully and make sure no servant of the LORD is here among you—only worshipers of Baal.”

Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Meanwhile, Jehu had posted eighty men outside and commanded, “If any man lets one of those I am bringing into your hands escape, his life shall be forfeited for the life of the one who escapes.”

As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guards and officers, “Go in and kill them; let no one escape.” So they put them to the sword, and the guards and officers threw the bodies out and went into the inner chamber of the house of Baal.
They brought out the sacred pillar from the house of Baal and burned it.
They tore down the pillar of Baal, demolished the temple of Baal, and made it a latrine, which it remains to this day.
Thus Jehu eradicated Baal worship from Israel.
But Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he had caused Israel to commit—the golden calves at Bethel and Dan.

And the LORD said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in My eyes and have dealt with the house of Ahab according to all that was in My heart, your sons will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.”
But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart; he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, by which he had made Israel sin.
In those days the LORD began to reduce the territory of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout all Israel's borders:
from the Jordan eastward—all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, the Reubenites, and the Manassites—from Aroer by the Arnon Gorge through Gilead and Bashan.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehu, all that he did, and all his might—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.
The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
When Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, saw that her son was dead, she rose up and destroyed the whole royal line.

But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash, the son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were being put to death. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom, concealing him from Athaliah so that he was not killed.
So Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD for six years, while Athaliah reigned over the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, and the guards, and had them brought to him into the house of the LORD, and in the house of the LORD he made a covenant with them, put them under oath, and showed them the king’s son.
He commanded them, “This is what you are to do: A third of you who come on duty on the Sabbath are to guard the king’s palace.
A third are to be at the Sur gate, and a third at the gate behind the guards. You are to guard the temple.
The two divisions that would normally go off duty on the Sabbath are to guard the house of the LORD for the king.

You must surround the king on every side, each man with his weapon in hand. Anyone who breaches the ranks is to be put to death. Stay with the king wherever he goes, when he leaves and when he returns.”
So the commanders of hundreds did everything that Jehoiada the priest commanded. Each man took his men—those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty—and came to Jehoiada the priest.
Then the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in the house of the LORD.
The guards stood with weapons in hand around the king, from the south side of the house of the LORD to the north side, near the altar and the house of the LORD.

Then Jehoiada brought out the king’s son, placed the crown on him, gave him the Testimony, and proclaimed him king. They anointed him, and the people clapped their hands and shouted, “Long live the king!”
When Athaliah heard the noise of the guards and the people, she went into the house of the LORD to see the people.

She looked and saw the king standing by the pillar, according to custom, with the officers and trumpeters beside the king. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and cried out, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest ordered the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army, “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.”
So they seized her, and she went by way of the horse gate to the king’s palace, where she was put to death.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they would be the LORD’s people, and also between the king and the people.

All the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed its altars and idols to pieces, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altars. Then Jehoiada the priest posted guards over the house of the LORD.

He took with him the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD and entered the king’s palace by way of the gate of the guards. The king sat on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They put Athaliah to death with the sword at the king’s palace.
Joash was seven years old when he became king.
In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah of Beersheba.
Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD throughout all his days, because Jehoiada the priest had instructed him.
Nevertheless, the high places were not removed, and the people continued to sacrifice and burn incense on the high places.

Jehoash said to the priests, “All the silver brought into the house of the LORD as sacred gifts—the silver assessed for each person, and all the silver that anyone willingly brings to the house of the LORD—
let the priests take it, each from his associate, and use it to repair every breach found in the house of the LORD.”
But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had not repaired the breaches of the house of the LORD.

So King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and asked them, “Why have you not repaired the breaches of the house of the LORD? Now take no more silver from your associates; instead, hand it over for the repair of the house of the LORD.”
The priests agreed to receive no more silver from the people and to stop repairing the house themselves.

Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD. The priests who guarded the threshold put into it all the silver brought into the house of the LORD.
Whenever they saw that the chest held a large amount of silver, the king’s secretary and the high priest would come, count the silver found in the house of the LORD, and put it in bags.
They then gave the weighed silver to those supervising the work on the house of the LORD, and these men paid it to the carpenters and builders working on the house of the LORD,
as well as to the masons and stonecutters. They also bought timber and dressed stone to repair the breaches of the house of the LORD, and they funded everything else needed to strengthen the house.
However, no silver cups, snuffers, basins, trumpets, or any gold or silver vessels were made for the house of the LORD from the money brought into the house of the LORD.
Instead, they gave it to the workmen, who used it to repair the house of the LORD.
Moreover, they did not require an accounting from the men into whose hands they entrusted the silver to pay the workmen, because those men acted faithfully.
The silver from guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.
Then Hazael king of Aram marched up, fought against Gath, and captured it. Afterward, Hazael turned his forces toward Jerusalem.

King Jehoash of Judah took all the sacred objects that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, kings of Judah, had dedicated, along with his own sacred objects, and all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and sent them to Hazael king of Aram; so Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem.
As for the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
His servants conspired against him and struck down Joash at the house of Millo, on the road that descends to Silla.
Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer, his servants, struck him, and he died. They buried him with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Amaziah reigned in his place.
In the twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned seventeen years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD by walking in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he had caused Israel to commit, and he did not depart from them.
So the LORD's anger burned against Israel, and throughout those days He delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Aram and into the hand of Ben-Hadad his son.
Then Jehoahaz implored the LORD, and the LORD heeded him, because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram was inflicting upon Israel.
The LORD granted Israel a deliverer, so that they escaped from the power of Aram, and the Israelites dwelt in their homes as they had formerly.
Nevertheless, they did not turn aside from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he had caused Israel to commit, but persisted in them; moreover, the Asherah remained standing in Samaria.
For the king of Aram had reduced the army of Jehoahaz to a mere fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, having destroyed the rest and reduced them to dust, as grain is threshed.
As for the remaining acts of Jehoahaz, all that he did and his might, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Jehoahaz slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Joash reigned in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned sixteen years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not depart from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he had caused Israel to commit, but persisted in them.

As for the remaining acts of Jehoash, all that he did and his might, including the war he waged against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Jehoash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam ascended his throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
Now Elisha had fallen ill with the sickness that would kill him. Jehoash king of Israel went down to him and wept over him, crying, “My father! My father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!”
Elisha said to him, “Take a bow and arrows,” so he took a bow and arrows.
“Take the bow in your hands,” he said to the king of Israel. When he had taken it, Elisha laid his hands upon the king's hands.

“Open the east window,” he said, and he opened it. “Shoot!” Elisha commanded, and he shot. “The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram!” Elisha proclaimed. “You will completely destroy the Arameans at Aphek.”
Then he said, “Take the arrows,” and he took them. “Strike the ground,” Elisha told him. He struck it three times and then stopped.
The man of God grew angry with him and said, “You should have struck the ground five or six times; then you would have completely destroyed Aram. But now you will defeat it only three times.”
Elisha died and was buried. Now bands of Moabite raiders were invading the land each spring.

Once, as some Israelites were burying a man, they suddenly saw a raiding band, so they threw the man's body into Elisha's tomb. When the body touched Elisha's bones, the man revived and stood on his feet.
Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout all the days of Jehoahaz.

But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them; He turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to this day He has neither destroyed them nor cast them from His presence.
Hazael king of Aram died, and his son Ben-Hadad reigned in his place.

Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-Hadad son of Hazael the cities that he had seized in battle from his father Jehoahaz. Three times Jehoash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.
In the second year of Joash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash began to reign as king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he ascended the throne, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jehoaddan, a native of Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, though not as David his father had done; instead, he followed in every respect the example his father Joash had set.
Nevertheless, the high places were not removed, and the people continued to sacrifice and burn incense on them.
Once his authority was firmly established, he executed the servants who had assassinated his father the king.

Yet he did not put the murderers’ children to death, in obedience to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; rather, each person shall die for his own sin.”
He also struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, captured Sela in battle, and renamed it Joktheel, the name by which it is still known.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, with this challenge: “Come, let us meet in battle.”

Jehoash king of Israel sent back this reply to Amaziah king of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon sent word to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son in marriage.’ Then a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thistle.
You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart is lifted up with pride. Enjoy your glory and remain at home. Why provoke calamity, so that you fall—you and Judah with you?”
But Amaziah refused to listen. So Jehoash king of Israel advanced, and the two kings met in battle at Beth-shemesh in Judah.
Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled home.

At Beth-shemesh, Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash, son of Ahaziah. He then marched on Jerusalem and tore down its wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, a distance of four hundred cubits.
He seized all the gold and silver and every vessel found in the house of the LORD and in the royal treasuries, together with the hostages, and then returned to Samaria.
The remaining deeds of Jehoash—his accomplishments, his valor, and his war with Amaziah king of Judah—are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and his son Jeroboam succeeded him.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of Amaziah’s deeds are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
A conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish; but his pursuers followed him there and killed him.
They carried him back on horses and buried him in Jerusalem with his fathers in the City of David.
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and proclaimed him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after Amaziah’s death.
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years.
He did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from any of the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit.

He restored Israel’s border from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, in accordance with the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.
For the LORD had seen the bitter affliction of Israel—there was no one left to help them, bond or free, and no helper for Israel.
Yet the LORD had not decreed the obliteration of Israel’s name from under heaven; instead, He delivered them through Jeroboam son of Joash.
The remaining deeds of Jeroboam—all that he accomplished, his military exploits, and his recovery of Damascus and Hamath for Israel—are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam died and was buried with the kings of Israel, and his son Zechariah succeeded him.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam’s reign over Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah became king of Judah.
He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah, and she was from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done.
Only the high places were not removed; the people continued to sacrifice and burn incense on the high places.
The LORD struck the king with leprosy, and he remained a leper until his death. He lived in seclusion, while his son Jotham governed the royal household and judged the people of the land.
The rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Azariah died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Jotham succeeded him as king.
In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned six months.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done; he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had caused Israel to sin.
Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him and struck him down before the people, killing him; then he reigned in his place.
The rest of the acts of Zechariah are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
This was the word of the LORD that He had spoken to Jehu, saying, “Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel.” And so it was.
In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah’s reign over Judah, Shallum son of Jabesh became king, and he reigned one month in Samaria.
Menahem son of Gad marched up from Tirzah to Samaria, struck down Shallum son of Jabesh there, killed him, and reigned in his place.
The rest of the acts of Shallum, including the conspiracy he formed, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then Menahem attacked Tiphsah and all who were in it, along with its territory, because they refused to open their gates to him; he sacked the city and ripped open all its pregnant women.
In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Menahem son of Gad became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned ten years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD throughout his days; he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had caused Israel to sin.
Pul, king of Assyria, invaded the land, and Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver so that Pul would support him and strengthen his grip on the kingdom.

Menahem exacted the money from Israel—from every wealthy and influential man—fifty shekels of silver apiece, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria withdrew and did not remain in the land.
The rest of the acts of Menahem, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Menahem died and was buried with his fathers, and his son Pekahiah succeeded him as king.
In the fiftieth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD; he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had caused Israel to sin.

Pekah son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him and struck him down in Samaria, in the citadel of the royal palace, with the help of Argob, Arieh, and fifty Gileadites; he killed him and reigned in his place.
The rest of the acts of Pekahiah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD; he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had caused Israel to sin.

During the reign of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria invaded and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and the whole territory of Naphtali; he carried their inhabitants into exile in Assyria.
Hoshea son of Elah conspired against Pekah son of Remaliah, struck him down, killed him, and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah.
The rest of the acts of Pekah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah’s reign over Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done.
Only the high places were not removed; the people continued to sacrifice and burn incense on the high places. He built the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD.
The rest of the acts of Jotham, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.
Jotham died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David, his father’s city, and his son Ahaz succeeded him as king.
In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. Unlike David his forefather, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
Instead, he walked in the way of the kings of Israel and even made his son pass through the fire, following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the sons of Israel.
He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and beneath every leafy tree.
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, marched up to wage war. They besieged Jerusalem against Ahaz, yet they could not overpower him.
At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram and drove the Judeans from Elath; the Arameans came to Elath and have lived there to this day.

Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Aram and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are rising against me."
Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house, and he sent them as a bribe to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria listened to him and marched against Damascus, captured it, deported its people to Kir, and put Rezin to death.

King Ahaz traveled to Damascus to meet Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria. There he saw the altar at Damascus, and King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a sketch of the altar, along with a model of its design and all its workmanship.
Uriah the priest built the altar in accordance with everything King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, finishing it before King Ahaz returned from Damascus.
When the king returned from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and offered sacrifices on it.
He burned his burnt offering and his grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
He moved the bronze altar that stood before the LORD from the front of the temple—between the new altar and the house of the LORD—and set it on the north side of the altar.

King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, "Burn on the great altar the morning burnt offering and the evening burnt offering, the king's grain offering and his burnt offering, and the grain offering and burnt offerings of all the people of the land, with their drink offerings. Sprinkle on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and all the blood of the sacrifices. The bronze altar, however, will be for me to seek guidance."
Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the basins from them. He took down the Sea from the bronze bulls that supported it and set it on a stone pavement.
He also removed from the house of the LORD the Sabbath canopy that had been built there, along with the royal entryway, because of the king of Assyria.
As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz, all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place.
In the twelfth year of Ahaz’s reign over Judah, Hoshea son of Elah ascended to the throne of Israel in Samaria and reigned nine years.
He perpetrated evil in the sight of the LORD, though not to the extent of the kings of Israel who had preceded him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria campaigned against him, and Hoshea became his vassal, paying him tribute.

But the king of Assyria discovered Hoshea’s conspiracy—his envoys to So king of Egypt—and his failure to remit tribute as in previous years. Accordingly, the king of Assyria arrested and imprisoned him.
The king of Assyria then overran the whole land, advanced upon Samaria, and besieged it for three years.
In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and deported the Israelites to Assyria, settling them in Halah, in Gozan on the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes.

All this transpired because the Israelites sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up from the land of Egypt, out from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had venerated other gods
and conformed to the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites, as well as to the practices instituted by the kings of Israel.
The Israelites clandestinely committed acts against the LORD their God that were not right. From watchtower to fortified city, they erected high places in every city.
They set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and beneath every verdant tree.
They burned incense on all the high places, as the nations had done whom the LORD had driven out before them, and they did wicked things, provoking the LORD.
They served idols, although the LORD had said to them, “You shall not do this thing.”

Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah, saying, “Turn from your evil ways and keep My commandments and statutes, according to all the law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets.”
But they would not listen; rather, they stiffened their necks like their fathers, who had not believed in the LORD their God.

They rejected His statutes and the covenant He had made with their fathers, together with the decrees He had given them. They pursued worthless idols and thereby became worthless themselves; they followed the surrounding nations, although the LORD had commanded them not to imitate them.
They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God and made for themselves two cast-metal calves. They made an Asherah pole, worshiped the whole host of heaven, and served Baal.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire and practiced divination and soothsaying. They devoted themselves to doing evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him.
So the LORD was exceedingly angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence; only the tribe of Judah remained.
Yet even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but followed the practices Israel had introduced.
Therefore the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel. He afflicted them and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, until He had banished them from His presence.
When the LORD had torn Israel away from the house of David, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king; Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD and caused them to commit a great sin.
The Israelites walked in all the sins Jeroboam had committed, and they did not turn from them
until the LORD removed Israel from His presence, just as He had declared through all His servants the prophets. So Israel was carried away from its land to Assyria, where they remain to this day.

Then the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria and settled in its cities.
At the beginning of their residence there, they did not fear the LORD, so the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions killed some of them.

So they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The people you have resettled in the cities of Samaria do not know the customs of the God of the land. Therefore He has sent lions among them, and the lions are killing them.”
Then the king of Assyria commanded, “Send back one of the priests you carried off from there, and let him go and live there and teach them the customs of the God of the land.”
So one of the priests who had been carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and he taught them how to fear the LORD.

Nevertheless, the people of each nation continued to make their own gods and placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritans had made. Each nation made gods in the cities where it lived.
The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; the men of Hamath made Ashima.
The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
So they feared the LORD, but they also appointed priests from among themselves for the high places, and those priests sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places.
They feared the LORD, yet they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away.

To this day they persist in their former practices: they do not fear the LORD, nor do they follow the statutes, ordinances, law, and commandments that the LORD gave to the descendants of Jacob, whom He named Israel.
The LORD had made a covenant with them and commanded them: “Do not fear other gods; do not bow down to them; do not serve them; and do not sacrifice to them.
Instead, fear the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Bow down to Him and sacrifice to Him.
And you must carefully observe the statutes, ordinances, law, and commandments He wrote for you. Do not fear other gods.
Do not forget the covenant I have made with you, and do not fear other gods.
Rather, fear the LORD your God, and He will deliver you from the hand of all your enemies.”
But they would not listen; instead, they persisted in their former practices.
So these nations feared the LORD, but they also served their carved images. To this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did.
In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-nine years; his mother was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done.

He removed the high places, smashed the sacred stones, and cut down the Asherah poles. He also broke into pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it up to that time; he called it Nehushtan.
He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before or after him.
He held fast to the LORD and did not turn away from following Him; he kept the commands the LORD had given through Moses.
The LORD was with him, and he prospered in everything he undertook. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.
He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its surrounding territory, from watchtower to fortified city.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria advanced against Samaria and besieged it.
At the end of three years they captured it; Samaria fell in the sixth year of Hezekiah and the ninth year of Hoshea, king of Israel.
The king of Assyria deported Israel to Assyria and settled them in Halah, in Gozan on the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes.

This happened because they had not obeyed the LORD their God but had violated His covenant—everything that Moses, the servant of the LORD, had commanded. They neither listened to those commands nor carried them out.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

Then Hezekiah king of Judah sent this message to the king of Assyria at Lachish: “I have done wrong. Withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand.” So the king of Assyria imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah a tribute of three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in the temple of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace.
At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts he had overlaid, and he gave it to the king of Assyria.

Then the king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh, along with a large army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. They advanced, came to Jerusalem, and took their stand by the aqueduct of the Upper Pool on the road to the Fuller's Field.
They called for the king, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went out to meet them.
Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah that the great king, the king of Assyria, asks, ‘What confidence are you relying on?’
You claim to have counsel and strength for war, but those are empty words. On whom are you now relying, that you have rebelled against me?
Look, you are relying on Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff, which pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who trust in him.”

“And if you say to me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?
Come now, make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses if you can put riders on them.
How then can you repulse even one of my master's least officers, even though you are relying on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
Furthermore, have I come to attack and destroy this place without the LORD's sanction? The LORD Himself told me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.”

But Rabshakeh replied, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who, like you, will eat their own filth and drink their own urine?”
Then Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in Hebrew, “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!”
“This is what the king says: ‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you from my hand.’
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD by saying, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: ‘Make peace with me and come out to me. Then each of you will eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink water from his own cistern,

until I come and take you to a land like your own—a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive oil and honey—so that you may live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying the LORD will deliver us.’
Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did any of them deliver Samaria from my hand?
Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?”
The people remained silent and did not answer a word, because the king had commanded, “Do not answer him.”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD.
He sent Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the scribe, and the senior priests, all clothed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They said to him, “This is what Hezekiah says: ‘Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace, for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to taunt the living God, and will rebuke him for the words the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.’”
So the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master, ‘This is what the LORD says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me.
Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.’”
When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish and was fighting against Libnah, he returned and found him there.
Now Sennacherib had heard that Tirhakah king of Cush was marching out to fight against him, so he sent messengers to Hezekiah with this message:
“Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.
Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be rescued?
Did the gods of the nations my fathers destroyed deliver them—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar?
Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?”
Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers' hands and read them. Then he went up to the house of the LORD and spread them out before the LORD.
“O the LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.
Incline Your ear, O the LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O the LORD, and see. Listen to the words Sennacherib has sent to insult the living God.
Truly, O the LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands.
They have thrown their gods into the fire, for they were not gods but only wood and stone, fashioned by human hands.
Now, O the LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O the LORD, are God.”
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Because you have prayed to Me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, I have heard.”
“This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind your back.
Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel.

By your messengers you have reproached the Lord, and you have said that with your many chariots you ascended the heights of the mountains, the utmost heights of Lebanon, that you would cut down its tallest cedars and choicest cypresses, and that you would enter its farthest lodge and densest forest.
I dug wells and drank foreign waters; with the soles of my feet I dried up all the streams of Egypt.”
“Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it. Now I have brought it to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into piles of rubble.
Therefore their inhabitants, powerless, are dismayed and ashamed. They are like grass of the field, green plants, tender grass on the rooftops, scorched before it grows.
But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me.
Because you rage against Me and your arrogance has reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back by the way you came.”
“This will be a sign to you: This year you will eat what grows by itself, and in the second year what springs from that, but in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
The surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above.
For a remnant will go out from Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.”
“Therefore this is what the LORD says concerning the king of Assyria: He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow here; he will not come before it with a shield or build a siege ramp against it.
He will return by the way he came and will not enter this city.
For I will defend this city and save it, for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.”
That night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp. When the people arose early in the morning, there were all the dead bodies.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. Then his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.
In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “Thus says the LORD: ‘Set your affairs in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’”
He turned his face toward the wall and interceded with the LORD, saying,
“Please, O LORD, remember how I have lived before you in integrity and with an undivided heart, and how I have done what is good in your sight.” Then Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Before Isaiah had departed the middle courtyard, the word of the LORD came to him:

“Go back and say to Hezekiah, the leader of My people, ‘Thus says the LORD, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you, and on the third day you shall ascend to the house of the LORD.
I will extend your life by fifteen years, and I will rescue you and this city from the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.’”
Then Isaiah said, “Take a cake of figs.” So they took it and applied it to the boil, and he recovered.
Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I shall ascend to the house of the LORD on the third day?”
Isaiah replied, “This is the sign to you from the LORD that the LORD will fulfill what He has promised: Shall the shadow advance ten steps, or retreat ten steps?”
Hezekiah answered, “It is a trivial matter for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. No—let the shadow retreat ten steps.”
So Isaiah the prophet cried out to the LORD, and He made the shadow retreat ten steps from the point to which it had descended on the stairway of Ahaz.
At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, because he had heard of Hezekiah's illness.

Hezekiah received the messengers and showed them his entire treasury—silver, gold, spices, precious oil, his armory, and everything found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or throughout his realm that Hezekiah did not display to them.
Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked, “What did these men say, and from where have they come to you?” Hezekiah replied, “They have come from a distant land, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What have they seen in your house?” Hezekiah answered, “They have seen everything in my house. There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.”
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD:
Behold, the days are coming when everything in your house—and what your fathers have accumulated to this day—will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.
And some of your sons, descendants you yourself will father, will be taken away and made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “Will there not be peace and truth in my days?”

The remaining deeds of Hezekiah, all his might, and how he constructed the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city—are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Hezekiah died and was gathered to his ancestors, and his son Manasseh reigned in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD, after the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.

For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed, and he erected altars for Baal, and made an Asherah, as Ahab king of Israel had done, and worshiped and served all the host of heaven.
And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD said, “In Jerusalem I will put My name.”
And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.
He sacrificed his son in the fire, practiced soothsaying and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did much evil in the eyes of the LORD, provoking Him to anger.

He set the carved image of the Asherah that he had made in the house of which the LORD said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put My name forever.

And I will not again cause Israel to wander from the land that I gave to their fathers, if only they will be careful to do according to all that I commanded them, and according to all the Law that My servant Moses commanded them.”
But they did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray to do more evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the people of Israel.
The LORD spoke through His servants the prophets, saying,
“Because Manasseh king of Judah has done these abominations—he has acted more wickedly than all that the Amorites did who were before him—and has made Judah sin with his idols,
therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: ‘Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah that whoever hears of it will be utterly appalled.’
I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of the house of Ahab, and I will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down.
I will forsake the remnant of My inheritance and give them into the hand of their enemies, and they shall become a prey and a spoil to all their enemies,
because they have done evil in My sight and have provoked Me to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day.”
Moreover, Manasseh shed very much innocent blood, until he had filled Jerusalem from one end to the other, besides his sin by which he made Judah sin, to do evil in the eyes of the LORD.
Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and all that he did, and his sin that he sinned, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
And Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza. And Amon his son reigned in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Meshullemeth the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done.
He walked in all the way that his father walked, and served the idols that his father had served, and worshiped them.
He forsook the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD.
The servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his own house.
But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon, and the people made Josiah his son king in his place.
Now the rest of the acts of Amon that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
And they buried him in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah his son reigned in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah daughter of Adaiah, from Bozkath.
He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, walking in all the ways of his ancestor David and not turning aside to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the scribe, to the house of the LORD, saying,
“Go up to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count the money brought into the house of the LORD, which the keepers of the threshold have collected from the people.
Let it be given into the hand of those appointed to do the work in the house of the LORD, and let them give it to the workmen who are in the house of the LORD to repair the damage to the house—
to the carpenters, builders, and masons—and for buying timber and cut stone to repair the house.
But no accounting shall be made with them for the money given into their hand, because they deal faithfully.”
Then Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD.” And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.

Then Shaphan the scribe went to the king and brought back a report, saying, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house and have given it into the hand of the workmen appointed in the house of the LORD.”
Moreover, Shaphan the scribe told the king, “Hilkiah the priest has given me a book.” And Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.
Then the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,

“Go and inquire of the LORD for me and for the people and for all Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found; for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers did not obey the words of this book, to do according to all that is written concerning us.”

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went and spoke to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter.

She said to them, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to Me, ‘Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am bringing disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants—all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read—
because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods, provoking Me to anger with all the work of their hands. My wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched.
But to the king of Judah who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus you shall say to him, ‘Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Concerning the words that you have heard,

because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I spoke against this place and its inhabitants, that it should become a desolation and a curse, and you tore your clothes and wept before Me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.
Therefore, behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place.’”
And they brought the word back to the king.
Then the king summoned every elder of Judah and Jerusalem.

He ascended to the house of the LORD with all the men of Judah, all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest, and he read aloud in their hearing every word of the Book of the Covenant that had been discovered in the house of the LORD.

The king stood beside the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD, pledging to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and all his soul, and to establish the words of this covenant written in this book. Then all the people stood firm in the covenant.

The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the doorkeepers to remove from the temple of the LORD all the vessels made for Baal, Asherah, and all the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel.

He abolished the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had installed to burn incense on the high places in the cities of Judah and in the environs of Jerusalem—those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, to the moon, to the constellations, and to all the host of heaven.
He brought the Asherah pole out of the house of the LORD to the Kidron Valley beyond Jerusalem, where he burned it, ground it to dust, and scattered its dust upon the graves of the common people.
He demolished the quarters of the male cult prostitutes that were in the house of the LORD, where women wove hangings for Asherah.

Then Josiah gathered all the priests from the cities of Judah and defiled the high places where they had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba. He broke down the high places at the gates, including the high place at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which stood on the left at the city gate.
Although the priests of the high places did not ascend to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem, they ate unleavened bread among their brethren.
He defiled Topheth in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, so that no one might make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech.

He removed from the entrance to the house of the LORD the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun; they stood in the court near the chamber of Nathan-melech, an official. He also burned the chariots of the sun.

He tore down the altars that the kings of Judah had erected on the roof of the upper chamber of Ahaz, along with the altars Manasseh had erected in the two courts of the house of the LORD. He pulverized them on the spot and cast their dust into the Kidron Valley.

The king defiled the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Corruption, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
He shattered the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their sites with human bones.
