They buried him in the tomb he had cut out for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bed filled with spices and various kinds of perfumes blended by the perfumers’ art, and they made a very great fire in his honor.
His son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place, and he strengthened himself against Israel.
He stationed troops in all the fortified cities of Judah, and he put garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the former ways of his father David and did not seek the Baals.
Instead, he sought the God of his father and walked by His commandments rather than according to the practices of Israel.
So the LORD established the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, so that he had an abundance of riches and honor.
His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD, and he removed the high places and the Asherah poles from Judah.
In the third year of his reign, Jehoshaphat sent his officials—Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah—to teach in the cities of Judah.
With them were the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah, along with the priests Elishama and Jehoram.
They taught in Judah, having with them the Book of the Law of the LORD, and they went throughout all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
And the dread of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands surrounding Judah, so that they did not make war against Jehoshaphat.
Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat tribute and silver as a load, and the Arabs also brought him seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred goats.
Jehoshaphat grew stronger and stronger, and he built in Judah fortresses and store cities.
He had a great deal of property in the cities of Judah, and men of war—mighty men of valor—in Jerusalem.
These are their numbers according to their fathers’ houses for Judah: the commanders of thousands, Adnah the commander, and with him 300,000 mighty men of valor.
Next to him was Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000.
Next to him was Amasiah son of Zichri, who volunteered himself to the LORD, and with him 200,000 mighty men of valor.
From Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with 200,000 men armed with bow and shield.
Next to him was Jehozabad, with 180,000 ready for battle.
These were the men who served the king, in addition to those he stationed in the fortified cities throughout Judah.
Now Jehoshaphat had wealth and honor in abundance, and he allied himself with Ahab.
And after some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered for him and for the people with him many sheep and oxen, and persuaded him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

And Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat said to him, “I am as you are, and my people as your people; and we will be with you in the war.”
And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire today for the word of the the LORD.”

So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, four hundred men, and said to them, “Shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?” They said, “Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king.”
But Jehoshaphat said, “Is there not here besides a prophet of the the LORD, that we may inquire of him?”

And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the the LORD, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil. He is Micaiah the son of Imla.” And Jehoshaphat said, “Let not the king say so.”
Then the king of Israel called an officer and said, “Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imla.”

Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting each on his throne, arrayed in their robes, and they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets were prophesying before them.
And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron, and said, “Thus says the the LORD, ‘With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are consumed.’”
And all the prophets prophesied so, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and prosper, for the the LORD will give it into the hand of the king.”

And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “Behold, the words of the prophets are uniformly good for the king. Please let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak good.”
But Micaiah said, “As the the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak.”
And when he came to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?” And he said, “Go up and prosper, and they shall be given into your hand.”
And the king said to him, “How many times must I adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the the LORD?”
And he said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, like sheep that have no shepherd; and the the LORD said, ‘These have no master; let each of them return to his house in peace.’”
And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?”
And he said, “Therefore hear the word of the the LORD: I saw the the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing on His right hand and on His left.
“And the the LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one said this, and another said that.
“Then a spirit came forward and stood before the the LORD and said, ‘I will entice him.’ “And the the LORD said to him, ‘How?’
“And he said, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ “And He said, ‘You shall entice him, and you shall also prevail. Go out and do so.’
“Now therefore, behold, the the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets, and the the LORD has spoken disaster concerning you.”
Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, “Which way did the Spirit of the the LORD go from me to speak to you?”
And Micaiah said, “Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself.”
And the king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son,
and say, ‘Thus says the king, “Put this man in prison and feed him with bread of affliction and water of affliction until I return in peace.”’”
And Micaiah said, “If you ever return in peace, the the LORD has not spoken by me.” And he said, “Hear, O peoples, all of you!”
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and go into the battle, but you put on your robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into the battle.
Now the king of Aram had commanded the captains of his chariots, saying, “Do not fight with small or great, but only with the king of Israel.”

And when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “It is the king of Israel!” And they turned to fight against him; and Jehoshaphat cried out, and the the LORD helped him, and God turned them away from him.
And when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

And a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. And he said to the driver of his chariot, “Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am wounded.”
And the battle grew fierce that day, and the king of Israel held himself up in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening; and at sunset he died.
King Jehoshaphat of Judah returned safely to his home in Jerusalem.

Jehu son of Hanani, the seer, went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the the LORD? Because of this, the wrath of the the LORD is upon you.
Nevertheless, good things are found with you, for you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart to seek God.”
Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem, and he went out again among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brought them back to the the LORD, the God of their fathers.
He appointed judges in the land, in all the fortified cities of Judah.
He said to the judges, “Consider what you are doing, for you are not judging for man but for the the LORD, and He is with you in the matter of judgment.
Now let the fear of the the LORD be upon you; be careful and act, for with the the LORD our God there is no injustice, no partiality, and no accepting of bribes.”
In Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat also appointed some of the Levites, priests, and heads of Israelite families to judge for the the LORD and to settle disputes, and they returned to Jerusalem.
He commanded them, “Thus you shall act in faithfulness and with a whole heart, in the fear of the the LORD.

In every dispute that comes to you from your brothers who dwell in their cities—whether it involves bloodshed, law, commandment, statute, or judgment—warn them so that they do not incur guilt before the the LORD, and wrath will not come upon you and upon your brothers. Do this, and you will not be guilty.

Behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the the LORD, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in all matters of the king, and the Levites and officers are before you. Act with courage; the the LORD will be with those who do good.”
After this, the Moabites and Ammonites, along with some of the Meunites, came to wage war against Jehoshaphat.
Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A vast army is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the Sea. It is already at Hazazon-tamar (that is, En-gedi)."
Alarmed, Jehoshaphat resolved to inquire of the LORD, and he proclaimed a fast for all Judah.
The people of Judah came together to seek help from the LORD; indeed, they came from every town in Judah to seek Him.
Then Jehoshaphat stood up in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem at the temple of the LORD in the front of the new courtyard.
He said: "the LORD, God of our ancestors, are You not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. Power and might are in Your hand, and no one can withstand You.
Our God, did You not drive out the inhabitants of this land before Your people Israel and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham, Your friend?
They have lived in it and have built in it a sanctuary for Your Name, saying,
'If disaster comes upon us—sword, judgment, plague, or famine—we will stand before this house that bears Your Name and cry out to You in our distress, and You will hear us and save us.'
"But now here are men from Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, whose territory You would not allow Israel to invade when they came from Egypt; so they turned away from them and did not destroy them.
See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession You gave us as an inheritance.
Our God, will You not judge them? For we have no power to face this vast army that is attacking us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on You."
All the men of Judah, with their wives and children and little ones, stood there before the LORD.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, a Levite from the descendants of Asaph, as he stood in the assembly.

He said: "Listen, King Jehoshaphat and all who live in Judah and Jerusalem! This is what the LORD says: 'Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this vast army, for the battle is not yours but God's.
"Tomorrow march down against them. They will be climbing up by the Pass of Ziz, and you will find them at the end of the gorge in the Desert of Jeruel.

You will not have to fight this battle. Take up your positions; stand firm and see the deliverance the LORD will give you, Judah and Jerusalem. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged. Go out to face them tomorrow, and the LORD will be with you."
Jehoshaphat bowed down with his face to the ground, and all the people of Judah and Jerusalem fell down in worship before the LORD.
Then some Levites from the Kohathites and Korahites stood up and praised the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.

Early in the morning they left for the Desert of Tekoa. As they set out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Listen to me, Judah and people of Jerusalem! Have faith in the LORD your God and you will be upheld; have faith in His prophets and you will be successful."

After consulting the people, Jehoshaphat appointed men to sing to the LORD and to praise Him for the splendor of His holiness as they went out at the head of the army, saying, "Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever."
As they began to sing and praise, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir who were invading Judah, and they were defeated.
The Ammonites and Moabites rose up against the men from Mount Seir to destroy and annihilate them. After they finished slaughtering the men from Seir, they helped to destroy one another.
When the men of Judah came to the place that overlooks the desert and looked toward the vast army, they saw only dead bodies lying on the ground; no one had escaped.

So Jehoshaphat and his men went to carry off their plunder, and they found among them a great amount of equipment, clothing, and also articles of value—more than they could take away. There was so much plunder that it took them three days to collect it.
On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Berakah, where they praised the LORD. This is why it is called the Valley of Berakah to this day.
Then, led by Jehoshaphat, all the men of Judah and Jerusalem returned joyfully to Jerusalem, for the LORD had given them cause to rejoice over their enemies.
They entered Jerusalem and went to the temple of the LORD to the accompaniment of harps, lyres, and trumpets.
The fear of God came on all the surrounding kingdoms when they heard how the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.
And the kingdom of Jehoshaphat was at peace, for his God gave him rest on every side.
As for Jehoshaphat, he was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years. His mother's name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the ways of his father Asa and did not stray from them; he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD.
The high places, however, were not removed, and the people still had not set their hearts on the God of their ancestors.
As for the other events of Jehoshaphat's reign, from beginning to end, they are written in the annals of Jehu son of Hanani, which are included in the book of the kings of Israel.
Later, Jehoshaphat king of Judah made an alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel, who was guilty of wickedness.
He agreed with him to construct a fleet of trading ships. After building the ships at Ezion-geber,

Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have made an alliance with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." The ships were wrecked and were not able to set sail to trade.
When Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, his son Jehoram reigned in his place.
He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Israel.
Their father gave them many gifts of silver, gold, and precious things, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn.
When Jehoram had established himself over his father's kingdom and strengthened his position, he killed all his brothers with the sword, along with some of the princes of Israel.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done, for Ahab's daughter was his wife; and he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.
Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He had made with David, and because He had promised to preserve his dynasty for him and his descendants forever.
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah and set up a king over themselves.
Then Jehoram went out with his officers and all his chariots; the Edomites had surrounded him, but he and his chariot commanders rose up by night and struck them.
So Edom has been in revolt against Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from under his hand, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers.
Moreover, he made high places in the mountains of Judah, caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit spiritual adultery, and led Judah astray.

Then a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, “Thus says the LORD, the God of your father David: ‘Because you have not walked in the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or in the ways of Asa king of Judah,

but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have caused Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit spiritual adultery, as the house of Ahab committed spiritual adultery, and have also killed your brothers—those of your father's house—who were better than you,
behold, the LORD will strike your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions with a great plague;
and you will have severe sickness, a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the sickness, day by day.’”
Then the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabians who were near the Cushites.
They came up into Judah, invaded it, and carried away all the possessions found in the king's house, along with his sons and his wives, so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest.
After all this, the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.
In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of his sickness, and he died in great agony. His people did not make a funeral fire for him, as they had for his fathers.

He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. He passed away to no one's regret, and they buried him in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, because the raiding party that had come with the Arabs to the camp had killed all his older brothers. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign.
Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, daughter of Omri.
He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother counseled him to act wickedly.
He did evil in the sight of the the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for after his father's death they became his counselors to his ruin.
He also followed their counsel and went with Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, to war against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram.

Joram returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds he had received at Ramah in the battle against Hazael king of Aram. Then Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, because Joram was ill.
But Ahaziah's downfall came from God: when he came to Joram, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the the LORD had anointed to exterminate the house of Ahab.
While Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he discovered the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers who served Ahaziah, and he killed them.

He searched for Ahaziah, and they caught him while he was hiding in Samaria. They brought him to Jehu and killed him, then buried him, because they said, "He is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the the LORD with all his heart." Thus the house of Ahaziah had no strength to retain the kingdom.
When Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah, saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal heirs of the house of Judah.

But Jehoshabeath, the king's daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from the king's sons who were being slain, and she placed him and his nurse in a bedroom. Because Jehoshabeath, daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, was Ahaziah's sister, she hid him from Athaliah so that she did not kill him.
He remained hidden with them in the house of God for six years, while Athaliah reigned over the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada consolidated his authority and brought into covenant with him the commanders of hundreds—Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
They traveled throughout Judah, gathered the Levites from every city in Judah and the heads of Israel’s ancestral houses, and came to Jerusalem.
The whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. Jehoiada said to them, “Indeed, the king’s son will reign, just as the LORD has declared concerning the sons of David.
This is what you are to do: a third of you who are priests and Levites, those entering service on the Sabbath, shall serve as gatekeepers at the thresholds;
a third shall be at the royal palace, and a third at the Foundation Gate, while all the people remain in the courts of the house of the LORD.
“No one may enter the house of the LORD except the priests and Levites on duty; they may enter because they are consecrated, but all the people must observe the LORD’s mandate.
The Levites shall surround the king on every side, each with his weapon in hand, and anyone who enters the temple shall be put to death. You must stay with the king wherever he goes.”

So the Levites and all Judah did everything Jehoiada the priest commanded. Each man took his men—both those coming on duty and those going off duty on the Sabbath—for Jehoiada the priest had not dismissed any of the divisions.
Then Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears, shields, and bucklers of King David that were in the house of God.
He stationed all the people, each with his weapon in hand, around the king—from the south side of the temple to the north side, near the altar and the temple.
Then they brought out the king’s son, placed the crown on him, gave him the Testimony, and proclaimed him king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and cried, “Long live the king!”
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went to the people in the house of the LORD.

She looked and saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, with the officers and trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, while the singers, accompanied by musical instruments, led the praise. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and shouted, “Treason! Treason!”

Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army and said to them, “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.”
So they seized her, and when she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate of the royal palace, they put her to death there.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king that they would be the LORD’s people.
So all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down. They smashed its altars and idols, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars.

Moreover, Jehoiada entrusted the priests and the Levites whom David had assigned to the house of the LORD with the service of the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and singing, according to David’s arrangement.
He stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD, so that nothing unclean might enter.

He took with him the commanders of hundreds, the nobles, the rulers of the people, and all the people of the land, and brought the king down from the house of the LORD. They entered the royal palace through the Upper Gate and seated the king on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to death by the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah, from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD throughout the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada chose two wives for him, and he fathered sons and daughters.
Afterward Joash resolved in his heart to restore the house of the LORD.

He gathered the priests and Levites and said to them, “Go into the cities of Judah and collect, year by year, the money due from all Israel for repairing the house of your God, and see that you carry out the matter without delay.” But the Levites did not act promptly.

So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest and asked him, “Why have you not required the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the tax that Moses, the servant of the LORD, imposed on Israel for the tent of testimony?”
For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God and had even used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.
At the king’s command they made a chest and placed it outside, at the gate of the house of the LORD.
Then they issued a proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem, calling the people to bring to the LORD the tax that Moses, the servant of God, had imposed on Israel in the wilderness.
All the leaders and all the people rejoiced; they brought their contributions and cast them into the chest until it was full.

Whenever the Levites brought the chest to the king’s officials, and when they saw that there was much money, the king’s secretary and the officer of the chief priest would come, empty the chest, and carry it back to its place. They did this day after day, and they gathered money in abundance.

The king and Jehoiada gave it to those who were doing the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and they hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD, as well as ironworkers and bronzeworkers to strengthen it.
The workmen labored, and the restoration progressed under their hands; they restored the house of God to its original design and reinforced it.

When they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, and it was made into vessels for the house of the LORD—vessels for the service and for the burnt offerings, and dishes, and vessels of gold and silver. All the days of Jehoiada, burnt offerings were presented continually in the house of the LORD.
Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and he died at the age of one hundred thirty years.
They buried him with the kings in the City of David, because he had done good in Israel, both toward God and toward His house.
After Jehoiada’s death, the leaders of Judah came and paid homage to the king, and the king listened to them.
They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and the idols; and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem because of this guilt of theirs.
Yet He sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD, and they testified against them; but they would not listen.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood above the people and said to them, “Thus says God: Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.”
But they conspired against him, and at the king’s command they stoned him in the court of the house of the LORD.
King Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had shown him, but killed his son. As he died, he said, “May the LORD see and avenge.”
At the turn of the year, the army of Aram came up against him; they came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the leaders of the people, and sent all their plunder to the king of Damascus.

Although the army of Aram had come with only a small force, the LORD delivered a very great army into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. So they executed judgment on Joash.

When they departed from him—for they left him gravely wounded—his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in the City of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings.
These were the conspirators against him: Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonitess, and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabitess.

As for his sons, the many prophecies concerning him, and the restoration of the house of God, behold, they are recorded in the commentary on the book of the kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not with a whole heart.
Once the kingdom was firmly established under him, he killed the servants who had struck down his father the king.

Yet he did not execute their sons, because it is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, which the LORD commanded: “Fathers shall not die for their sons, nor sons die for their fathers; instead, each shall die for his own sin.”

Amaziah gathered Judah and assigned them by ancestral houses under commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds for all Judah and Benjamin. He mustered those twenty years old and older and found three hundred thousand chosen men able to go to war, bearing spear and shield.
He also hired one hundred thousand mighty warriors from Israel for one hundred talents of silver.
Then a man of God came to him and said, “O king, do not let Israel's army go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel—not with any of the Ephraimites.
But if you go, be strong for battle; God will make you fall before the enemy, for God has power both to help and to overthrow.”
Amaziah asked the man of God, “But what are we to do about the hundred talents I have already given to Israel's troops?” “The LORD can give you much more than this.”
So Amaziah dismissed the troops who had come to him from Ephraim and sent them home. They were furious with Judah and returned home in a rage.
Amaziah strengthened himself and led his people to the Valley of Salt, where he struck down ten thousand men of Seir.
The men of Judah captured another ten thousand alive, took them to the top of the rock, and threw them down from the summit, so that all of them were dashed to pieces.
Meanwhile, the troops Amaziah had sent back from the battle raided the cities of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon, killing three thousand people and carrying off great plunder.
After Amaziah returned from defeating the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the Seirites, set them up as his own gods, bowed down to them, and offered sacrifices to them.
The LORD's anger burned against Amaziah, and He sent a prophet to him, who said, “Why have you sought the gods of a people who could not deliver their own people from your hand?”

While the prophet was still speaking, the king said to him, “Have we appointed you as counselor to the king? Stop! Why should you be struck down?” “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel.”
After taking counsel, Amaziah king of Judah sent messengers to Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us meet face to face.”

Joash king of Israel replied to Amaziah king of Judah, “A thornbush in Lebanon sent to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son for a wife,’ but a wild beast in Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush.
You say, ‘Look, I have defeated Edom,’ and your heart has lifted you up in boasting. Now stay at home. Why should you provoke trouble and fall, you and Judah with you?”
But Amaziah would not listen, for this turn of events was from God, so that He might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom.
So Joash king of Israel advanced, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah.
Judah was defeated before Israel, and every man fled to his home.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, a distance of four hundred cubits.
He took all the gold, silver, and vessels found in the house of God, together with Obed-edom, the treasures of the king's house, and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel?
From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish; but they pursued him there and put him to death.
They carried him back on horses and buried him with his fathers in a city of Judah.
The whole people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Eloth and restored it to Judah after Amaziah had died.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem; his mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.
He devoted himself to seeking God in the days of Zechariah, who was adept in the visions of God; and as long as he sought the the LORD, God granted him prosperity.
He campaigned against the Philistines, dismantling the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, and he founded cities in Ashdod and throughout Philistine territory.
God sustained him against the Philistines, against the Arabs dwelling in Gur-baal, and against the Meunites.
The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his renown extended to the approaches of Egypt, for his power had grown immense.
Moreover, Uzziah erected towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle, reinforcing them.

He built towers in the wilderness and excavated numerous cisterns, because he owned extensive herds in the Shephelah and on the plain; he employed farmers and vinedressers in the highlands and in Carmel, for he cherished the soil.
Uzziah maintained an army of warriors who marched out in divisions, tallied by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer under the authority of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders.
The aggregate of the ancestral chieftains, valiant men, numbered 2,600.
At their disposal stood an army of 307,500 men, exercising formidable martial power to assist the king against his adversaries.
Uzziah outfitted them—the entire force—with shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and sling stones.

He also devised in Jerusalem ingenious war machines, crafted by skilled artisans, to be mounted on the towers and corners for discharging arrows and hurling massive stones. His renown reached distant lands, for he received extraordinary assistance until he had grown powerful.
Yet once he had become powerful, pride swelled in his heart to his ruin; he acted unfaithfully against the the LORD his God by entering the the LORD's temple to burn incense on the altar of incense.
Azariah the priest followed him in, accompanied by eighty priests of the the LORD—men of valor.

They confronted King Uzziah and declared, “It is not your prerogative, Uzziah, to burn incense to the the LORD; that privilege belongs to the priests, the sons of Aaron, who have been consecrated for this rite. Leave the sanctuary at once, for you have trespassed; nor will this bring you honor from the the LORD God.”
Then Uzziah grew furious, and while his anger raged against the priests, leprosy erupted on his forehead in the presence of the priests within the the LORD's house, beside the altar of incense.

When Azariah the chief priest and all the priests turned toward him and saw that he was leprous on his forehead, they expelled him from the premises; he himself hastened to depart, because the the LORD had afflicted him.
King Uzziah remained a leper until his death. He lived in an isolated dwelling, barred from the the LORD's house, and his son Jotham oversaw the royal palace, governing the people of the land.
The remaining deeds of Uzziah, from first to last, were recorded by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors in the royal burial field, because, as they acknowledged, he was a leper. His son Jotham succeeded him.
Upon ascending the throne at twenty-five years of age, Jotham reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years; his mother was Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok.

He conducted himself uprightly in the sight of the LORD, emulating all that his father Uzziah had done, with the sole exception that he did not enter the temple of the LORD; nevertheless, the populace persisted in corrupt conduct.
He erected the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD and undertook extensive work on the wall of Ophel.
He also established cities throughout the hill country of Judah, together with fortresses and watchtowers, and he constructed edifices within the forested regions.

He waged war against the king of the Ammonites and subdued them; in that same year, the Ammonites rendered to him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. They remitted an identical tribute during the second and third years as well.
Thus Jotham increased in power, for he established his conduct before the LORD his God.
The remaining deeds of Jotham—encompassing all his military campaigns and his personal conduct—are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and his reign in Jerusalem spanned sixteen years.
Jotham slept with his fathers and was entombed in the City of David, whereupon his son Ahaz succeeded him.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.
Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even cast molten images for the Baals.
He burned incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and burned his sons in the fire, following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.

Therefore the LORD his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Aram, who defeated him, took a great number of captives, and brought them to Damascus. He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with a great slaughter.
For Pekah son of Remaliah killed one hundred twenty thousand in Judah in a single day—all valiant men—because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah, the king’s son; Azrikam, the officer over the palace; and Elkanah, second to the king.
The Israelites carried away two hundred thousand captives—women, sons, and daughters—and they also seized a great deal of plunder, which they brought to Samaria.

But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there, and he went out before the army that was coming to Samaria and said to them, “Because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, He gave them into your hand, and you have killed them in a rage that reaches to heaven.
And now you intend to subjugate the sons and daughters of Judah and Jerusalem as male and female slaves for yourselves. Are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?
Now therefore hear me, and return the captives you have taken from your brothers, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you.”

Then certain men of the leaders of the Ephraimites—Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—stood up against those returning from the war

and said to them, “You shall not bring the captives here, for you are proposing to bring guilt upon us from the LORD, adding to our sins and guilt; for our guilt is great, and fierce wrath is against Israel.”
So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the princes and the whole assembly.

The men designated by name rose up, took the captives, and from the plunder clothed all who were naked; they clothed them, gave them sandals, food and drink, and anointed them. They put all the feeble on donkeys and brought them to Jericho, the City of Palms, near their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.
At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help.
The Edomites came again, struck Judah, and carried away captives.

The Philistines raided the cities of the lowland and the Negev of Judah; they captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and Gimzo with its villages, and settled there.
For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD.
Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and distressed him instead of strengthening him.
Although Ahaz took a portion from the house of the LORD, from the king’s house, and from the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria, it did not help him.
In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him, for he said, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram help them, I will sacrifice to them so that they help me.” But they became the cause of his downfall and of all Israel’s.
Ahaz gathered the utensils of the house of God, cut them in pieces, shut the doors of the house of the LORD, and made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem.
In every city of Judah he made high places to burn incense to other gods, provoking the LORD, the God of his fathers.
The rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, but they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah reigned in his place.
Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he ascended the throne, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
He acted uprightly in the sight of the the LORD, following the example of his father David in every respect.
During the first month of the first year of his reign, he threw open the doors of the the LORD’s house and restored them.
He summoned the priests and the Levites and assembled them in the eastern square.
“Listen to me, Levites,” he said. “Consecrate yourselves at once, and consecrate the house of the the LORD, the God of your fathers. Purge every impurity from the sanctuary.

For our fathers acted treacherously and did evil in the sight of the the LORD our God. They abandoned Him, averted their faces from the dwelling place of the the LORD, and turned their backs upon Him.
They also closed the doors of the portico and extinguished the lamps; they offered neither incense nor burnt offerings in the Holy Place to the God of Israel.
Therefore the wrath of the the LORD has fallen upon Judah and Jerusalem, and He has made them an object of terror, horror, and derision, as you can plainly see.
Our fathers have fallen by the sword, while our sons, daughters, and wives have been carried into captivity.
Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the the LORD, the God of Israel, so that His fierce anger may turn away from us.
My sons, do not now be negligent, for the the LORD has chosen you to stand before Him, to serve Him, to minister before Him, and to burn incense.”

Then the Levites rose to the task: from the Kohathites, Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah; from the Merarites, Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehalelel; from the Gershonites, Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah;
from the Asaphites, Zechariah and Mattaniah; from the Hemanites, Jehiel and Shimei; and from the Jeduthunites, Shemaiah and Uzziel.
They assembled their brothers, consecrated themselves, and entered to cleanse the house of the the LORD, in accordance with the king’s command and the words of the the LORD.

They began the consecration on the first day of the first month; by the eighth day they had reached the vestibule of the the LORD, and in eight more days they had consecrated the the LORD’s house, finishing on the sixteenth day of the first month.

Then the priests entered the inner part of the the LORD’s house to purify it. They removed into the courtyard of the the LORD’s house every unclean thing they discovered in the temple, and the Levites bore them away to the Kidron Valley.

Hezekiah dispatched couriers throughout Israel and Judah, and he also composed letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, urging them to assemble at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem and observe the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.
The king, his officials, and the whole assembly in Jerusalem had resolved to celebrate the Passover in the second month,
for they could not celebrate it at the appointed time, because too few priests had been consecrated and the people had not yet gathered in Jerusalem.
The proposal pleased the king and the entire assembly.

So they decreed that a proclamation should be sent throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, summoning the people to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, because they had not observed it in large numbers as prescribed.

According to the king’s command, the couriers traveled throughout Israel and Judah carrying letters from the king and his officials. They read: “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to the remnant of you who escaped the power of the Assyrian kings.
Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their fathers, and whom He therefore consigned to ruin, as you can see.

Do not stiffen your necks as your fathers did. Yield yourselves to the LORD, enter His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, so that His fierce anger may turn away from you.

For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and your sons will find mercy before their captors and return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn His face from you if you return to Him.”
The couriers went from city to city through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, as far as Zebulun, but the people laughed at them and mocked them.
Nevertheless, some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
Moreover, the hand of God was on Judah, giving them one heart to carry out the command of the king and the officials in accordance with the word of the LORD.
A very great assembly gathered in Jerusalem in the second month to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
They rose and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem; they also removed all the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley.

They slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and Levites were ashamed, so they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings to the house of the LORD.
They took their positions according to the ordinance, as the law of Moses, the man of God, required: the priests sprinkled the blood, receiving it from the Levites.
Because many in the assembly had not consecrated themselves, the Levites were charged with slaughtering the Passover lambs for everyone who was not clean, in order to consecrate them to the LORD.

For a great many of the people—especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun—had not purified themselves, yet they ate the Passover contrary to what was written. But Hezekiah prayed for them, saying, “May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers,
even though he is not cleansed according to the sanctuary’s purity.”
And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.

The Israelites who were present in Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, while the Levites and priests praised the LORD day by day with resounding instruments dedicated to the LORD.

Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who had shown good understanding in the service of the LORD. They ate the festival food for seven days, offering peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Then the whole assembly agreed to celebrate for another seven days, and they kept the feast for seven more days with joy.

For Hezekiah king of Judah had contributed to the assembly one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep, and the officials had contributed one thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep; and many priests consecrated themselves.

All the assembly of Judah rejoiced, together with the priests and Levites and all the assembly that had come from Israel, as well as the sojourners who had come from the land of Israel and those who lived in Judah.
There was great joy in Jerusalem, for nothing like this had occurred in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.
Then the priests and Levites stood and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer reached His holy dwelling in heaven.

When all this had ended, the Israelites who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke the sacred stones, cut down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all; then all Israel returned to their own cities, each to his own property.

Hezekiah reestablished the divisions of the priests and Levites, assigning each to his duties—priests and Levites alike—for burnt offerings and peace offerings, for ministry, for giving thanks, and for singing praises at the gates of the LORD.

The king also contributed from his own wealth for the morning and evening burnt offerings, as well as for the burnt offerings on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD.
Moreover, he commanded the people living in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and Levites, so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD.

As soon as the command was issued, the Israelites gave generously the firstfruits of grain, new wine, oil, honey, and all the produce of the field, and they brought in a great abundance—a tithe of everything.

The Israelites and Judahites who lived in the cities of Judah also brought a tithe of their herds and flocks and a tithe of the holy things consecrated to the LORD their God, and they piled them in heaps.
They began building the heaps in the third month and finished in the seventh month.
When Hezekiah and his officials came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and His people Israel.
Hezekiah then inquired of the priests and Levites concerning the heaps,

and Azariah the chief priest of the house of Zadok answered him, "Since the people began bringing their contributions into the house of the LORD, we have had enough to eat and plenty remains, because the LORD has blessed His people; this great abundance is what is left."
Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD, and they did so.
They faithfully brought in the contributions, tithes, and dedicated gifts. Conaniah the Levite was in charge of them, and his brother Shimei was second.

Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were supervisors under Conaniah and his brother Shimei, by appointment of King Hezekiah and of Azariah the chief official of the house of God.
Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the keeper of the East Gate, was in charge of the freewill offerings to God, to distribute the contributions to the LORD and the consecrated things.

Under his authority, Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah faithfully distributed the portions to their brothers in the cities of the priests, according to their divisions, to great and small alike,
as well as to those enrolled by genealogy—males three years of age and older—for everyone who entered the house of the LORD to perform the daily service according to their duties and divisions.
As for the priests, they were enrolled according to their families in the genealogical records, and the Levites twenty years of age and older, according to their duties and divisions.
The genealogy included all their little ones, wives, sons, and daughters throughout the whole assembly, for they were faithful in consecrating themselves.

As for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who lived in the pasturelands around their cities, men were designated by name to distribute a portion to every male among the priests and to every Levite listed in the genealogical records.
So Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, doing what was good and right and true before the LORD his God.
In every work that he began in the service of the house of God, in the law and in the commandment, to seek his God, he did with all his heart, and he prospered.
After these faithful deeds, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, invaded Judah and besieged its fortified cities, intending to seize them for himself.
When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come to make war against Jerusalem,
he consulted with his officials and warriors about stopping up the water from the springs outside the city, and they supported his plan.
A large crowd assembled and stopped up every spring and the stream that flowed through the land, asking, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find an abundance of water?"

Hezekiah then worked resolutely to rebuild every broken section of the wall, raise towers upon it, construct an additional outer wall, strengthen the supporting terraces of the City of David, and manufacture an abundance of weapons and shields.
He appointed military commanders over the people and gathered them in the square at the city gate, where he encouraged them, saying,
"Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria or before the vast army with him, for there is a greater power with us than with him.
With him is merely the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God to help us and to fight our battles." The people gained confidence from the words of Hezekiah, king of Judah.

Later, while Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and all his forces besieged Lachish, he sent his servants to Jerusalem with this message for Hezekiah, king of Judah, and for all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem:
"This is what Sennacherib, king of Assyria, says: On what are you relying, that you remain under siege in Jerusalem?
Is not Hezekiah misleading you into surrendering yourselves to die by famine and thirst when he says, 'The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria'?
Did not Hezekiah himself remove His high places and altars and say to Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship before one altar, and on it you must burn sacrifices'?
Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands? Were the gods of those nations ever able to deliver their land from my hand?
Who among all the gods of these nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand? How then can your God deliver you from my hand?

Now, therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you, and do not let him mislead you in this way. Do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you from my hand!"
His servants spoke further against the LORD God and against His servant Hezekiah.

He also wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel, and speaking against Him, saying, "Just as the gods of the nations did not deliver their people from my hand, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver His people from my hand."
Then the Assyrians called out in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might capture the city.
They spoke about the God of Jerusalem as they had about the gods of the other peoples of the earth—the work of human hands.
In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, cried out to heaven in prayer.

Then the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty warrior, commander, and officer in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he withdrew to his own land in disgrace, and when he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons struck him down with the sword.
Thus the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and from the hand of all others. He gave them rest on every side.
Many brought offerings to Jerusalem for the LORD and valuable gifts for Hezekiah, king of Judah, and from then on he was exalted in the eyes of all nations.
In those days Hezekiah became ill and was at the point of death. He prayed to the LORD, who answered him and gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah's heart was proud, and he did not respond to the kindness shown him; therefore wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah repented of the pride of his heart—he and the people of Jerusalem—so the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah.
Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made treasuries for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuable articles.
He also built storehouses for the harvest of grain, new wine, and oil, as well as stalls for all kinds of livestock and pens for the flocks.
He made cities for himself and acquired flocks and herds in abundance, for God gave him very great wealth.
It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon Spring and channeled the water down to the west side of the City of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all that he did.
When envoys were sent by the rulers of Babylon to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left Hezekiah to test him, that He might know all that was in his heart.
As for the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his deeds of loving devotion, they are recorded in the vision of the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

Hezekiah rested with his fathers and was buried on the upper slopes of the tombs of David. All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death, and his son Manasseh reigned in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.
He acted wickedly in the sight of the LORD, following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had dispossessed before the Israelites.
He reversed course and rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down; he erected altars to the Baals, fashioned Asherah poles, and bowed down to and served the entire host of heaven.
He built altars in the temple of the LORD, the very house of which the LORD had declared, “My Name will remain in Jerusalem forever.”
In the two courts of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven.

He made his sons pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom; he practiced soothsaying, divination, and sorcery; he consulted mediums and spiritists; and he did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger.

He set up the carved image of the idol he had made in the house of God, the very place of which God had said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will put My Name forever.
I will never again banish Israel from the land I appointed for your fathers, provided they take care to do all that I commanded them through Moses—all the law, statutes, and ordinances.”
Yet Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, so that they committed more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they paid no heed.
Therefore the LORD brought against them the commanders of the Assyrian king’s army, who captured Manasseh with hooks, bound him with bronze chains, and carried him off to Babylon.
In his distress he entreated the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.
Manasseh prayed to Him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his supplication; He restored Manasseh to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.

Afterward he built an outer wall for the City of David on the west side of Gihon in the valley, extending to the entrance of the Fish Gate; he encircled the Ophel and raised it to a great height. He also stationed military commanders in all the fortified cities of Judah.

He removed the foreign gods and the carved image from the house of the LORD, along with all the altars he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he cast them outside the city.
He restored the altar of the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings on it; he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.
Nevertheless, the people continued to sacrifice on the high places, but only to the LORD their God.
The rest of the acts of Manasseh, his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD God of Israel are recorded in the annals of the kings of Israel.

His prayer and how he was heard, along with all his sin and trespass, and the sites where he built high places and set up Asherah poles and carved images before he humbled himself, are written in the records of the seers.
Manasseh died and was buried in his palace; his son Amon succeeded him.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done; Amon sacrificed to all the carved images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them.
He did not humble himself before the LORD, as his father Manasseh had humbled himself; instead, Amon increased his guilt.
His servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house.
But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD and walked in the ways of David his father, without turning aside to the right or to the left.

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a youth, he began to seek the God of David his father; and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved images, and the cast images.

In his presence they tore down the altars of the Baals; the incense altars that stood above them he cut down; and the Asherah poles, the carved images, and the cast images he smashed and ground to powder, then scattered the dust over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.
He burned the bones of the priests on their altars and so cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.
He did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins all around them.
He broke down the altars and beat the Asherah poles to pieces; he pulverized the carved images and cut down all the incense altars throughout the land of Israel, and then returned to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, after purifying the land and the temple, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz the recorder, to repair the house of the the LORD his God.

They came to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites who guarded the threshold had collected from Manasseh, Ephraim, and the whole remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

They put it into the hands of the workmen appointed to oversee the house of the the LORD, and these workmen gave it to those who were repairing the house of the the LORD, to restore and strengthen it.
They gave it to the carpenters and builders to purchase quarried stone and timber for braces, and to floor the houses that the kings of Judah had destroyed.

The men did the work faithfully. Over them were appointed the Levites Jahath and Obadiah of the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam of the sons of Kohath, to supervise; and the other Levites, all of them skilled musicians,
were over the burden bearers and directed all who did the work in every service; and some of the Levites were scribes, officers, and gatekeepers.
When they brought out the money that had been brought into the house of the the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the the LORD given by Moses.
Hilkiah said to Shaphan the scribe, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan brought the book to the king and reported, "Your servants are carrying out everything entrusted to them."
They melted down the money found in the house of the the LORD and handed it over to the overseers and the workmen.
Then Shaphan the scribe told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes.
The king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying,

"Go and inquire of the the LORD for me and for the remnant in Israel and Judah concerning the words of the book that has been found, for great is the wrath of the the LORD that has been poured out on us, because our fathers did not keep the word of the the LORD, to do all that is written in this book."

So Hilkiah and those the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter. They spoke to her about this.
She said to them, "Thus says the the LORD, the God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me,
Thus says the the LORD: I am bringing disaster on this place and on its inhabitants—all the curses written in the book that was read before the king of Judah.
Because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods, provoking Me to anger by all the works of their hands, My wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.
But to the king of Judah who sent you to inquire of the the LORD, you shall say this: Thus says the the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the words you have heard:

Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard His words against this place and its inhabitants, and because you humbled yourself before Me and tore your clothes and wept before Me, I have heard you, declares the the LORD.

Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace; your eyes will not see all the disaster I am bringing on this place and on its inhabitants.' Then they brought this word back to the king.
The king sent and gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

The king went up to the house of the the LORD with all the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, the Levites, and all the people, from the greatest to the least; and he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the the LORD.

The king stood in his place and made a covenant before the the LORD to walk after the the LORD and to keep His commandments, His testimonies, and His statutes with all his heart and all his soul, and to perform the words of the covenant written in this book.
He made all who were found in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand to it. The inhabitants of Jerusalem acted according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers.

Josiah removed all the abominations from all the lands belonging to the Israelites, and he made all who were found in Israel serve the the LORD their God. All his days they did not turn aside from following the the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Josiah observed the Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem, and the Passover lambs were slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He stationed the priests in their divisions and strengthened them for the service of the house of the LORD.

To the Levites, who taught all Israel and were holy to the LORD, he said, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built. You no longer have a burden to carry on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and His people Israel.
Prepare yourselves according to your ancestral houses and divisions, as written by David king of Israel and by Solomon his son.
Stand in the holy place according to the divisions of the fathers' houses of your brothers, the lay people, and according to the division of a fathers' house of the Levites.
Slaughter the Passover, sanctify yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, so that you may carry out the word of the LORD given through Moses."
King Josiah contributed from his own possessions thirty thousand lambs and young goats, and three thousand bulls, all for the Passover offerings for all the people who were present.

His officials contributed willingly for the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave the priests two thousand six hundred lambs and kids and three hundred bulls for the Passover offerings.

Conaniah, along with his brothers Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave the Levites five thousand lambs and kids and five hundred bulls for the Passover offerings.
So the service was prepared. The priests stood in their places, and the Levites in their divisions, according to the king's command.
They slaughtered the Passover lambs. The priests sprinkled the blood from their hands, while the Levites skinned the animals.

They set aside the burnt offerings to be distributed to the divisions of the fathers' houses of the lay people, so that they could offer them to the LORD, as written in the Book of Moses; they did the same with the bulls.
They roasted the Passover over the fire according to the ordinance, boiled the holy offerings in pots, cauldrons, and pans, and carried them quickly to all the people.

Afterward they prepared portions for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were occupied with offering burnt offerings and fat portions until nightfall; the Levites prepared portions for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron.

The singers, the sons of Asaph, stood in their places according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer. The gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not have to leave their posts, because their fellow Levites prepared portions for them.
Thus all the service of the LORD was prepared that day for observing the Passover and for offering burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah.
The Israelites who were present kept the Passover at that time and celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had ever kept a Passover such as this one, which Josiah kept with the priests, the Levites, all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
This Passover was kept in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign.
After all this, when Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco king of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates. Josiah went out to meet him.

Neco sent messengers to him, saying, "What do you have against me, king of Judah? I am not coming against you today, but against the house with which I am at war. God has commanded me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, so that He does not destroy you."

But Josiah did not turn away from him. Instead, he disguised himself to fight against him. He did not listen to the words of Neco, which came from the mouth of God, but went to fight in the Valley of Megiddo.
The archers shot King Josiah, and the king said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded."

His servants took him out of his chariot and put him in his second chariot, then brought him to Jerusalem. There he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah, and to this day all the male and female singers speak of Josiah in their laments. They made these laments an ordinance in Israel, and they are written in the Book of Laments.
The rest of the acts of Josiah, along with his deeds of faithful love, are written according to the Law of the LORD.
His first and last acts are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.
The king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and imposed on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.
The king of Egypt made Eliakim, his brother, king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. The king of Egypt took Jehoahaz, his brother, and carried him off to Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD his God.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him and bound him in bronze shackles to take him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar also carried to Babylon some of the articles from the house of the the LORD and put them in his temple in Babylon.
The rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, the abominations he committed, and what was found against him, are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.
Jehoiachin was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD.

At the turn of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and brought him to Babylon, along with the precious articles of the house of the the LORD, and made Zedekiah his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the the LORD.
He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He stubbornly refused and hardened his heart against turning to the the LORD, the God of Israel.

All the leaders of the priests and the people likewise increased in unfaithfulness, following all the abominations of the nations, and they defiled the house of the the LORD that He had consecrated in Jerusalem.
The The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent to them again and again by His messengers, because He had compassion on His people and on His dwelling place.
But they mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the the LORD rose against His people, until there was no remedy.

Therefore He brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged; He gave them all into his hand.
All the articles of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the the LORD and the treasures of the king and his officials, he brought to Babylon.
They burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem; they burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious articles.
He carried into exile those who escaped the sword to Babylon, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power.
So the land enjoyed its Sabbaths; all the days of desolation it kept Sabbath, to fulfill the word of the the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until seventy years were completed.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the the LORD spoken by Jeremiah, the the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and put it in writing, saying:

“Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has appointed me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to His people, may the the LORD his God be with him, and let him go up.”

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, so that the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia. He made a proclamation throughout his entire kingdom and also put it in writing, saying:
“Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has appointed me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.
Who among you is of all His people? May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel—He is the God who is in Jerusalem.

And every survivor, wherever he sojourns, shall be assisted by the men of his place with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, together with the freewill offering for the house of God that is in Jerusalem.”

Then the heads of the fathers’ houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, rose up—everyone whose spirit God had stirred—to go up and build the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.
And all their neighbors strengthened their hands with vessels of silver and gold, with goods and livestock, and with precious things, besides all that was freely offered.
King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his god.
Cyrus king of Persia brought them out by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.
This was their number: thirty gold basins, a thousand silver basins, twenty-nine knives,
thirty gold bowls, four hundred ten silver bowls of a second kind, and a thousand other articles.
All the vessels of gold and silver numbered five thousand four hundred. Sheshbazzar brought up all of them with the exiles who were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

These are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exile, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away to Babylon; they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.
