When the gates of Jerusalem were nearing closure before the Sabbath, I commanded that the portals be closed and not reopened until after the Sabbath. I stationed several of my attendants at the gates so that no burden might be imported on the Sabbath day.
On one or two occasions the merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods encamped beyond Jerusalem.
But I admonished them, “Why are you encamping outside the wall? Should you repeat this, I will have you arrested.” Thereafter they did not come on the Sabbath.

Then I directed the Levites to consecrate themselves and keep watch at the gates in order to sanctify the Sabbath day. “Remember me for this as well, O my God, and extend mercy to me in accordance with Your abundant loving devotion.”
In those days I also saw Jews who had married Ashdodite, Ammonite, or Moabite women.
Half of their offspring spoke the language of Ashdod or the tongue of each respective people, but none was able to speak the language of Judah.

So I confronted them and denounced them and struck certain of them and plucked out their hair. I compelled them to swear an oath before God: “You must not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves.”

“Did not Solomon, king of Israel, transgress in these matters? No king among the nations surpassed him, and he was beloved of his God, who appointed him king over all Israel—yet foreign women led him into sin.
Are we now to hear that you are committing this great evil, acting treacherously toward our God by marrying foreign women?”
Moreover, one of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest had become son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite, so I expelled him from my presence.
“Remember them, O my God, because they defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.”
Accordingly, I cleansed them of all foreign elements and assigned the priests and Levites to their respective duties.
I also arranged for the wood offering at the prescribed times and for the firstfruits. “Remember me, O my God, for good.”
In the days of Xerxes—that is, the Xerxes who reigned over one hundred twenty-seven provinces stretching from India to Cush—
during those days King Xerxes sat upon his royal throne in the citadel of Susa.
In the third year of his reign, he held a feast for all his officials and servants; the military leaders of Persia and Media were present, together with the nobles and princes of the provinces.
For one hundred eighty days he displayed the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness.
When those days had ended, the king held a banquet lasting seven days in the courtyard of the royal palace in Susa, for all the people from the least to the greatest who were present in the citadel.

White and blue linen hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble pillars; couches of gold and silver were arranged on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and other costly stones.
Drinks were served in golden goblets, each one unlike the others, and royal wine flowed abundantly, according to the king's generosity.
The drinking was conducted according to law; no one was compelled, for the king had instructed every official of his household to do as each person desired.
Queen Vashti likewise gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes.
On the seventh day, when the king's heart was gladdened by wine, he commanded the seven eunuchs who served in his presence—Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas—
to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing the royal crown, to display her beauty to the people and the officials, for she was remarkably beautiful.
Queen Vashti, however, refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. Then the king became furious, and his anger burned within him.
Then the king consulted the wise men who knew the times, for it was customary for him to confer with all who knew law and justice.

Those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who had privileged access to the king and ranked highest in the kingdom.
"According to law," he asked, "what should be done to Queen Vashti, since she has failed to obey the command of King Xerxes delivered by the eunuchs?"
Memucan replied in the presence of the king and his nobles, "Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but also all the officials and all the peoples in every province of King Xerxes.
For the queen's conduct will become known to all women, causing them to despise their husbands and say, 'King Xerxes ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she refused to come.'
This very day the noblewomen of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's conduct will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be no end of contempt and discord.

"So if it pleases the king, let a royal decree be issued and written into the laws of Persia and Media, which cannot be repealed, that Vashti is never again to enter the presence of King Xerxes, and that her royal position be given to a woman more worthy than she.
Then the king's decree will be published throughout his vast kingdom, and all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands."
The king and his nobles were pleased with this advice, and the king did as Memucan had advised.
He sent letters to all the king's provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language, proclaiming that every man should be master in his own household.
After these events, King Ahasuerus's wrath had subsided; once his anger cooled, he remembered Vashti—both what she had done and the decree issued against her.
Then the king's personal attendants proposed, "Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king.

Let the king appoint commissioners in every province of his realm to gather all these beautiful young women into the harem at the citadel of Susa. Place them under the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch who oversees the women, and let beauty treatments be provided for them.
Then let the young woman who pleases the king be queen in Vashti's place." This counsel pleased the king, and he put it into effect.
Now in the citadel of Susa there was a Jew named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite,
who had been exiled from Jerusalem with the captives taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away.

Mordecai had raised his cousin Hadassah—that is, Esther—because she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was lovely in form and beautiful in appearance, and when her parents died, Mordecai adopted her as his own daughter.

When the king's order and edict had been proclaimed, many young women were brought to the citadel of Susa and placed under Hegai's supervision. Esther, too, was taken into the king's palace and entrusted to Hegai, who was in charge of the women.

She pleased him and won his favor, so he promptly provided her with beauty treatments and special food. He assigned her seven attendants chosen from the king's palace, moved her and her attendants to the best quarters in the harem, and treated them better than the rest.
Esther did not disclose her people or her family background, because Mordecai had commanded her not to.
Every day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the courtyard of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was being done to her.

Before a young woman's turn came to go in to the king, she had to complete twelve months of beauty treatments prescribed for the women: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and cosmetics.
When she went to the king, she was given whatever she requested to take with her from the women's quarters to the king's palace.

She would go in the evening and return in the morning to a second set of women's quarters, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch in charge of the concubines. She would not return to the king unless he was pleased with her and summoned her by name.

When Esther's turn came—she was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, whom Mordecai had taken as his own daughter—she requested nothing except what Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, advised. And Esther won the favor of everyone who saw her.
She was brought to King Ahasuerus in his royal residence in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.

The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she found greater favor and kindness in his sight than any of the other virgins, so he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.
Then the king gave a great banquet—Esther's banquet—for all his nobles and officials. He proclaimed a holiday throughout the provinces and distributed gifts with royal generosity.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still had not revealed her family background or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed her; she continued to follow Mordecai's instructions as she had when he was raising her.
During the days when Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, became enraged and conspired to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
The matter came to Mordecai's knowledge, and he told Queen Esther; Esther then reported it to the king in Mordecai's name.
When the report was investigated and found true, the two men were hanged on a gallows, and the incident was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence.
After these events, King Ahasuerus elevated Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, promoting him and placing his seat above all the officials who served with him.
All the king's servants who were at the gate bowed and prostrated themselves before Haman, for the king had commanded that they do so; yet Mordecai neither bowed nor prostrated himself.
The king's servants at the gate asked Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?"
Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen; so they reported the matter to Haman to see whether Mordecai's defiance would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would neither kneel nor bow before him, he was filled with rage.

Because they had told him who Mordecai's people were, Haman regarded it as beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone; instead, he sought to annihilate all the Jews throughout the realm of Ahasuerus—the people of Mordecai.
In the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, in the first month, Nisan, the lot—Pur—was cast before Haman from day to day and from month to month, and it fell on the twelfth month, Adar.

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people, scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom, whose laws differ from those of every other people and who do not observe the king's laws. It is not in the king's interest to tolerate them.
If it pleases the king, let it be written that they be destroyed, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury for those who execute the task."
The king removed his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "The silver is given to you, along with the people, to do with them as you see fit."

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's scribes were summoned, and in accordance with all that Haman commanded, they wrote to the king's satraps, to the governors over each province, and to the leaders of each people—each province in its own script and each people in its own language. The decree was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with orders to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews—young and old, women and children—on a single day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, and to plunder their goods.
A copy of the text of the edict was to be issued as law in every province and made public to all peoples, so that they might be ready for that day.

The couriers went out, pressed forward by the king's command, and the decree was proclaimed in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, while the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.

When Mordecai learned the full extent of what had transpired, he tore his garments, donned sackcloth and ashes, and proceeded into the city's central thoroughfare, uttering a loud and bitter lamentation.
He advanced only to the king's gate, since no one clad in sackcloth was permitted to enter it.
Throughout every province, wherever the royal command and decree reached, the Jews sank into profound mourning—fasting, weeping, and wailing—while many reclined in sackcloth and ashes.
Upon receiving this report, Queen Esther was seized by acute anguish. She dispatched garments for Mordecai to wear in place of his sackcloth, but he refused them.
Consequently, Esther summoned Hathach, one of the eunuchs whom the king had appointed to serve her, and directed him to ascertain from Mordecai the cause and meaning of these events.
Hathach then went out to Mordecai in the open square before the king's gate.
Mordecai disclosed to him all that had befallen him, including the precise sum of silver Haman had pledged to deposit into the royal treasuries in exchange for the annihilation of the Jews.

He also entrusted Hathach with a copy of the written decree promulgated in Susa for their destruction, instructing him to exhibit it to Esther, explicate its implications, and command her to approach the king, supplicate his favor, and intercede on behalf of her people.
Hathach returned and relayed Mordecai's message to Esther.
Then Esther instructed Hathach to convey this reply to Mordecai:

"All the king's servants and the subjects of every province recognize that any man or woman who enters the king's inner court unsummoned incurs one immutable penalty—death—unless the king extends the golden scepter to that person, thereby granting life. As for me, I have not been summoned to the king these thirty days."
Hathach reported these words to Mordecai.
Mordecai responded with this message: "Do not think to yourself that you will find sanctuary in the royal palace any more than the rest of the Jews.

For if you persist in silence at this critical juncture, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another quarter, yet you and your father's household will perish. Moreover, who can discern whether you have attained royal authority for a moment precisely like this?"
Esther then directed them to answer Mordecai:

"Go, assemble every Jew in Susa, and observe a fast on my behalf; abstain from food and drink for three days and nights. I and my attendants will fast in the same manner. Thereafter, I shall approach the king, notwithstanding that it contravenes the law; and if it costs me my life, so be it."
Mordecai departed and executed all of Esther's instructions.

On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner courtyard of the king's palace, directly opposite the king's residence. The king was seated on his royal throne in the hall of the palace, facing the entrance.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the courtyard, she won his favor, and he extended the golden scepter in his hand toward her. Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
The king asked her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom will be given to you."
Esther replied, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for him."
The king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may carry out Esther's request." So the king and Haman went to the banquet Esther had prepared.
At the banquet of wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition? It will be granted. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be done."

Esther answered, "My petition and my request are these: if I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, then let the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them, and I will do as the king has said."
Haman left that day joyful and glad of heart. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate refusing to stand or tremble before him, he was filled with rage against Mordecai.
Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home. He sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh.

Haman boasted to them about his glorious wealth, his many sons, and all the honors the king had bestowed on him, including his promotion above the officials and servants of the king. He added, "Even Queen Esther invited no one but me to accompany the king to the banquet she prepared, and tomorrow I am invited again with the king."
"Yet all of this means nothing to me," he said, "as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

His wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Have a gallows built, seventy-five feet high, and in the morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go to the banquet with the king in good spirits." This advice pleased Haman, so he had the gallows constructed.
That very night, sleep eluded the king, so he commanded that the chronicle of memorable deeds—the book recording the days' events—be brought and read aloud in his presence.
There it was found recorded that Mordecai had disclosed the plot of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold and who had sought to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
The king asked, "What honor or distinction has been conferred upon Mordecai for this?" His servants replied, "Nothing has been done for him."
The king inquired, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had entered the outer court of the royal palace, intending to petition the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had erected for him.
The king's servants answered, "Haman stands in the court." The king said, "Let him enter."
When Haman entered, the king asked him, "What should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor?" Haman thought to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
So Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor,
let royal robes be brought that the king himself has worn, and a horse on which the king has ridden, with a royal crown placed upon its head.

Let the robe and horse be entrusted to one of the king's most noble officials, and let them array the man whom the king delights to honor; then let them lead him on horseback through the city square and proclaim before him, 'Thus shall it be done for the man whom the king delights to honor.'"

The king then said to Haman, "Make haste; take the robe and the horse, exactly as you have spoken, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Let nothing of all that you have spoken fail."
So Haman took the robe and the horse, clothed Mordecai, led him on horseback through the city square, and proclaimed before him, "Thus shall it be done for the man whom the king delights to honor."
Afterward Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried home, mourning, with his head covered.

Haman recounted to his wife Zeresh and to all his friends everything that had befallen him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom your downfall has already begun, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him; rather, you will certainly fall before him."
While they were still speaking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hastened to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman came to drink with Queen Esther.

On the second day, at the wine banquet, the king said to Queen Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It will be granted to you. And what is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it will be done."
Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor with you, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be granted to me as my petition, and my people as my request.

For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and annihilated. If we had merely been sold as slaves and maidservants, I would have kept silent, for no enemy could compensate for the king's loss."
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"
Esther said, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.
In his wrath the king rose from the wine banquet and went into the palace garden, while Haman stood up to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king had decreed his ruin.

When the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther lay. The king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my own house?" As soon as the word left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs before the king, said, "Look, the gallows that Haman made for Mordecai, who spoke in the king's favor, stands in Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it!"
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's wrath subsided.
On that day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king, because Esther had revealed his relationship to her.
The king removed his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai, and Esther placed Mordecai over the house of Haman.
Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet, wept, and implored him to avert the evil scheme of Haman the Agagite and the plot he had devised against the Jews.
When the king extended the golden scepter to Esther, she rose and stood before the king.

She said, “If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the matter seems right to the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king’s provinces.
For how could I bear to see the calamity that would befall my people? Or how could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?”
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, “Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and he was hanged on the gallows because he attacked the Jews.

But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king’s ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king’s ring cannot be revoked.”

The king’s scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. An edict was written according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps, the governors, and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia—127 provinces in all—to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and language.
It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet ring. Letters were sent by couriers mounted on swift horses used in the king’s service, bred from the royal stud.

The letters said that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, including children and women, and to plunder their possessions,
on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the document was to be issued as law in every province and proclaimed to all peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to avenge themselves on their enemies.
The couriers, mounted on the royal horses, rode out in haste, urged on by the king’s command, and the decree was proclaimed in Susa the citadel.
Then Mordecai left the king’s presence wearing royal garments of blue and white, with a large crown of gold and a robe of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor.

In every province and in every city, wherever the king’s command and decree arrived, the Jews had gladness and joy, a feast and a holiday. Many peoples of the land declared themselves Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—the month of Adar—the king’s command and decree were to be carried out. On that day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but the outcome was reversed, and the Jews gained power over those who hated them.

The Jews assembled in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to strike those who sought their harm. No one could withstand them, because dread of them had fallen on all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and the king’s administrators supported the Jews, because fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.
For Mordecai was great in the king’s house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces; indeed, the man Mordecai grew greater and greater.
So the Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and they did to those who hated them as they pleased.
In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not seize the plunder.
On that day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, including the ten sons of Haman. What have they done in the rest of the king’s provinces? Now what is your petition? It will be given to you. And what further request do you have? It will be fulfilled.”
Esther replied, “If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa be allowed to do tomorrow also according to today’s decree, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows.”
So the king commanded that this be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
The Jews in Susa assembled on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa, but they did not seize the plunder.

The rest of the Jews who were in the king’s provinces assembled, defended themselves, and found relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not seize the plunder.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Adar the Jews fought, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews in Susa had assembled on the thirteenth and fourteenth, and on the fifteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.

Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns, observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday, and a day for sending portions to one another.
Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to all the Jews throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far,
obliging them to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar each year

as the days on which the Jews found relief from their enemies, and the month that was turned for them from sorrow into joy and from mourning into a holiday. They were to make these days days of feasting and joy, of sending portions to one another, and of giving gifts to the poor.
So the Jews agreed to continue the celebration they had begun, doing what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast the lot (Pur) to crush and destroy them.

But when Esther came before the king, he commanded in writing that Haman’s wicked scheme, which he had devised against the Jews, should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
Therefore these days are called Purim, after the name Pur. Therefore, because of everything written in this letter, and because of what they had witnessed and what had happened to them,

the Jews established and took upon themselves and their descendants and all who joined them that they would not fail to celebrate these two days according to their regulation and at their appointed time every year.

These days are to be remembered and observed in every generation, by every family, in every province, and in every city; and these days of Purim are never to cease among the Jews, nor is their memory to perish from their descendants.
Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, words of peace and truth,

to establish these days of Purim at their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established for them, and as they had established for themselves and for their descendants, with regard to their fasting and their lamentation.
And Esther’s command confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was written in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tribute upon the mainland and upon the islands of the sea.

As for all the power and might of Mordecai, together with the full account of his greatness to which the king advanced him, are not these things written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?

For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus; he was great among the Jews and well regarded by the majority of his brothers, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants.
There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil.
Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.

His livestock included seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, along with very many servants. He was the greatest of all the men of the East.
His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his own day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting had run their course, Job would send for them and consecrate them; rising early in the morning, he would offer burnt offerings for each of them, for Job said, "Perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." Job did this continually.
One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.
The LORD said to Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD, "From roaming through the earth and walking back and forth in it."
Then the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered My servant Job? There is no one on earth like him—blameless and upright, one who fears God and turns away from evil."
Satan answered the LORD, "Is Job's reverence for God really selfless?
Have You not put a hedge around him, his household, and everything he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock have multiplied in the land.
But stretch out Your hand and touch everything he owns, and he will surely curse You to Your face."
The LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your power; only do not stretch out your hand against him." Then Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.
Now on a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were feeding beside them,
when the Sabeans attacked and carried them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants. I alone have escaped to tell you."

While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three raiding parties and swept down on the camels, carrying them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, yet another messenger came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
when a mighty wind swept in from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people, and they died. I alone have escaped to tell you."
Then Job arose, tore his robe, shaved his head, and fell to the ground in worship.
He said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
In all this Job did not sin, nor did he charge God with wrongdoing.
On a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.
The LORD asked Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD, "From roaming throughout the earth and ranging across it."

The LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered My servant Job? There is no one like him on the earth—a blameless and upright man who fears God and shuns evil. He still maintains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to destroy him without cause."
Satan answered the LORD, "A man will relinquish everything he owns to preserve his own life.
But stretch out Your hand and strike his bone and flesh, and he will curse You to Your face."
The LORD said to Satan, "He is in your power, but you must spare his life."
So Satan departed from the presence of the LORD and afflicted Job with severe boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself while he sat among the ashes.
Then his wife said to him, "Do you still maintain your integrity? Curse God and die."
He answered her, "You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. Shall we accept prosperity from God and not adversity?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

When Job's three friends—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite—heard of all the calamity that had befallen him, each came from his own region. They agreed to meet together to offer him sympathy and comfort.
When they raised their eyes from afar and did not recognize him, they wept aloud. Each tore his robe and sprinkled dust on his head toward heaven.
They sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they perceived that his suffering was exceedingly great.
After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.
Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night that said, ‘A man is conceived.’
Let that day be darkness; let God not regard it from above, nor let light shine upon it.
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it; let a cloud settle over it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. “
As for that night, let darkness seize it; let it not rejoice among the days of the year, nor enter the number of the months.
Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful shout enter it.
Let those who curse days curse it—those prepared to rouse Leviathan.
Let the stars of its twilight be dark; let it wait for light, but have none, and let it not see the eyelids of the dawn,
because it did not shut the doors of my womb or hide trouble from my eyes. “
Why did I not die at birth and perish as I came from the womb?
Why did knees receive me, and why breasts, that I should nurse?
For now I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept, and then I would have been at rest,
with kings and counselors of the earth who built ruins for themselves,
or with princes who had gold and filled their houses with silver,
or why was I not hidden like a stillborn child, like infants who never saw light? “
There the wicked cease from turmoil, and there the weary are at rest.
There prisoners are at ease together; they do not hear the voice of the taskmaster.
Small and great are there, and the slave is free from his master. “
Why is light given to one in misery, and life to the bitter in soul,
who long for death, but it does not come, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?
Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
For my sighing comes before I eat, and my groanings pour out like water.
For the thing I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.
I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, for turmoil comes.”
"If someone presumes to speak a word to you, will you grow weary? Yet who can keep from speaking?
Surely you have instructed many, and you have strengthened feeble hands.
Your words have upheld those who were stumbling, and you have made firm the knees that gave way.
But now adversity has come to you, and you are weary; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
Is not your reverence your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
"Remember now: who is the innocent man who perished? Where were the upright ever cut off?
As I have seen, those who cultivate iniquity and sow trouble reap what they have sown.
By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.
The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
"Now a word was brought to me secretly, and my ear caught a whisper of it.
In thoughts from night visions, when deep sleep falls on people,
dread and trembling seized me and made all my bones shake.
A spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood on end.
It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form stood before my eyes; there was silence, and then I heard a voice:
"'Can mortal man be righteous before God? Can a man be pure before His Maker?
Behold, He puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error.
How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed as easily as a moth!
Between morning and evening they are broken; they perish forever without anyone regarding.
Are not their lives uprooted? They die, and not in wisdom.'"
Call out now—will anyone answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For wrath slays the fool, and envy destroys the simple.
I have seen a fool take root, yet suddenly I cursed his dwelling.
His sons are driven far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and no one delivers them.
The hungry consume his harvest, seizing it even from among thorns, while the thirsty pant after his wealth.
For misery does not spring from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the soil.
Yet man is born to trouble, as surely as sparks fly upward.” “
But I would seek God and lay my case before Him.
He does great things beyond searching out, wonders without number.
He gives rain to the earth and sends water over the fields.
He sets the lowly on high, and those who mourn He lifts to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so their hands accomplish nothing.
He catches the wise in their own cunning, and the counsel of the crooked is swept away.
Darkness overtakes them at noon; at midday they grope as in the night.
He saves the needy from their cutting words and from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.” “
Blessed is the man whom God corrects; therefore do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.
For He wounds, yet He binds up; He shatters, yet His hands heal.
He will rescue you from six calamities; in seven no harm will befall you.
In famine He will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be shielded from the scourge of the tongue and will not fear when destruction comes.
You will laugh at destruction and famine, and you will not fear the beasts of the earth.
For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is secure; you will inspect your property and find nothing missing.
You will know that your children are many, and your descendants like the grass of the earth.
You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf gathered in its season.” “
We have searched this out, and it is true. Hear it, then, and apply it to yourself.”
“If only my anguish were weighed, and my calamity laid together in the balances,
for then it would outweigh the sand of the seas—no wonder my words have been rash.
“For the arrows of the Almighty are in me, and my spirit drinks their venom; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.
Does a wild donkey bray over grass, or an ox bellow over its fodder?
Is tasteless food eaten without salt, or is there flavor in the white of an egg?
My soul refuses to touch them; they are like loathsome food to me.
“Oh, that I might have my request, and that God would grant my desire!
That it would please God to crush me, to loose His hand and cut me off!
Then I would still have this consolation—my joy in unrelenting pain—that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
“What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should prolong my life?
Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze?
Is my help not within me, and has sound wisdom been driven from me?
A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers have proved as treacherous as a brook, like torrents of brooks that vanish—
darkened with ice, in which snow hides itself;
but when they are scorched, they vanish, and in the heat they are consumed from their place.
The caravans turn aside from their path; they wander into the wasteland and perish.
The caravans of Tema looked for them; the traveling companies of Sheba waited for them.
They were confounded because they had trusted; they came there and were ashamed.
“For now you have become nothing; you see a terror and are afraid.
Did I ever say, ‘Give me something,’ or, ‘Pay a ransom for me from your wealth’?
Or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the adversary, or redeem me from the hand of the ruthless’?
Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand wherein I have erred.
How forceful are honest words! But what does your reproof actually prove?
Do you intend to reprove mere words, the speeches of a desperate man, which are only wind?
You would even cast lots for the fatherless and barter away your friend.
But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face.
Turn back, I beg you; let there be no injustice; turn back, for my righteousness still stands.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can my palate not discern mischief?”
Is not man consigned to hard service on earth? Are not his days like those of a hired worker?
As a slave pants for shade, so a hired worker waits for his wages.
Thus I have been allotted months of futility, and nights of affliction have been assigned to me.
When I lie down I ask, ‘When will I rise?’ The night drags on, and I toss restlessly until dawn.
My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin festers and oozes.” “
My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle and come to an end without hope.
Remember that my life is but a breath; my eye will never again see good.
The eye that now sees me will see me no more; Your eyes will be upon me, but I will be gone.
As a cloud fades and vanishes, so one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.
He returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.” “
Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that You set a guard over me?
When I say, ‘My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,’
then You frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions,
so that my soul chooses strangulation and death rather than this body of bones.
I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.” “
What is man, that You magnify him, and that You set Your heart upon him,
visiting him every morning and testing him every moment?
How long will You not look away from me, nor leave me alone for even a moment?
If I have sinned, what have I done to You, You who watch over mankind? Why have You made me Your target? Why have I become a burden to You?
Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For soon I will lie in the dust; You will seek me, but I will be no more.”
How long will you persist in this torrent of words? Your speech is but a gale of empty rhetoric.
Would God subvert justice, or would the Almighty distort righteousness?
If your children sinned against Him, He delivered them into the power of their own transgression. “
If you would seek God with earnest diligence and plead with the Almighty,
if you are pure and upright, He will surely rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your rightful estate.
Though your beginnings were humble, your latter days would abound in prosperity.
For inquire, I pray, of the former generations, and give heed to what their fathers discovered.
For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, because our days upon the earth are but a shadow.
Will they not teach you and declare to you, bringing forth words from their inmost understanding? “
Can papyrus grow without a marsh? Can reeds flourish without water?
While yet in bloom and not cut down, they wither before any other vegetation.
So are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless man perishes.
His confidence proves frail, and his trust is but a spider's web.
He leans upon his house, yet it does not stand; he clings to it, yet it does not endure.
He is verdant before the sun, and his shoots spread across his garden.
His roots entwine a heap of stones; he gazes upon a house of stones.
If he is swept away from his place, then it disowns him, saying, ‘I have never seen you.’
Behold, this is the joy of his course; and out of the dust others spring up. “
Behold, God will not spurn a blameless man, nor will He uphold the hand of evildoers.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more.”
"Truly I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God?
If He should choose to contend with him, he could not answer Him one time in a thousand.
"He is wise in heart and mighty in strength; who has hardened himself against Him and prospered?
He moves mountains without their knowing it and overturns them in His anger.
He shakes the earth from its place, and its pillars tremble.
He commands the sun, and it does not rise; He seals up the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens and treads upon the waves of the sea.
He makes the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, and the hidden constellations of the south.
He does great things beyond searching out and wonders beyond number.
"If He passes by me, I do not see Him; if He moves on, I do not perceive Him.
If He snatches away, who can restrain Him? Who can say to Him, 'What are You doing?'
God does not turn back His anger; the allies of Rahab bow beneath Him.
"How much less, then, can I answer Him and choose my words before Him?
Though I were righteous, I could not answer; I would plead for mercy to my Judge.
If I called and He answered me, I would not believe that He was listening to my voice.
For He crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause.
He will not let me catch my breath, but fills me with bitterness.
If it is a matter of strength, behold, He is mighty; if of justice, who can summon Him?
If I am righteous, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, He would declare me perverse.
I am blameless, yet I do not know myself; I despise my life.
It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'
When calamity strikes suddenly, He mocks the suffering of the innocent.
The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He covers the faces of its judges. If it is not He, then who is it?
"My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away without seeing good.
They pass by like papyrus skiffs, like an eagle swooping down on prey.
If I say, 'I will forget my complaint; I will change my expression and be cheerful,'
I dread all my suffering; I know You will not acquit me.
I am guilty; why then should I toil in vain?
If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye,
You will plunge me into the pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.
For He is not a man like me, that I should answer Him, that we should come together in judgment.
There is no arbiter between us, to lay his hand upon us both.
Let Him remove His rod from me, and let not His terror make me afraid.
Then I would speak without fear of Him, but that is not how I am."
“I loathe my very life; I will give free rein to my complaint and speak in the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God, ‘Do not condemn me; show me why You contend with me.’
Does it please You to oppress, to reject the work of Your hands and favor the schemes of the wicked?
Do You have eyes of flesh? Do You see as a man sees?
Are Your days like those of a mortal, or Your years like those of a man,
that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin?
Although You know that I am not guilty, and there is no one who can deliver me from Your hand.”
“Your hands shaped and fashioned me; yet now You turn and destroy me.
Please remember that You molded me like clay. Will You now return me to dust?
Did You not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.
You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit.
Yet You have hidden these things in Your heart; I know that this was Your plan.”
“If I sinned, You would take note, and would not acquit me of my iniquity.
If I am wicked, woe to me; and if I am righteous, I cannot lift my head. I am full of shame; see my affliction.
If I hold my head high, You stalk me like a lion, and again You display Your power against me.
You renew Your witnesses against me and increase Your anger toward me; Your armies are assembled against me.”
“Why then did You bring me out of the womb? Oh, that I had perished and no eye had seen me!
If only I had never come to be, but had been carried from the womb to the grave.
Are my days not few? Withdraw, that I may enjoy a little relief
before I go—never to return—to a land of darkness and gloom,
to a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, where even the light is like darkness.”
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:
"Should a torrent of words go unanswered, and should a man of many speeches be vindicated?
Should your idle talk silence men, and when you scoff, should no one put you to shame?
For you say, 'My teaching is pure, and I am clean in Your eyes.'
"But oh, that God would speak and open His lips against you,
and disclose to you the secrets of wisdom—for true wisdom has a double measure. Know, then, that God exacts from you less than your guilt deserves.
Can you discover the deep things of God? Can you find the limit of the Almighty?
It is higher than the heavens—what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know?
Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
If He passes through, imprisons, and summons to judgment, who can restrain Him?
For He knows deceitful men; when He sees iniquity, does He not take note?
An empty-headed man will never gain understanding, no more than a wild donkey can bear a human child.
"If you prepare your heart and spread out your hands to Him,
if you put away the iniquity in your hand and do not let wickedness dwell in your tents,
then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will stand firm and not fear.
You will forget your misery, remembering it only as water that has flowed past.
your life will shine brighter than noonday; even its darkness will be like the morning.
You will be secure, because there is hope; you will look about and lie down in safety.
You will lie down, and no one will make you afraid; many will seek your favor.
"But the eyes of the wicked will fail, escape will elude them, and their hope will be a dying gasp."
"Truly you are the people, and wisdom will perish with you.
I also possess understanding, just as you do; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things?
I have become a laughingstock to my neighbor, though I called upon God and He answered me—a righteous and blameless man made into a spectacle.
In the mind of one at ease, calamity is contemptible, yet it is prepared for those whose feet slip.
The tents of robbers remain secure, and those who provoke God dwell in safety, because they trust in their own power.
"But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens will tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; the fish of the sea will declare it to you.
Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?
In His hand is the life of every living creature and the breath of all mankind.
Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?
Wisdom is found with the aged, and understanding in length of days.
"With Him are wisdom and might; counsel and understanding belong to Him.
If He tears down, no one can rebuild; if He imprisons a man, no one can release him.
If He withholds the waters, they dry up; if He sends them forth, they overwhelm the earth.
Strength and effective wisdom are His; both the deceived and the deceiver belong to Him.
He leads counselors away stripped of their dignity and makes judges into fools.
He looses the bonds of kings and binds a sash around their waists.
He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty.
He removes the speech of trusted men and takes discernment from the elders.
He pours contempt upon princes and weakens the strong.
He reveals deep things out of darkness and brings utter darkness into the light.
He makes nations great and then destroys them; He enlarges nations and leads them away.
He takes understanding from the leaders of the earth and makes them wander in a pathless wasteland.
They grope in darkness without light, and He makes them stagger like drunkards."
Indeed, my eye has seen all this; my ear has heard and understood it.
What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.
Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and to argue my case with God.
You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians.
If only you would be completely silent, for that would be your wisdom!
Hear now my argument, and listen to the pleas of my lips.
Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf and speak deceitfully for Him?
Will you show Him partiality? Will you contend for God?
Would it be well if He examined you? Could you deceive Him as you deceive a man?
Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.
Would not His majesty terrify you, and the dread of Him fall upon you?
Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
Be silent before me so that I may speak; then let come to me what may.
Why do I put myself in jeopardy and take my life in my hands?
Behold, He will slay me; I will have no hope, yet I will argue my ways before His face.
He also is my salvation, for no godless man will come before Him.
Listen carefully to my words; let my declaration be in your ears.
See now, I have prepared my case; I know that I am right.
Who can contend with me? If I were to yield now, I would die.
Only grant me these two things, O God, and then I will not hide from You:
Withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me.
Then summon me, and I will answer; or let me speak, and You reply.
How many are my iniquities and sins? Reveal to me my transgression and sin.
Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy?
Will You frighten a windblown leaf? Will You chase after dry chaff?
For You record bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
You put my feet in the stocks and stand watch over all my paths; You set a limit for the soles of my feet.
So man wastes away like something rotten, like a garment eaten by moths.
A person born of a woman lives only a short time and is full of trouble.
He springs up like a flower and then withers; he flees like a shadow and does not endure.
You have opened Your eyes upon me, and You bring me into judgment with You. “
Who can bring what is clean from the unclean? No one.
If his days are determined, and the number of his months is with You, and You have set his limit so that he cannot pass beyond it,
then turn Your gaze from him and leave him alone, until he completes his day like a hired laborer.” “
At least there is hope for a tree: if it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its shoots will not fail.
Though its root grows old in the earth and its stump dies in the dust,
yet at the scent of water it will bud and put forth branches like a newly planted tree. “
But a man dies and lies powerless; a human being breathes his last, and where is he?
As water disappears from the sea and a riverbed becomes parched and dry,
so a man lies down and does not rise again; until the heavens are no more, they will not awake or be roused from their sleep.” “
Oh, that You would hide me in Sheol and conceal me until Your anger passes! Oh, that You would set me an appointed time and then remember me!
If a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my hard service I will wait until my renewal comes.
You will call, and I will answer You; You will long for the work of Your hands. “
Surely then You would count my steps, but You would not keep watch over my sin.
My transgression would be sealed in a bag, and You would cover over my iniquity.” “
But a falling mountain crumbles away, and a rock is removed from its place;
water wears away stones, and its torrents wash away the soil of the earth—so You destroy the hope of a man.
You overpower him forever, and he passes away; You change his face, and You send him away. “
His sons come to honor, but he does not know it; they are brought low, but he does not perceive it.
He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself.”
"Should a wise man answer with empty knowledge and fill his belly with empty words?
Should he argue with unprofitable words and speeches that accomplish nothing?
Indeed, you undermine reverence and diminish devotion before God.
For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty.
Your own mouth condemns you, and your lips testify against you."
"Were you the first man born? Were you brought forth before the hills?
Have you heard the secret counsel of God, that you should limit wisdom to yourself?
What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not with us?
Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father.
Are God's consolations too small for you, even a gentle word spoken to you?
Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash?
so that you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?"
"What is man, that he should be pure? Or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?
If He puts no trust in His holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in His sight,
how much less a man who is abominable and corrupt, who gulps down iniquity as easily as water!
Listen to me; I will show you, and what I have seen I will declare,
what wise men have declared, hiding nothing from their fathers,
to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them."
"The wicked man writhes in pain all his days; the number of years is fixed for the ruthless.
Sounds of terror are in his ears; in peace the destroyer comes upon him.
He does not believe he will return from darkness; he is marked for the sword.
He wanders in search of bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is prepared.
Distress and anguish terrify him; they overpower him, like a king ready for battle.
Because he has stretched out his hand against God and acts arrogantly against the Almighty,
rushing at Him with a stiff neck, with the thick bosses of his shields.
Though he has covered his face with fat and made his loins heavy with fat,
he will dwell in desolate cities, in houses no one inhabits, which are destined to become heaps of rubble.
He will not grow rich, and his wealth will not endure; his possessions will not spread over the earth.
He will not escape from darkness; a flame will wither his shoots, and by the breath of His mouth he will depart.
Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his reward.
It will be accomplished before his time, and his branch will not be green.
He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive.
For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.
They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb prepares deceit."
"I have heard plenty of talk like this; all of you are miserable comforters.
Will these windy speeches never end? What drives you to keep answering?
"I could speak as you do if you were in my place; I could pile up words against you and shake my head at you.
I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would ease your pain.
If I speak, my pain is not eased; and if I fall silent, how much of it leaves me?
"Surely now He has worn me out; You have devastated my entire household.
You have bound me, and it has become a witness; my frailty rises up against me and testifies to my face.
His anger has torn and hounded me; He has gnashed His teeth at me; my adversary sharpens His eyes against me.
They gape at me with their mouths; they strike my cheeks with contempt; they mass together against me.
God has delivered me to the ungodly and cast me into the hands of the wicked.
I was at ease, but He shattered me; He seized me by the neck and broke me apart. He has set me up as His target.
His archers surround me; He pierces my kidneys without mercy and pours my gall on the ground.
He breaks me with wound upon wound; He rushes at me like a warrior.
"I have sewn sackcloth over my skin and buried my dignity in the dust.
My face is flushed with weeping, and the shadow of death lies over my eyelids.
Although my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure.
"O earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.
Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high.
My friends mock me, but my eyes pour out tears to God.
Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his fellow man!
For when a few years have passed, I will go the way of no return."
My spirit is shattered, my days are extinguished, and the grave stands ready for me.
Surely mockers hem me in, and my eyes must dwell on their insolence.
Please stand as my guarantor with Yourself; who else will pledge himself to me?
For You have hidden their hearts from discernment; therefore You will not exalt them.
Whoever informs against friends to claim a share of the spoils will see his children's eyes grow dim.
He has made me a byword among the peoples; I am a man in whose face they spit.
My eyes have grown dim with grief, and my whole body is but a shadow.
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stir themselves up against the godless.
Yet the righteous will hold fast to his way, and he who has clean hands will grow stronger.
But as for all of you, come back now; I will not find a wise man among you.
My days have passed; my plans are broken; the desires of my heart are shattered.
They turn night into day and say, "Light is near in the face of darkness."
If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I spread my bed in darkness,
I have called to corruption, "You are my father," and to the worm, "You are my mother and my sister."
Where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?
Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we descend together into the dust?
“How long will you keep hunting for words? Gain understanding, and then we will speak.
Why are we counted as cattle, and regarded as stupid in your eyes?
You who tear yourself apart in anger—should the earth be abandoned for your sake, or should a rock be moved from its place?
“Indeed, the light of the wicked is extinguished, and the spark of his fire does not shine.
The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out.
His strong steps are shortened, and his own counsel brings him down.
For his feet are caught in a net, and he walks into a snare.
A trap seizes his heel, and a snare grips him.
A noose is hidden in the ground, and a trap lies across his path.
Terrors frighten him on every side and hound him at every step.
His strength is starved, and calamity stands ready at his side.
It devours the limbs of his body, and the firstborn of death devours his limbs.
He is torn from the safety of his tent and led away to the king of terrors.
Fire dwells in his tent, and brimstone is scattered over his dwelling.
His roots dry up beneath him, and his branches wither above.
His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land.
He is driven from light into darkness and banished from the inhabited world.
He has no offspring or posterity among his people, and no survivor remains in his dwelling.
Those in the west are appalled at his fate, while those in the east are seized with horror.
Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked, and this is the place of one who does not know God.”
"How long will you torment me and crush me with words?
Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me.
Even if I have truly erred, my error remains my own concern.
If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me,
then understand that God has wronged me and drawn His net around me."
"Though I cry out that I have been wronged, I receive no answer; though I plead for justice, there is none.
He has blocked my path so I cannot pass; He has veiled my ways in darkness.
He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head.
He tears me down on every side until I am gone; He uproots my hope like a tree.
His anger burns against me, and He counts me among His enemies.
His troops advance together; they build a siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent."
"He has removed my brothers from me, and my acquaintances have become strangers to me.
My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me.
My guests and maidservants count me as a stranger; I am an alien in their sight.
I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth.
My breath is repulsive to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own children.
Even young boys scorn me; when I rise, they deride me.
All my close friends abhor me, and those I love have turned against me.
My bones cling to my skin and flesh; I have survived by the narrowest margin."
"Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me.
Why do you pursue me as God does? Will you never be satisfied with my flesh?"
"Oh, that my words were recorded, that they were inscribed in a book,
that with an iron stylus and lead they were engraved in rock forever!
But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the dust.
Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.
I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!"
"If you say, 'How shall we persecute him, since the cause is found in him?'
then you should fear the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment."
"Therefore, my thoughts compel me to answer, for the agitation within me will not be subdued.
I hear a rebuke that dishonors me, and my understanding insists upon a reply.
"Do you not know that from antiquity, since humanity was placed upon the earth,
the triumph of the wicked is ephemeral and the joy of the godless endures only a moment?
Though his arrogance ascends to the heavens and his head touches the clouds,
he perishes forever, like his own refuse; those who once beheld him ask, 'Where is he?'
He vanishes like a dream and is never recovered; he is driven away like a nocturnal vision.
The eye that saw him sees him no more, and his place no longer acknowledges him.
"His sons oppress the poor, and his hands must restore his wealth.
His bones, once saturated with youthful vigor, lie down with him in the dust.
"Though evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it beneath his tongue,
though he spares it and refuses to relinquish it, keeping it in the roof of his mouth,
yet his food turns sour in his stomach and becomes the venom of cobras within him.
He swallows wealth, but he vomits it up; God compels it from his belly.
He sucks the poison of cobras; the fangs of a viper slay him.
"He will not see the streams—the rivers flowing with honey and curds.
He must restore what he labored to acquire without consuming it; he does not rejoice in the profits of his commerce.
For he has oppressed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house he never built.
Because his appetite remains insatiable, he preserves nothing he desired.
Nothing remains for him to devour; consequently, his prosperity cannot endure.
"In the midst of his abundance, he is distressed; every hand of the afflicted assails him.
When he is about to fill his belly, God sends His fierce anger upon him and rains it down while he eats.
Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze bow pierces him.
He draws it out, and it emerges from his back; the gleaming point comes from his liver. Terrors overwhelm him.
Total darkness is reserved for his treasures; an unfanned fire consumes him and devours what remains in his tent.
"The heavens expose his iniquity, and the earth rises up against him.
The increase of his house departs; his goods flow away in the day of God's wrath.
This is the wicked man's portion from God—the inheritance appointed to him by God."
"Listen carefully to my words, and let this be your comfort.
Bear with me while I speak; after I have spoken, you may mock.
As for me, is my complaint against a human being? Why, then, should I not be impatient?
Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth.
When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.
"Why do the wicked live on, grow old, and increase in power?
Their children are secure around them, and their descendants are before their eyes.
Their homes are safe from dread, and God's rod does not strike them.
Their bulls breed without fail; their cows calve and do not miscarry.
They send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children skip about.
They sing to the tambourine and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.
They spend their days in prosperity and descend to Sheol in peace.
They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire knowledge of Your ways.
What is the Almighty, that we should serve Him? What do we gain by praying to Him?'
Behold, their prosperity is not in their own hands; the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
How often is the lamp of the wicked extinguished, and calamity overtakes them? He allots suffering in His anger.
They are like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm.
You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let Him repay them, that they may know it.
Let their own eyes see their ruin, and let them drink the wrath of the Almighty.
For what do they care about their house after them, when the number of their months has been cut short?
Will anyone teach God knowledge, when He judges those on high?
"One person dies in full vigor, completely at ease and secure.
His sides are full of milk, and the marrow of his bones is moist.
Another dies with a bitter soul, never having tasted prosperity.
They lie down together in the dust, and worms cover them.
"Behold, I know your thoughts and the schemes you devise against me.
For you say, 'Where is the prince's house? Where is the tent of the wicked?'
Have you not asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their testimony
that the wicked are spared in the day of calamity and rescued in the day of wrath?
Who confronts him to his face? Who repays him for what he has done?
When he is carried to the grave, a watch is kept over his tomb.
The grave is pleasant to him; all humanity follows him, and countless go before him.
How then will you comfort me with empty words, when your answers remain nothing but falsehood?"
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:
“Can a mortal be of any use to God? Can even a wise man add to His prosperity?
Does the Almighty find pleasure in your righteousness? Does He gain anything when your ways are blameless?
Is it out of fear of you that He rebukes you, or that He brings you into judgment?
Is not your wickedness immense, and are not your iniquities without end?
For you have exacted pledges from your brothers without cause and stripped the naked of their clothing.
You have given no water to the weary and withheld bread from the hungry.
Yet the land belongs to the powerful, and the favored dwell in it.
You have sent widows away empty-handed, and the arms of the fatherless have been crushed.
Therefore snares surround you, and sudden terror overwhelms you;
or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
Is not God in the heights of heaven? Look at the highest stars—how lofty they are!
Yet you say, “What does God know? Can He judge through the thick darkness?
Thick clouds veil Him, so that He does not see; He walks about on the vault of heaven.”
Will you keep to the ancient path that wicked men have trodden—
men who were snatched away before their time, whose foundations were washed away by a flood?
They said to God, “Depart from us,” and, “What can the Almighty do to us?”
Yet He filled their houses with good things. Far be it from me to embrace the counsel of the wicked.
The righteous see it and rejoice, and the innocent mock them,
saying, “Surely our adversaries are cut off, and fire has consumed their wealth.”
Reconcile now with Him and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.
Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored; if you banish iniquity from your tent,
and lay your gold in the dust—even the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks—
then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.
You will pray to Him, and He will hear you; you will fulfill your vows.
You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.
When men are brought low, you will say, “There is exaltation!” He will save the humble.
He will deliver the innocent; yes, they will be delivered by the purity of your hands.
“Even today my complaint is bitter; my hand weighs heavily because of my groaning.
Oh, that I knew where I might find Him, that I might come to His seat!
I would lay my case before Him and fill my mouth with arguments.
I would know what words He would answer me with, and understand what He would say to me.
Would He contend with me in great power? No—He would pay attention to me.
There an upright man could reason with Him, and I would be delivered forever from my Judge.”
“Behold, I go forward, but He is not there; I go backward, but I do not perceive Him.
When He works on the left, I cannot grasp Him; He turns to the right, but I do not see Him.
But He knows the way that I take; when He has tried me, I shall come out as gold.
My foot has held fast to His steps; I have kept His way and not turned aside.
I have not departed from the commandment of His lips; I have treasured the words of His mouth more than my daily bread.”
“But He is unchangeable, and who can turn Him? What His soul desires, that He does.
For He will complete what He has appointed for me, and many such things are with Him.
Therefore I am terrified at His presence; when I consider, I am in dread of Him.
God has made my heart faint, and the Almighty has terrified me,
for I am not silenced by the darkness, nor by the thick darkness that covers my face.”
Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Why may those who know Him not see His days?
There are those who move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks.
They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and take the widow’s ox in pledge.
They push the needy off the road; the poor of the land are forced into hiding. “
Indeed, like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go out to their toil, seeking food; the wasteland is food for their children.
They gather fodder in the fields and glean the vineyards of the wicked.
Without clothing, they spend the night naked; they have no covering against the cold.
Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rock for lack of shelter. “
The fatherless are snatched from the breast, and the infant of the poor is taken as a pledge.
Without clothing, they wander about naked. They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry.
They crush olives within their walls; they tread the winepresses, but still are thirsty.
From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, yet God charges no one with wrongdoing. “
Then there are those who rebel against the light; they do not know its ways or stay on its paths.
The murderer rises at daybreak to kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.
The eye of the adulterer watches for twilight. ‘No eye will see me,’ he says, and he conceals his face.
In the dark they dig through houses; by day they seal themselves in; they never see the light.
For to them, deep darkness is their morning; they are friends with the terrors of darkness. “
He is but foam on the surface of the water; his portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward his vineyards.
As drought and heat consume the melted snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned.
The womb forgets him; the worm feeds on him; he is no longer remembered. So injustice is broken like a tree.
He preys on the barren and childless, and does not show kindness to the widow.
Yet God drags away the mighty by His power; though rising up, they have no assurance of life.
He gives them a sense of security, and they rest in it, but His eyes are on their ways.
They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they wither like heads of grain.
If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?”
“Dominion and awe are His; He establishes peace in His celestial heights.
Can His troops be numbered? Upon whom does His light not shine?
How then can a man be righteous before God, or one born of woman be pure?
If even the moon does not shine and the stars are not pure in His eyes,
how much less a mortal, who is but a maggot, and a son of man, who is but a worm!”
“How have you helped the powerless? How have you rescued an arm bereft of strength?
How have you counseled one devoid of wisdom, and how have you made sound insight abundantly known?
To whom have you uttered words, and whose breath proceeded from you?”
“The shades tremble beneath the waters, together with those who dwell there.
Sheol lies naked before Him, and Abaddon has no covering.
